## I / 一
===Original===

Vernon’s

The Banking House of the Vernons was known through all the Home Counties as only second to the Bank of England in stability and strength. That is to say, the people who knew about such matters, the business people, the professional classes, and those who considered themselves to be acquainted with the world, allowed that it ought to be considered second: but this opinion was not shared by the greater proportion of its clients, the shopkeepers in Redborough and the adjacent towns, the farmers of a wide district, and all the smaller people whose many united littles make up so much wealth. To them Vernon’s bank was the emblem of stability, the impersonation of solid and substantial wealth. It had risen to its height of fame under John Vernon, the grandfather of the present head of the firm, though it had existed for two or three generations before him. But John Vernon was one of those men in whose hands everything turns to gold. What the special gift is which determines this it is difficult to tell, but there can be little doubt that it is a special gift, just as it is a particular genius which produces a fine picture or a fine poem. There were wiser men than he, and there were men as steady to their work and as constantly in their place, ready for all the claims of business, but not one other in whose hands everything prospered in the same superlative way. His investments always answered, his ships always came home, and under his influence the very cellars of the banking-house, according to the popular imagination, filled with gold. At one period of his career a panic seized the entire district, and there was a run upon the bank, by which it was evident anybody else must, nay, ought, to have been ruined; but John Vernon was not ruined. It was understood afterwards that he himself allowed that he did not understand how he had escaped, and nobody else could understand it: but he did escape, and as a natural consequence became stronger and richer, and more universally credited than ever. His son after him had not the same genius for money, but at least he had the genius for keeping what he had got, which is next best.

===Chinese===

弗农银行（Vernon's）

弗农家的这家银行（The Banking House of the Vernons）在整个伦敦周边诸郡无人不晓，其稳固与实力公认仅次于英格兰银行（Bank of England）。也就是说，懂行的人——生意人、专业人士，以及那些自认为见过世面的人——承认它理应名列第二；但它的绝大多数主顾却不这么看。对雷德伯勒（Redborough）及邻近城镇的店主们、对一片广阔地区的农户们，以及所有那些以其涓滴之力汇聚成巨富的小民百姓来说，弗农银行是稳固的象征，是殷实财富的化身。它是在本行现任掌门的祖父约翰·弗农（John Vernon）手中臻于极盛的，尽管在他之前这家银行已经营了两三代人。但约翰·弗农是那种万事到了他手里都点石成金的人。这种禀赋究竟是什么，很难说清；但毋庸置疑，它确是一种特殊的天赋，正如产出一张好画或一首好诗靠的是一种独特的天才一样。世上有比他更明智的人，也有像他一样勤于职守、时刻坐镇行中、随时应付认领业务的人，但再没有第二个人，能让万事在他手中同样出类拔萃地兴旺发达。他的投资总是获利，他的船队总能满载而归；在他的治下，照民间的想象，连银行的地下室都堆满了黄金。在他生涯的某个时期，恐慌席卷了整个地区，银行遭到挤兑，换了别人——不但必然、而且理应——早已倾家荡产；但约翰·弗农没有倒。事后据他自己承认，他也不明白自己是如何逃过这一劫的，旁人更无从理解：但他确实逃过去了，并且自然而然地变得比以往更强大、更富有、更受信赖。他之后的儿子没有他那样生财的天才，但至少有守成的天才，这已是次佳的了。

===Original===

Edward Vernon, however, was not so fortunate in his family as in his affairs. He had two sons, one of whom died young, leaving a little daughter to be brought up by her grandfather; the other “went wrong.” Oh, never-ending family tragedy, never ending, still beginning, the darkest anguish that exists in the world! The younger son went wrong, and died also in his father’s lifetime, leaving a helpless little family of children, and a poor wife stupefied with trouble. She did her best, poor soul, to bring up her boy to ways the very opposite of those in which his father had stumbled and fallen, and it was supposed that he would marry his cousin Catherine Vernon, and thus unite once more all the money and prestige of the house. He too was John Vernon, and resembled the golden great-grandfather, and great things were hoped of him. He entered the bank in old Mr. Vernon’s time, and gave every promise of being a worthy successor as long as the senior partner, the head of the house, lived. But when the old gentleman died and John Vernon became in his turn the head of the house, there very soon appeared signs of change. In the first place the marriage with his cousin never came to pass; things had seemed to promise fairly so long as the grandfather with whom she lived was alive. But after, there was an immediate cooling of sentiment. Whose fault this was nobody knew. She said nothing on the subject even to her dearest friends; nor did he say anything; but he laughed and waved aside all questions as a man who “could an if he would”﻿—. His mother, for her part, said a great deal. She ran between them like an excited hen, shaking her tail-feathers and cackling violently. What did they mean by it? What was it for? She asked her son how he could forget that if Catherine’s money went out of the business it would make the most extraordinary difference? and she bade Catherine remember that it would be almost dishonest to enrich another family with money which the Vernons had toiled for. Catherine, who was not by any means an ordinary girl, smiled upon her, perhaps a little sadly, and entered into no explanations. But her son, as was natural, scoffed at his mother. “What should you know about the business?” he said. Poor Mrs. Vernon thought she had heard enough of it to understand it, or at least to understand the intentions of those who understood it.

===Chinese===

然而爱德华·弗农（Edward Vernon）在家庭事务上却不似在生意上那般幸运。他有两个儿子：一个早亡，留下一个由祖父抚养的小女儿；另一个则“走了歪路”。啊，这永无休止的家庭悲剧，永不终结，又不断重演，这是人世间最深沉的痛苦！小儿子走了歪路，也在父亲生前死去，撇下一群无依无靠的孩子，和一个被苦难折磨得麻木的贫妻。可怜的人，她竭尽全力，要把儿子培养成人，走的恰是他父亲失足跌倒的那条路的反面；人们原指望他会娶表妹凯瑟琳·弗农（Catherine Vernon），从而把全家的钱财与声望重新合为一体。他也叫约翰·弗农，酷似那位点石成金的曾祖父，人们对他寄予厚望。他在老弗农先生在世时就进了银行，只要这位资深合伙人、这一家银行的掌门人还活着，他处处显示出配得上继承人的样子。但等老先生去世、约翰·弗农轮到自己成为一家之主后，很快就显出了变化的迹象。首先，与表妹的婚事终究没有成。只要与她同住的祖父在世，事情看起来还挺有指望。但祖父一死，情分立刻冷了下来。这该怪谁，谁也不知道。对这个话题，她连最亲密的朋友也不吐露半句；他也不置一词，只是笑着把一切询问挥到一边，像个“能而不为”的人。他的母亲则不然，话说了个没完。她像一只激动的母鸡在他们两人之间跑来跑去，抖着尾巴上的羽毛，咯咯地叫个不停。他们这是什么意思？图的是什么？她问儿子，怎么能忘记：凯瑟琳的钱一旦从生意中抽走，就会造成天大的差别？她叮嘱凯瑟琳记住，把弗农家辛苦挣来的钱去养肥别家，那几乎是不诚实的。凯瑟琳绝非寻常女子，对着她微笑，也许还带着几分伤感，却不作任何解释。而她的儿子，正如自然之理，对母亲嗤之以鼻。“你懂什么生意？”他说。可怜的弗农太太自以为听得多到足以懂了，或至少懂了那些懂行的人的意图。

===Original===

But what is the use of a mother’s remonstrances? The new generation will please itself and take its way. She scolded and wept for years after, poor soul, in vain, and yet could never learn that it was in vain, but began anew day after day weeping, entreating, remonstrating, falling into nervous crises of passion a hundred and a hundred times over. How much better for her to have held her tongue! but how could she help it? She was not of that placid and patient nature which can be wise. And gradually things began to go badly with John. He married a young lady belonging to a county family, but with no money to keep up her pretensions. He had his stables full of horses and his house full of company. “What is it all to come to?” cried his poor, anxious, angry, disappointed, despairing mother, seeking opportunities to have a few words with him, to speak to him seriously, to remind him of his duty. To be sure she did a great deal more harm than good. She drew many a blow upon herself which she might have escaped had she been content to allow that his life had passed far beyond her guidance; but the poor lady would not be taught. And it was quite true what John Vernon said. It would take a long time, he told her, before a few horses and pleasant company would affect Vernon’s bank. As the head of that establishment he was expected to be hospitable, and keep almost open house; the country which trusted in him knew he could afford it. The Redborough people went further, and liked to see the confidence with which he spent his money. What could that do to Vernon’s? He had never lived up to his income yet, he believed. So he told his mother, who was never satisfied, and went on till the day of her death always seeking a few words with him﻿—an opportunity of speaking seriously to her son. Poor mother! nothing went very well with her; perhaps she was not clever either at managing her children or her money. The partisans of the Vernons said so at least; they said so of all the wives that were not Vernons, but interlopers, always working harm. They said so also of Mrs. John, and there his mother thought they were not far wrong. But none of her children turned out very satisfactorily; the girls married badly; Edward, her younger son, went into the Church, and never was more than a vicar, and their money matters would not go right. Certainly she was not a fortunate woman.

===Chinese===

可是一位母亲的规劝又有什么用呢？新一代自有主张，要走自己的路。此后多年，她徒劳地又骂又哭，可怜的人，却永远学不会这是徒劳，日复一日地重新开始哭泣、恳求、规劝，成百上千次地陷入狂乱的情绪发作。她要是闭住嘴该多好！可她怎么忍得住呢？她天生不是那种沉得住气、有耐心、因而能明智处事的性子。渐渐地，约翰的景况开始不妙了。他娶了一位郡中世家的年轻小姐，但她没有钱财支撑她的排场。他的马厩里养满马匹，家里宾客盈门。“这一切到头来会怎样？”他那可怜、焦急、愤怒、失望、绝望的母亲喊道，寻找机会同他说上几句话，同他严肃地谈谈，提醒他尽自己的本分。的确，她做的坏事比好事多得多。她给自己招来了许多打击，倘若她甘心承认儿子的生活早已远远脱离了她的管教，这些打击本是可以躲开的；但这可怜的太太不肯受教。而约翰·弗农说的话倒是千真万确。他告诉她，要等区区几匹马和几场欢宴影响到弗农银行，还早着呢。作为这家银行的掌门，他本就该好客，几乎就该门庭大开；信任他的乡野知道他供得起。雷德伯勒的人更进一步，乐于看到他花钱时那份自信。那对弗农银行能有什么损害？他相信，他还从未入不敷出过呢。他这样告诉永不满足的母亲；而她直到去世的那一天，还在寻求与儿子说几句话的机会——一次同儿子严肃谈谈的机会。可怜的母亲！她的诸事没有一件顺遂；也许她既不擅长管教儿女，也不擅长打理钱财。弗农家的拥趸们至少是这么说的；他们对所有不是弗农家出身、而是外来的、总在惹祸的媳妇都是这么说的。他们对约翰太太也这么说，而在这一点上，连他母亲都觉得他们说得不算离谱。但她的儿女没有一个很有出息：女儿们婚事不如意；小儿子爱德华进了教会，终身不过是个牧师；他们的钱财事务也总不顺畅。的确，她不是个有福的女人。

===Original===

But she died, happily for her, before anything material happened to realise her alarms in respect to John.

It is astonishing how money grows when it is in the way of growing﻿—when it has got the genuine impulse and rolls every kindred atom near it, according to some occult law of attraction, into itself. But just as wonderfully as money grows does it melt away when the other﻿—the contrary process﻿—has begun. John Vernon was quite right in saying that the bank justified, nay, almost demanded, a certain amount of expenditure from its chief partner. And he was more, much more, than its chief partner. Catherine, though she was as deeply interested in it as himself, took no responsibility whatever﻿—how should she, a girl who knew as much about money as her pony did? She took less interest, indeed, than in ordinary circumstances she would have done, for there was certainly something, whatever it might be, which had interrupted the natural intercourse between the two cousins. They were not at ease with each other like brother and sister, as everything suggested they ought to have been﻿—not sufficiently at ease to consider their mutual interests together, as partners ought to have done. This, one of them at least thought, would have been ridiculous in any case. When his lawyers asked what Catherine thought on this or that subject, he laughed in their faces.

“What should she think? What should she know? Of course she leaves all that to me,” he said. “How can a girl understand banking business?”

But this did not satisfy the respectable firm of solicitors who advised the banker.

“Miss Vernon is not a girl any longer,” said Mr. Pounce, who was its head; upon which John Vernon laughed, one of those offensive laughs with which a coarse-minded man waves the banner of his sex over an unmarried woman.

“No,” he said, “Catherine’s growing an old maid. She must look alive if she means to get a husband.”

Mr. Pounce was not a sentimentalist, and no doubt laughed sometimes too at the unfortunate women who had thus failed in the object of their life; but he respected Miss Vernon, and he was very doubtful of her cousin.

“Husband or no husband, I think she ought to be consulted,” he said.

“Oh, I will take Catherine in my own hands,” was the cousin’s reply.

===Chinese===

不过她死得倒算幸运，赶在任何实质变故发生、坐实她对约翰的种种忧惧之前。

钱这东西，处在滋长的路上时长得惊人——一旦有了真正的势头，便按照某种神秘的引力法则，把近旁每一个同类原子都滚进自己怀里。可一旦那相反的过程开始，钱的消融也同样神奇。约翰·弗农说银行养得起、甚至几乎需要它的首席合伙人有一定的开销，这话说得不错。而且他远不止是首席合伙人。凯瑟琳虽然同他一样与银行利害攸关，却不承担任何责任——她能承担什么呢？一个对钱的了解同她的小马驹一样的姑娘？她对银行的兴趣，实际上比在正常情况下本该有的还要少，因为这两位表兄妹之间的自然往来，确确实实被某种东西——管它是什么——中断了。他们相处不像兄妹那样自在，尽管种种迹象都表明他们本该如此——他们自在不到能够像合伙人本该的那样，一起商量共同利益的程度。这一点，至少其中一人认为，无论如何都是荒谬的。当他的律师们问起凯瑟琳对这样或那样的事情怎么想时，他当面笑话他们。

“她会怎么想？她能知道什么？她当然把这一切都交给我，”他说。“一个姑娘家怎么会懂银行业务？”

但这满足不了为银行家出主意的那家体面律师事务所。

“弗农小姐（Miss Vernon）已经不是姑娘了，”事务所的掌门人庞斯先生（Mr. Pounce）说；约翰·弗农听了大笑，那是粗鄙之人向未婚女人挥舞男性大旗时发出的一种无礼的笑。

“是啊，”他说，“凯瑟琳快成老姑娘了。她想嫁人就得抓紧喽。”

庞斯先生并非多愁善感之人，无疑有时也会取笑那些在人生目标上如此失利的可怜女人；但他敬重弗农小姐，而且对银行家的这位表弟很不放心。

“嫁人不嫁人的，我认为应当同她商量，”他说。

“哦，凯瑟琳的事我自己来管，”那位表弟答道。

===Original===

And thus life went on, very gay, fast, amusing, and expensive on one side; very quiet and uneventful on the other. John Vernon built himself a grand new house, in which there were all the latest improvements and scientific luxuries, which the most expensive upholsterers filled with the most costly furniture, and for which the skilfullest gardeners all but created ready-made trees and shrubberies. He filled it with fine company﻿—names which the clerks at the bank felt were a credit to the establishment, and which the townsfolk looked upon with admiring awe: and there was nothing in the county to equal Mrs. John Vernon’s dresses and diamonds. What is all that to a great bank, gathering money every hour?﻿—nothing! Even Mr. Pounce acknowledged this. Personal extravagance, as long as it is merely hospitality and show, must go a very long way indeed before it touches the great revenue of such a business. It was not the diamonds nor the feasts that they were afraid of. But to be lavish with money is a dangerous fault with a man who is a business man. It is a very common sin, but there is nothing more perilous. In Manchester or Liverpool, where they turn over a fortune every day, perhaps this large habit of sowing money about does not matter. People there are accustomed to going up and down. Bankruptcy, even, does not mean the end of the world in these regions. But a banker in a country town, who has all the money of a district in his hands, should not get into this reckless way. His clients are pleased﻿—up to a certain limit. But when once the first whisper of suspicion has been roused it flies fast, and the panic with which rural depositors rush upon a bank which has awakened the ghost of an apprehension, is even more cruel and unreflecting than other panics. It went on a long time, and where it was that the first suggestion came from, nobody ever knew. Probably it did not come from anyone﻿—it was in the air, it struck two people, all at once, talking to each other, and the electricity of the contact found a single syllable of utterance. When that was done, all was done. Everybody had been waiting for this involuntary signal; and when it came, it flew like lightning through all Redborough, and out into the roads and lanes﻿—to distant farmhouses, into the rectories and vicarages, even to the labourer’s cottage.

===Chinese===

于是日子就这样过下去：一边非常快活、放纵、有趣而奢侈；另一边则非常平静、无事发生。约翰·弗农给自己盖了一座堂皇的新宅，屋里有一切最新的改良和科学的奢华，最昂贵的家具商用最贵的家具将它填满，最巧的园艺师几乎为它造出了现成的树木和灌木丛。他以上宾满座——那些名字连银行的职员们都觉得为本行增光，镇民们怀着叹服的敬畏仰望：全县没有一样东西比得上约翰·弗农太太的衣裙和钻石。这对一家每小时都在聚敛金钱的大银行算得了什么？——算不了什么！连庞斯先生也承认这一点。只要个人挥霍仅仅是好客与排场，要走很远很远才碰得到这种生意庞大收益的边。他们害怕的不是钻石，也不是盛宴。但对一个生意人来说，挥霍成性是一种危险的毛病。这是极常见的罪过，但没有比它更凶险的了。在曼彻斯特或利物浦，人们每天倒手一笔家财，也许这种撒钱的大手大脚无关紧要。那里的人习惯了起起落落。甚至在那些地方，破产也不意味着世界末日。但一个小镇上的银行家，一区之财尽握于手，就不该沾染这种无所顾忌的做派。他的主顾们高兴——直到某个限度。可是一旦疑虑的第一声耳语被唤起，它便飞快传开；乡间的存户们冲向一家唤起一丝疑影的银行时的那种恐慌，比别的恐慌更冷酷、更盲目。这样过了很久；最初的暗示究竟来自何处，谁也说不清。也许它并非来自任何人——它在空气中，同时击中两个正在交谈的人，接触的电火花找到了一个音节吐露出来。这一吐露，一切便都定了。人人都在等着这个不自觉的信号；信号一来，它便如闪电一般传遍整个雷德伯勒，传到大路小径上——传到遥远的农舍，传进教区长住宅和牧师寓所，甚至传到雇工的小屋。

===Original===

“It’s said as Vernon’s bank’s a-going to break,” the ploughmen in the fields said to each other. It did not matter much to them; and perhaps they were not sorry that the farmer, who grew fat (they thought) on their toil, should feel that he was also human. The farmers had something of the same feeling in respect to their landlords, but could not indulge it for the furious terror that took possession of themselves. Vernon’s bank! Safer than the Bank of England, was what they had all said exultingly. Very few of them had sufficient command of themselves to wait now and inquire into it and see how far the panic was well founded. To wait would have been to leave the chance of salvation to other men.

Mrs. John Vernon was considered very refined and elegant according to the language of the day, a young lady with many accomplishments. But it was the fashion of the time to be unpractical just as it is the fashion of our time that women should understand business and be ready for any emergency. To wear your hair in a high loose knot on the top of your head, with ringlets straying down your cheek, and across the always uncovered whiteness of your shoulders, and to sing the songs of Mr. Haynes Bayley, “Oh No, We Never Mention Her,” or “The Soldier’s Tear”﻿—could anything be more entirely inconsistent with business habits? Mrs. John would have considered it a slight to the delicacy of her mind to have been supposed to know anything about the bank; and when the head clerk demanded an audience at an unseasonable hour one summer evening she was entirely taken aback.

“Me! do you mean that it is me Mr. Rule wants to see?” she asked of the servant in consternation.

“He did ask for master, ma’am,” said the man, “but as master’s from home he said he must see my lady. He looks very flustered. I’ll say that for him,” he added.

To be sure William had heard the whisper in the air, and was more or less gratified that Mr. Rule should be flustered; but as for his lady, she saw no connection whatever between Mr. Rule’s excitement and herself.

“I do not see what good I can do him, William; and it’s not an hour at which I ever receive people. I am sure I don’t know what he can want with me.”

===Chinese===

“听说弗农银行要倒喽，”田里的犁田汉子们互相说。这对他们本身没多大干系；也许他们并不遗憾，那个（在他们看来）靠他们的劳作养肥的农场主也尝尝人间的滋味。农场主们对他们的地主也存着几分同样的心思，可自己心里那狂暴的恐惧占满了一切，顾不上幸灾乐祸。弗农银行！比英格兰银行还稳，他们从前都这样得意地说。此刻他们当中极少有人能有足够的自持，去等一等、打听打听、看看这场恐慌究竟有几分根据。等待就等于把获救的机会留给别人。

约翰·弗农太太按当时的话语来说被视为十分文雅精致，是一位多才多艺的年轻淑女。但那个时代的风尚是不切实际，正如我们这时代的风尚是女人要懂生意、随时应付急务一样。把头发在头顶挽成一个高高的松髻，鬈发垂在颊边，掠过总是袒露的雪白双肩，唱着海恩斯·贝利（Haynes Bayley）先生的歌，《哦不，我们从不提起她》（Oh No, We Never Mention Her）或者《士兵的眼泪》（The Soldier's Tear）——还有什么能比这与生意的习气更格格不入的呢？约翰太太会认为，若有人猜想她懂一点银行的事，那是对她心灵娇贵的冒犯；因此，当某个夏日的黄昏，首席职员在不合时宜的时刻求见时，她整个人都愣住了。

“我！你是说鲁尔先生（Mr. Rule）要见的是我？”她惊慌地问仆人。

“他本来是要见老爷的，太太，”那人说，“可老爷出门了，他说那就非见太太不可。他看上去慌得很。这一点我得说，”他补了一句。

威廉（William）自然听到了空气中的耳语，鲁尔先生慌张，他多少有点暗自得意；至于他的女主人，她一点也看不出鲁尔先生的激动与她有什么相干。

“我不明白我能帮得上他什么忙，威廉；而且这个钟点我从不会客。我真不知道他能找我什么事。”

===Original===

“It’s business, I think, ma’am,” said the servant, with a little eagerness. He wanted immensely himself to know what it was, and it did not occur to him as possible that his mistress, so much more interested than he, should be without anxiety or concern.

“Business!” said Mrs. John, “what do I know about business? However,” she added, “if he is so desirous, perhaps you had better show him up. Your master is always pleased when I pay a little attention to the clerks. He says it does good.”

“Yes, ma’am,” said William.

Being a reasonable human creature he was touched in spite of himself by the extraordinary sight of this poor, fine lady, sitting in her short sleeves on the edge of the volcano, and knowing nothing about it. It was too bad of master, William thought, if so be﻿—To leave the poor lady entirely in the dark so that she did not know no more than a baby what the clerk could want with her. William speculated, too, on his own circumstances as he went downstairs. If so be﻿—It was a good place, and he would be sorry to lose it. But he remembered that somebody had said the Sandersons were looking out for a butler.

“Mrs. Vernon will see you, sir,” he said in the midst of these thoughts; and Mr. Rule followed him eagerly upstairs.

===Chinese===

“是生意上的事，我想，太太，”仆人说，带着一点急切。他自己极想知道是什么事，而且他压根没想到，他的女主人比他利益攸关得多，居然会不着急不上心。

“生意！”约翰太太说，“我懂什么生意？不过，”她又说，“他要是一心想见，你还是领他上来吧。我对职员们稍加礼遇，你们老爷总是高兴的。他说这样有好处。”

“是，太太，”威廉说。

作为一个通情达理的人，他不由得被眼前这非同寻常的景象打动了：这位可怜的、优雅的太太，穿着短袖衣裳，坐在火山口上，对此却一无所知。威廉心想，老爷也未免太不像话，要是果真——把可怜的太太蒙在鼓里，让她像婴儿一样，不知道那职员找她能有什么事。下楼的时候，威廉也盘算起自己的处境来。要是果真——这是个好差事，丢了可惜。不过他记起有人说，桑德森家正在物色一个管家。

“弗农太太请您上去，先生，”他正想到这里说道；鲁尔先生急切地跟着他上了楼。

===Original===

But what could Mrs. John do? Her dress was spotted muslin, as most dresses were in those days; it was cut rather low on the shoulders, though she was not dressed for company. She had pretty little ringlets falling upon her cheeks, and short sleeves, and a band round her waist with a shining clasp. She was considered brilliant in conversation, and sang, “We Met, ’Twas in a Crowd,” and the songs previously mentioned, with so much feeling that people had been known to weep as they listened. The clerk had heard of all these accomplishments, and as he hurried in, his eye was caught by the harp in its corner, which was also one of the fashions of the time. He could not help being a little overawed by it, notwithstanding his dreadful anxiety. Poor lady! the thought passed through his mind as similar thoughts had passed through William’s﻿—Would all this be sold away from her? White muslin dresses with low necks have the advantage that they quite seem to separate their wearers from everyday life. We have no doubt that the dying out of chivalry, and the way in which women nowadays insist on doing their own business, and most likely other people’s too, is in great part to be put down to high dresses and long sleeves. In these habiliments a lady looks not so very much different from other people. She feels herself free to go into common life. But Mrs. John sat there helpless, ignorant, quite composed and easy in her mind, with pretty feet in sandalled slippers peeping from under her dress. Mr. Rule had time for all this distressed, regretful sympathy before he could stammer out in a hurry his anxious question﻿—or rather his hope﻿—that Mr. Vernon would be home tomorrow﻿—early?

“I am sure I don’t know,” said Mrs. John. “It would be scarcely worth his while to go away if he was to be back so soon. He said perhaps tomorrow, but more likely next week.”

“Next week!” cried Mr. Rule; “then he may just as well stay away altogether; it will then be too late.”

“Dear me!” said Mrs. John, politely, willing to show an interest; but she did not know what more to say.

“Perhaps you know where he is, ma’am?” said the anxious clerk: for this was the time when people said ma’am. “We might send an express after him. If he were here, things might still be tided over. Excuse me, Mrs. Vernon, but if you can give me any information﻿—”

===Chinese===

可约翰太太有什么办法呢？她穿的是细点花纱裙，那时候大多数裙子都是这个料子；虽不是会客的装束，肩头却裁得颇低。俏丽的小鬈发垂在双颊上，短短的袖子，腰间一条发亮的带扣腰带。她被公认谈吐出众，唱起《我们相遇，在人海之中》（We Met, 'Twas in a Crowd）和前面提到的那些歌来，感情充沛得让人听着听着就落了泪。职员对这些才艺早有耳闻；他匆匆进屋时，目光被角落里的竖琴吸引住了，那也是当时的风尚之一。他不由得对它生出几分敬畏，尽管心里焦急万分。可怜的太太！这个念头从他心里掠过，正如类似的念头掠过威廉的心头——这一切都会从她手里被卖掉吗？低领的白纱裙有一种好处：它们似乎真能把穿着它们的人与日常生活隔开。我们毫不怀疑，骑士精神的消亡，以及当今女人执意要亲手打理自己的事务、多半还要打理别人的事务，在很大程度上要归咎于高领衫和长袖子。穿着这类服饰，一位淑女看上去与旁人也就没多大分别。她自觉可以随便走进世俗生活。可约翰太太坐在那里，无助，无知，心里安然自在，穿着凉鞋式便鞋的秀足从裙裾下微微露出。鲁尔先生有工夫想完这满怀难过而惋惜的同情，才慌急地、结结巴巴道出他焦灼的询问——或者说是盼望——弗农先生明天——一早——能回家来？

“我真不知道，”约翰太太说。“要是这么快就回来，他也不值得出这趟门了。他说也许明天，多半是下星期。”

“下星期！”鲁尔先生喊道，“那他还不如干脆别回来了；到那时就太迟了。”

“天哪！”约翰太太客客气气地说，愿意显出点关心；可她不知道再说什么好。

“也许您知道他在哪儿，太太？”焦急的职员说：那还是人人称呼“太太”的年代。“我们可以派人快马追他去。他要是在这儿，事情也许还遮盖得过去。恕我冒昧，弗农太太，要是您能给我一点儿消息——”

===Original===

“Dear me,” said Mrs. John, “my husband was going to London, I think. Is it about business, or anything I may know?”

“All the world will know tomorrow,” cried the agitated clerk, “unless you can give me some assistance. I don’t like to trouble a lady, but what can I do? Mrs. Vernon, tomorrow is market day, and as sure as that day comes if he is not here to make some provision for it, we shall have a run on the bank.”

“A run on the bank!” said Mrs. John, dismayed. “What does that mean?”

“It means that we shall have to pay every note that is presented us in gold: and that everybody will rush upon us with our notes in their hands: and all the people who have deposit accounts will withdraw their money. It means Ruin,” said Mr. Rule, very much flustered indeed, wiping the perspiration from his brow. He had an account himself, and a considerable sum to his credit. Oh, the fool he had been to let it lie there instead of investing it! but then, he had been waiting for a good investment, and in the meantime, Vernon’s was as safe, safer than the Bank of England. He had believed that till today.

Mrs. John sat looking at him with bewildered eyes.

“I don’t understand,” she said. “The bank of course is for that, isn’t it? I never understand how you do it,” she added, with a little of the sprightliness for which she was distinguished. “It has always been a mystery to me what good it can do you to take all the trouble of paying people’s bills for them, and locking up their money, and having all that responsibility; but I cannot deny that it seems to answer,” she concluded with a little simper.

The harassed clerk looked at her with a pity that was almost tragic. If she had not been so handsome and so fine, and surrounded with all these luxuries, it is very likely he would have been impatient, and considered her a fool.

He replied gently﻿—

“I dare say, ma’am, it is difficult for you to form an idea of business; but I am almost forgetting, sitting talking to you, how dreadfully serious it is. If I knew where Mr. Vernon was, I would send a post-chaise directly. We are lost if he is not here. They will say﻿—God knows what they may not say. For God’s sake, ma’am, tell me how I am to find him?”

===Chinese===

“天哪，”约翰太太说，“我丈夫是要去伦敦，我想。是生意上的事吗，还是什么我能知道的事？”

“明天全世界都会知道，”激动的职员喊道，“除非您能给我一点帮助。我不愿搅扰一位太太，可我有什么法子？弗农太太，明天是集日，那一天一到，他要是不在这儿做点安排，银行就要遭到挤兑。”

“挤兑！”约翰太太惊慌地说。“那是什么意思？”

“意思是人家拿来多少钞票，我们就得用金子兑出多少：所有人都攥着我们的钞票冲我们来：所有立了存款账户的人都要把他们的钱提走。意味着毁灭，”鲁尔先生说，当真慌乱不堪，一边抹着额头上的汗。他自己也有个账户，名下还存着相当一笔款子。哦，自己真蠢，竟让那笔钱躺在那儿不拿去投资！不过，他一直在等一笔好的投资，而在此期间，弗农银行安稳——比英格兰银行还安稳。这话他一直信到今天。

约翰太太睁着一双茫然的眼睛望着他。

“我不明白，”她说。“银行本来就是干这个的，不是吗？你们怎么做这一套，我从来搞不懂，”她带着一点她素以出众的俏皮劲儿补充道。“你们替人付账单，把人家的钱锁起来，担着那么大的干系，这对你们到底有什么好处，我一向觉得是个谜；可我不能不承认，这买卖看着倒是有利可图，”她说完浅浅一笑。

被搅得心烦意乱的职员望着她，目光里的怜悯近乎悲壮。她若不是这样美貌、这样雍容、被这许多奢华环绕，他很可能会不耐烦，把她当成个傻瓜。

他温和地答道——

“我敢说，太太，生意上的事您确实难有概念；可同您坐着说话，我几乎忘了事情有多么严重。我要是知道弗农先生在哪儿，我马上就雇驿车追去。他不回来，我们就完了。人家会说——天知道人家会说出什么来。看在上帝份上，太太，告诉我怎样才能找到他？”

===Original===

“Indeed, Mr. Rule, I am very, very sorry. If I had known! but I rather encouraged him to go. He was looking so poorly. He was going to town, I am sure﻿—first: and then perhaps to Bath: or he might go across to France. He has been talking of that. France﻿—yes, I suggested it. He has never been on the Continent. But now I think of it, I don’t think he will go there, for he said he might be home tomorrow﻿—though more likely next week.”

“It seems very vague,” said Mr. Rule, looking at her with a steady look that began to show a gleam of suspicion; but this was entirely out of place. Mrs. John answered lightly without any perception even of what he could mean.

“Oh yes, it was vague! it is so much better not to be tied down. I told him he ought to take me; but it was settled in a hurry, he was feeling so poorly.”

“Then he has forsaken us!” cried the clerk in a terrible voice, which shook even her obtuse perceptions. She gazed at him with a little glow of anger.

“Forsaken you! Dear me, surely a little holiday never can matter. Why, the servants could go on without me for a time. It would never come into Mr. Vernon’s head that you could not manage by yourselves even for a single day.”

The clerk did not answer; it was all such a terrible muddle of ignorance and innocence, and perhaps of deep and deliberate guilt. But anyhow, there was the result beyond all uncertainty. The bank must come down. Vernon’s, which it had taken the work of generations to build up; Vernon’s, which was safer than the Bank of England. Mr. Rule had been a clerk there, man and boy, for about twenty years. He had been one of old Mr. Vernon’s staff. He had a pride in the bank as if it had been his own. To give up Vernon’s to destruction seemed more than giving himself up. But what could the clerks do without the principal? A lieutenant may fight his ship if the captain fails, or a subaltern replace his leader, but what can the clerks do without the head of the establishment? And he had no authority to act even if he had known how to act; and every two or three minutes there would come across him a poignant recollection of his own deposit. Oh, the Alnaschar hopes he had built upon that little fortune, the ways in which it was to serve him! He tried honestly, however, to put it away from his mind.

===Chinese===

“真的，鲁尔先生，我非常、非常抱歉。我要是知道就好了！可我还是怂恿他去的呢。他近来气色那么差。他先是要进城——这个我拿得准：然后也许去巴斯：要不然就渡海去法国。他一直念叨这个。法国——对，还是我提议的。他从来没去过大陆。可现在想想，我看他不会去了，因为他说也许明天就回家——虽然多半是下星期。”

“太渺茫了，”鲁尔先生说，眼睛直直地望着她，目光里开始露出一丝疑心；可这疑心全然放错了地方。约翰太太轻快地答道，压根没觉出他可能是什么意思。

“哦是的，是渺茫！不受拘束才好呢。我告诉他该带我一起去；可这趟出门定得匆忙，他身子又那么不舒服。”

“那么他是抛下我们不管了！”职员用可怕的声音喊道，连她那迟钝的知觉也为之一震。她瞪着他，眼里腾起一点怒火。

“抛下你们！天哪，放几天假总不至于有什么要紧吧。嗐，连仆人们都能一时半会儿没有我。弗农先生做梦也不会想到，你们连一天都撑不住。”

职员没有回答；这一团东西真是无知与天真、也许还有深藏而蓄意的罪愆掺和成的可怕的乱麻。可无论如何，结果是明明白白不容置疑的了。银行必倒无疑。弗农银行，那是几代人的心血建起来的；弗农银行，那比英格兰银行还稳当。鲁尔先生从孩提到成人，在这家银行当职员约摸二十年了。他曾是老弗农先生手下的人。他对这家银行怀有一种仿佛自家的自豪。把弗农银行交出去任其毁灭，比交出他自己还要难受。可没有老板，职员们能做什么呢？舰长倒下了，尉官还可以指挥军舰；长官阵亡了，下级军官还可以接替；可没有掌门的银行，职员们能做什么呢？况且即使他知道该怎么行动，他也没有行动的权限；每隔两三分钟，他自己那笔存款便像针一样刺上心头。哦，他曾在这笔小小的家财上筑起过多少白日梦般的指望，盘算过它将怎样为他效力！不过他还是老老实实地竭力把这事从心头排开。

===Original===

“We could have done well enough on an ordinary occasion,” he said, “and Mr. Vernon generally settles everything before he goes; but I thought he was only absent for the day. Mrs. Vernon,” he cried, suddenly, “can’t you help us? can’t you help us? It will be ruin for you too.”

She stared at him for a moment without speaking, and then﻿—

“You make me quite wretched. I don’t understand. I have only a little money in the house. Would that do any good?” she said.

“How much have you?” said the clerk in his trouble.

She ran to a pretty ornamental desk and opened it nervously.

“I dare say there may be about twenty pounds,” she said.

He laughed loudly, harshly, a laugh that seemed to echo through the large, unoccupied room.

“If it were twenty thousand it might do something,” he said.

“Sir!” said Mrs. John Vernon, standing in a fine attitude of displeasure by her desk, holding it open with one hand. She looked like a picture by Sir Thomas Lawrence, her scarf, for she wore a scarf, hanging half off her pretty white shoulders, caught upon one equally white arm, her ringlets waving on her cheek. His laugh was rude, and then he was only a clerk. She was all angry scorn from the high knot of brown hair on the top of her head to the point of her sandalled shoe.

Poor Mr. Rule was as penitent as man could be. He was shocked beyond measure by his own brutality. He had forgotten himself﻿—and before a lady! He made the most abject apologies.

“But my interest in the bank will, I hope, be some excuse. I feel half distracted,” he said; and he added, as he backed out at the door with painful bows, “Perhaps, ma’am, if you can think of any means of communicating with Mr. Vernon, you would let me know; or I will call later, if we could send an express; nothing is too much for the chance of having him back tomorrow.”

“Well,” said the lady, “you are strange managers, I must say, that cannot get on without my husband one day.”

“It is not that, ma’am; it is not that.”

“I don’t know what it is. I begin to think it is only making a fuss,” Mrs. John said.

===Chinese===

“寻常的日子我们本应付裕如，”他说，“弗农先生出门前一般总把一切都安排妥当；可我只当他出门一天。弗农太太，”他忽然喊道，“您就不能帮帮我们吗？就不能帮帮我们吗？对您这也是毁灭呀。”

她怔怔地望了他一会儿，没有作声，然后——

“您把我弄得难受极了。我不明白。我家里只有一点点现钱。那能顶什么用吗？”她说。

“您有多少？”职员在焦灼中问。

她跑到一张精致的饰柜前，紧张地打开它。

“大概总有二十来镑吧，”她说。

他放声大笑，笑声粗厉，仿佛在空荡荡的大屋子里回荡。

“要是两万还顶点用，”他说。

“先生！”约翰·弗农太太说着，在柜旁摆出一副愠怒的美妙姿态，一只手扶着敞开的柜门。她活像托马斯·劳伦斯爵士（Sir Thomas Lawrence）画中的人物——她披着一条披巾，那披巾半挂在漂亮的雪白双肩上，搭在同样雪白的一条手臂上，鬈发在颊边拂动。他的笑是无礼的，何况他还不过是个职员。从头顶那高高的棕色发髻，到凉鞋式便鞋的鞋尖，她浑身上下都是愤怒的轻蔑。

可怜的鲁尔先生悔恨得无以复加。他为自己的粗暴骇异万分。他忘形了——而且是在一位太太面前！他作了最卑躬的道歉。

“可我对银行的这片心，希望能多少算个理由。我都快急疯了，”他说；又一边连连躬身、倒退着出门，一边补充道：“太太，您若能想起什么法子与弗农先生通个信儿，望您告诉我；或者我们若能派专差，我晚些再来一趟；只要有一线指望他能明天回来，怎么都使得。”

“真是，”那位太太说，“你们可真是些奇怪的当家人，我可得说，离了我丈夫一天都转不动。”

“不是那么回事，太太；不是那么回事。”

“我不知道是什么回事。我倒开始觉得这不过是大惊小怪，”约翰太太说。

## II / 二
===Original===

Miss Catherine

Poor Mr. Rule rushed out into the night in a state of despair. It was a summer night, and the streets of Redborough were still full of the murmur of life and movement. He came down from the slope on which Mr. John Vernon’s grand new house was situated, into the town, turning over everything that it was possible to do. Should he go to the Old Bank, the lifelong rival of Vernon’s, and ask their help to pull through? Even such a humiliation he would have endured had there been any chance of success. Should he go to the agent of the Bank of England? He could not but feel that it was quite doubtful whether between them they could make up enough to meet the rush he expected; and were they likely to do it? Would not the first question be, “Where is Mr. Vernon?” And where was Mr. Vernon? Perhaps gone to Bath; perhaps to France, his wife said. Why should he go to France without letting anyone at the bank know, saying he was only to be absent for a day? There was no telegraph in those days, and if he confided Mr. Vernon’s story to the other banks, what would they think of him? They would say that Vernon was mad, or that he had﻿—gone away. There could be no doubt of what they would say. Rule was faithful to his old service, and to the honour of the house which had trained him. He would say nothing about France or Bath. He would allow it to be understood that Mr. Vernon had gone to London to get the assistance necessary, and would come back in a post-chaise before the offices were open in the morning. And perhaps, he said to himself, perhaps it was so. God grant it might be so! Very likely he had not thought it necessary to enter into the matter to a lady. Poor thing, with her twenty pounds! that showed how much she knew of business; but it was very high-minded and innocent of her to offer all she had. It showed there was at least no harm in her thoughts. It gave a momentary ease to the clerk’s mind to think that perhaps this was what Mr. Vernon must mean. He must have known for some time how badly things were going, and who could tell that the sudden expedition of which he had made so little, only saying when he left the bank the day before “I shall not be here tomorrow,” who could tell that it was not to help to surmount the crisis, that he had gone away?

凯瑟琳小姐（Miss Catherine）

可怜的鲁尔先生绝望地冲进夜色里。那是一个夏夜，雷德伯勒的街上还满是生活与走动的低语。他从约翰·弗农先生那座宏伟新宅所在的山坡上下来，走进镇里，心里翻来覆去盘算着一切可能做的事。要不要去找老银行——弗农银行一辈子的对头——求他们帮忙渡过难关？哪怕这样的屈辱他也肯忍受，只要有一线成功的希望。要不要去找英格兰银行的代理？他不能不觉得，他们两家合起来，也未必凑得够应付他预想的那场挤兑；何况他们肯吗？人家问的第一句岂不是：“弗农先生呢？”弗农先生又在哪里？也许去了巴斯；也许去了法国，他太太说。他为什么去法国不跟银行里任何人讲一声，只说出门一天就回？那时候还没有电报，他若把弗农先生的事托给别家银行，人家会怎么想？人家会说弗农疯了，要么就是——跑了。他们会怎么说，是毫无疑问的。鲁尔忠于他服务多年的老东家，忠于养他成人的这家银行的体面。法国也好，巴斯也好，他一个字也不会提。他只让人理解为：弗农先生上伦敦去筹措必要的援助去了，明早晨营业之前会坐驿车赶回来。也许，他对自己说，也许真是这样呢。但愿上帝保佑真是这样！很可能他只是觉得没有必要对一位太太细说这件事。可怜的人，就凭她那二十镑！可见她对生意懂得多少；可她愿意献出自己所有的一切，这心意极高贵、很天真。这说明她心里至少没有一点坏念头。想到弗农先生的用意也许正在于此，职员心头一时松快了些。事态败坏到这个地步，他必定早就心中有数；他临走时在银行里只轻描淡写地说了一句“我明天不来了”，谁能说这场突如其来的出行不是为了助他闯过这场危机呢？谁能说他不是为这个才走的呢？

Rule turned towards his own house under the solace of this thought, feeling that anyhow it was better to get a night’s rest, and be strong for whatever was to happen tomorrow. It would be a miserable tomorrow if Mr. Vernon did not bring help. Not only the bank that would go, but so many men with families that would be thrown upon the world. God help them! and that money which stood to his own credit, that balance of which two or three days before he had been so proud, to see it standing in his name on those well-kept beautiful books! All this hanging upon the chance that Mr. Vernon might have gone to town to get money! No, he could not go in, and sit down at the peaceful table where Mrs. Rule perhaps would be hemming a cambric ruffle for his shirt, or plaiting it delicately with her own fingers, a thing no laundress could do to please her﻿—and the children learning their lessons. He felt sure that he could not rest; he would only make her anxious, and why should she be made anxious as long as he could keep it from her. It is difficult to say how it was that the first suggestion of a new possibility took hold of Mr. Rule’s mind. He turned away when he was within a stone’s throw of his own house, saying to himself that he could not go in, that it was impossible, and walked in the opposite direction, where he had not gone far until he came in sight of the bank, that centre of so many years’ hard work, that pride of Redborough, and of everybody connected with it. Vernon’s! To think that Ruin should be possible, that so dark a shadow could hover over that sacred place. What would old Mr. Vernon have said, he who received it from his father and handed it down always flourishing, always prosperous to﻿—not to his son. If his son had lived, the eldest one, not he who had gone wrong, but the eldest, who was John too, called after his grandfather, he who was the father of﻿—It was at this point that Mr. Rule came to a dead stop, and then after a pause wheeled right round, and without saying another word to himself walked straight up Wilton Street, which as everybody knows was quite out of his way.

The father of —﻿—﻿—. Yes, indeed, indeed, and that was true! The recollection which called forth this fervour of affirmation was a pleasant one. All the youth of Redborough at one time had been in love with Catherine Vernon. The bank clerks to a man adored her. When she used to come and go with her grandfather﻿—and she did so constantly, bringing him down in the morning in her pony carriage, calling for him in the afternoon, running in in the middle of the day to see that the old gentleman had taken his biscuits and his wine﻿—she walked over their hearts as she crossed the outer office, but so lightly, so smoothly, that the hearts were only thrilled, not crushed by her footfall, so firm and swift, but so airy as it was. She knew them all in the office, and would give her hand to the head clerk, and send a friendly glance all round, unaware of the harm she was doing to the hapless young men. But after all it was not harm. It was a generous love they felt for her, like the love of chivalry for a lady unapproachable. That young princess was not for them. None of them grew mad with foolish hopes, but they thought of her as they never thought of anyone else. Mr. Rule was at the end of Wilton Street, just where it meanders out towards the edge of the common, before he took breath, and began to ask himself what Miss Vernon could do for him. Was not one lady enough to appeal to? She whom he had already seen had nothing for him﻿—no help, no advice, not a suggestion even. And yet she was more closely connected with the bank than Catherine Vernon, who had disappeared from all visible connection with it at her grandfather’s death, notwithstanding that a great deal of her money was in it, and that she had in fact a right to be consulted as a partner. So it had been settled, it was said, by the old man in his will. But she had never, so far as anybody knew, taken up this privilege. She had never come to the bank, never given a sign of having any active interest in it. What then could she be expected to do? What could she do even if she wished to help them? Mr. Rule was aware that there was no very cordial feeling between her cousin’s house and hers. They were friends, perfectly good friends, but they were not cordial. While he turned over these thoughts in his mind, however, he walked on steadily and quickly without the least hesitation in his step.

——的父亲。是啊，千真万确，一点不假！唤起这番热烈肯定的回忆是愉快的。当年雷德伯勒的年轻人一度个个都爱着凯瑟琳·弗农。银行的职员更是无一不倾慕她。她从前常伴着祖父来来去去——的确是常来常往：早晨用小马车送老人家下山，下午再来接他，中午还要跑进来瞧一瞧，看老先生有没有吃他的饼干、喝他的酒——她穿过外间办公处时，一路踏过众人的心，可她踏得那样轻、那样稳，那些心只是为之颤动，并不被她的脚步碾碎——她的脚步那样坚定、轻捷，又那样轻盈。她认得行里所有的人，会把手伸给首席职员，向四周投去友好的目光，浑然不觉自己正对那些不幸的年轻人施害。但说到底那并不是害。他们对她的爱是一种慷慨的爱，如同骑士对一位高不可攀的贵妇人的爱。那位年轻的公主不是给他们预备的。他们没有一个被愚蠢的希望逼疯，可他们想她，想得从不曾这样想过别人。鲁尔先生走到威尔顿街的尽头，走到那条街蜿蜒散向公地边缘的地方，才缓过一口气来，开始问自己：弗农小姐能帮他什么忙呢？求助一位太太还不够吗？他已见过头一位了，那位什么也帮不上——没有帮助，没有主意，连一点提示也没有。可她与银行的关系毕竟比凯瑟琳·弗农近得多；而凯瑟琳自祖父去世后，便从一切看得见的关联中隐去了，尽管她的许多钱投在这银行里，尽管她实际上有权作为合伙人参与谘议。据说老先生在遗嘱里就是这么定下的。但据人所知，她从未行使过这项权利。她从未到银行来过，从未流露过一丝积极的关切。那么又能指望她做什么呢？就算她愿意帮忙，她又做得了什么呢？鲁尔先生深知她表哥那一家与她之间并无多少热络的情分。他们是朋友，地道的好朋友，但算不上亲热。不过，尽管心里翻来覆去地想这些，他的脚步却走得又稳又快，没有半点迟疑。

There was even a sort of exhilarated excitement in him, a sentiment quite different from that with which he had been disconsolately straying about, and painfully turning over possibilities, or rather impossibilities. Perhaps it was a half romantic pleasure in the idea of speaking to Miss Vernon again, but really there was something besides that, a sense of satisfaction in finding a new and capable mind to consult with at least, if no more.

Miss Vernon lived in the house which her grandfather had lived in and his father before him. To reach it you had to make your way through the delta of little streets into which Wilton Street ran, and across a corner of the common. The Grange was an old house with dark red gables appearing out of the midst of a clump of trees. In winter you saw the whole mass of it, chiefly old bricks, though these were thrown up and made picturesque by the fact that the oldest part was in grey stone. Broad large Elizabethan windows glimmered, lighted up, through the thick foliage this evening; for by this time the summer night was beginning to get dark, and a good deal too late for a visit. Mr. Rule thought as he knocked at the door that it was very likely she would not see him. But this was not the case. When he sent in his name as the head clerk at the bank he was received immediately, and shown into the room with the Elizabethan windows where she was sitting. By this time she was of mature years, and naturally much changed from the young girl he had known. He had been one of the young clerks in the outer office, whom she would recognise with a friendly smiling look, and a nod of her head all round. Now, however, Miss Vernon came up to him, and held out her hand to Mr. Rule. “You need not have sent me word who you were,” she said with a smile. “I knew quite well who you were. I never forget faces nor names. You have not come to me at this time of night on a mere visit of civility. Don’t be afraid to tell me at once whatever there may be to say.”

“From the way you speak, ma’am,” said Mr. Rule, “I conclude that you have heard some of the wicked reports that are flying about?”

“That is exactly what I want to know,” she said, with all her old vivacity. “Are they wicked reports?”

“A report is always wicked,” said Mr. Rule sententiously, “which is likely to bring about the evil it imagines.”

弗农小姐住在祖父住过的宅子里，祖父之前又是曾祖住的。要去那里，得穿过威尔顿街尽头分岔出来的那些小街的迷阵，再斜穿过公地的一角。格兰奇宅（The Grange）是一座老宅，暗红色的人字山墙从一丛树木中间探出来。冬天看得见它整个的一大片，主要是老砖，不过最老的那一部分是灰石的，把全宅衬托得错落有致。今晚，宽大的伊丽莎白时代的窗户亮着灯，透过浓密的枝叶微微闪光；因为此刻夏夜已经开始黑下来，要拜访实在已太晚了。鲁尔先生一面叩门一面想，她多半不会见他。但并非如此。他递上“银行首席职员”的名帖，立刻被让了进去，领进那间有着伊丽莎白式窗户、她正坐着的屋子。此时她已是成熟的年纪，自然与他当年相识的少女大不相同了。他从前只是外间办公处的一个年轻职员，她认出他们时，会报以友好的微笑，朝四面点点头。而此刻，弗农小姐起身迎上前来，把手伸给鲁尔先生。“您本来不必报姓名，”她微笑着说。“我清清楚楚知道您是谁。人的脸和名字，我从不忘记。您这个钟点到我这里来，总不会只是拜访寒暄。不管有什么话，别怕，立刻对我说吧。”

“听您说话的口气，太太，”鲁尔先生说，“我断定外面乱飞的那些坏话，您已经听到了一些？”

“凡属可能招来它所臆想的祸事的风言风语，都是坏话。”鲁尔先生一本正经地说。

“Ah!” she cried. “Then it is no further gone than that; and yet it is as far gone as that?” she added, looking anxiously in his face.

“Miss Vernon,” said Rule solemnly, “I expect a run upon the bank tomorrow.”

“Good God!” she said, clasping her hands; which was not a profane exclamation, but the kind of half-conscious appeal which nature makes instinctively. “But you have made all preparations? Surely you can meet that.”

He shook his head solemnly. The credit of the bank was so much to him that when thus face to face with the event he dreaded, poor Rule could not articulate anything, and the water stood in his eyes.

“Good God!” she said again: but her face was not awestricken; it was that of a soldier springing instantly to the alert, rallying all his resources at the first word of danger; “but you don’t mean to say that my cousin﻿—does not John know this? They say everybody knows these things before the person concerned. Why, why did you not warn him, Mr. Rule?”

Rule shook his head.

“It isn’t possible that he could have been ignorant. How could he be ignorant, ma’am? God knows I have not a word to say against Mr. Vernon﻿—but to think he should forsake us in our moment of trial!”

“Forsake you!” A sudden flush flew over Miss Vernon’s face﻿—a spark shot out of her eyes. Indignation and yet doubt was in her face. “That is not possible,” she cried, holding her head high; and then she said anxiously, “Mr. Rule, tell me what you mean?”

“I dare say it is the falsity of appearances,” said poor Rule. “I am sure I hope so. I hope Mr. Vernon has gone away to get help, personally: you can do that so much better than writing; and that he may be back in time tomorrow.”

“Has he gone away?” she said in a low tone.

“Unfortunately, Miss Vernon﻿—I can’t help saying unfortunately, for it paralyses everybody else. We can do nothing at the bank. But I cling to the hope that he will be back before the bank is opened. Oh, yes, I cling to the hope. Without that﻿—”

“Everything will be lost?”

“Everything!” cried he, who was so proud of being the head clerk at Vernon’s, with tears in his eyes.

And then there was a pause. For a minute or two not a word was said. The daughter of the house was as much overcome by the thought as was its faithful servant. At last she said faintly, but firmly﻿—

“Mr. Rule, I cannot believe but that you will see John tomorrow when the bank is opened, with means to meet every demand.”

“Yes, Miss Vernon, that is my conviction too.”

But in what a faltering voice was this conviction stated! The room was not very light, and they did not distinguish very clearly each other’s faces.

“But in case of any failure﻿—” she said, “for of course one never can tell, the most tiresome nothings may detain you just when speed is most important; or he might not have succeeded as he hoped. In case of any﻿—delay﻿—I shall be there, Mr. Rule; you may calculate upon me, with every penny I can muster﻿—”

“You, Miss Vernon!” the clerk said, with a cry of relief and joy.

“Certainly; who else, when the credit of the bank is at stake? I have been living very quietly, you know. I spend next to nothing; my mother’s money has accumulated till it is quite a little fortune, I believe. What had I best do? send to Mr. Sellon and ask him to help us on that security? I don’t think he will refuse.”

“If you do that we are saved,” said Rule, half crying. “That is the thing to do. What a head for business you have!”

She smiled, and gave him a little nod, like one of those happy nods she used to give to the young clerks in her fine youthful days, in which there was a kind acknowledgment of their admiration, a friendly good fellowship with themselves.

“I hope I am not old Edward Vernon’s granddaughter for nothing,” she said, beginning to walk up and down the room with a buoyant impatience, as though longing for the moment of exertion to come. “I had better write to Mr. Sellon at once; there is no time to lose.”

“And if you will let me I will take the note directly, and bring you an answer.”

“Bravo! that is promptitude,” cried Miss Vernon; and she went up to him and held out her hand. “Between us we will keep the old place going,” she said, “whoever may give in.”

If Mr. Rule had not been the steady, bashful Englishman he was, he would have kissed that hand. He felt that there was in it enough to save everything﻿—the bank first, and then his own little bit of money, and his situation, and his children’s bread. He had not allowed himself to think of these things in the greatness of his anxiety in respect to Vernon’s; but he did think of them now, and was ready to cry in the relief of his soul.

===Chinese===

“鲁尔先生，我不信明天银行开门时您会看不到约翰带着应付一切提兑的钱回来。”

“是的，弗农小姐，这也是我的信念。”

可这信念说得多么颤巍巍啊！屋里光线不亮，彼此的脸都看不真切。

“但万一有闪失——”她说，“因为谁也说不准，越是急的时候，越是最恼人的鸡毛蒜皮绊住人；他也可能不像指望的那样顺利。万一有什么——耽搁——我会在那里，鲁尔先生；您可以指望我，把我能凑到的每一个便士都算上——”

“您，弗农小姐！”职员喊出声来，又是宽慰又是欢喜。

“当然；银行的名誉攸关之时，除了我还有谁？您知道，我一直过得非常清静。我几乎不花什么钱；我母亲的钱攒到今天，我想已经是一小笔家财了。我最好怎么办？派人去找塞隆先生（Mr. Sellon），请他凭这个作保帮我们一把？我想他不会拒绝。”

“您要是这样做，我们就得救了，”鲁尔说，几乎哭出来。“就该这么做。您多懂生意啊！”

她微微一笑，朝他轻轻点了点头，就像她当年风华正茂时给那些年轻职员们的得意的点头——那点头里含着对他们倾慕的好意领受，含着与他们的友好情谊。

“但愿我做老爱德华·弗农的孙女不是白做的，”她说着，开始在屋里踱来踱去，步子里带着一股轻快的急切，仿佛巴不得施展身手的时刻立刻到来。“我最好马上给塞隆先生写信；一刻也不能耽搁。”

“您若允许，我立刻把信送去，把回音带回来。”

“好极了！这才是雷厉风行，”弗农小姐喊道；她走上前，伸出手来。“咱们两个，定要把老家业撑住，”她说，“管它谁先撑不住。”

鲁尔先生若不是他那样一个稳重怕羞的英国人，真会吻那只手的。他觉得那只手里握着足以拯救一切的力量——先救银行，再救他自己那一点钱、他的职位、他孩子们的面包。方才为弗农银行的焦虑压倒一切，他不许自己想这些；此刻他想了，心底一松，几乎要哭出来。

===Original===

Never was an evening more full of occupation. Mr. Sellon, who was the agent of the Bank of England in Redborough, was fortunately at home, and responded at once to Miss Vernon’s appeal. Mr. Rule had the gratification of walking back with him to the Grange, whither he hastened to reply in person, and of assisting at the interview afterwards with a sense of pride and personal advancement which heightened the satisfaction of his soul. Miss Vernon insisted strongly on the point that all these preparations were by way of precaution merely.

“My cousin will no doubt be back in time, fully provided; but of course you never can be perfectly certain. Horses may break down, shafts be broken; the least little accident may spoil everything. Of course John put off such a step till the last moment, and thought it better to keep it entirely to himself.”

“Of course,” cried Rule, speaking out of his corner; and “Of course,” but much more faintly, Mr. Sellon said.

“That is so evident that it requires no repetition: but just as naturally Mr. Rule was alarmed, and had the good sense to come to me.”

All this was by way of convincing Mr. Sellon that the whole matter was perfectly simple, and that probably his resources would not be called upon at all. To be sure, as in every case of a similar kind, Miss Vernon might have saved herself the trouble, the circumstances being far more clearly known to Mr. Sellon than to herself. He was very sure that John Vernon would not return, and that his intention was to get himself out of it. Everybody had known it was coming. It was just as well to humour a lady, and accept her version as the right one; but he was not for a moment deceived.

“Of course the bank,” he said, “will make it up to you afterwards.”

“Of course,” she said; “and if not, I don’t know who is to stop me from doing what I like with my own.”

He asked a few questions further, in which there was a good deal of significance, as for instance something about Mrs. John Vernon’s marriage settlements, which neither of the others for the moment understood. Rule saw Mr. Sellon to the door, by Miss Vernon’s request, with great pride, and went back to her afterwards, “as if he were one of the family,” he described to his wife afterwards.

“Well,” she said, “are you satisfied?”

“Oh, more than satisfied, happier than I can tell you,” cried the clerk. “The bank is saved!”

===Chinese===

从来没有一个夜晚这么忙碌过。塞隆先生——英格兰银行驻雷德伯勒的代理——幸而在家，立刻响应了弗农小姐的求助。鲁尔先生有幸陪他走回格兰奇宅（塞隆先生急着亲自登门作复），又有幸随后列席了那场会谈，心里怀着一种自尊与升迁之感，愈发志得意满。弗农小姐执意强调一点：这一切准备只不过是防患于未然。

“我表弟无疑会及时赶回来，粮草齐备；可世事难保万全。马会失蹄，车辕会折；顶小的一点意外就可能坏了全局。约翰自然把这一步拖到最后一刻，自然觉得此事完全烂在自己肚子里才好。”

“自然，”鲁尔在他的角落里高声附和；“自然，”塞隆先生也说，声音却低得多。

“这道理明摆着，不必多说；可鲁尔先生照样着了慌，也算他有头脑，来找我。”

这番话全是说给塞隆先生听的，为的是让他相信事情再简单不过，多半根本用不着动用他的财力。当然，如同一切类似情形，弗农小姐本可省去这番口舌——塞隆先生对实情的了解远比她清楚。他十分有数：约翰·弗农不会回来了，此行的用意是把自己摘出去。人人都早知道会有这一天。不妨顺着一位太太，把她的说法当作正解；但他一刻也没受骗。

“当然，”他说，“事后银行会补偿您的。”

“当然，”她说；“若不补偿，我不知道谁拦得住我拿自己的钱随心所欲。”

他又问了几句，句句大有深意，比方说问到约翰·弗农太太的婚产协定，另外两位一时都没听懂。弗农小姐请鲁尔先生送塞隆先生到门口，他满怀着自豪送去，回来时“就像自家人一样”——他后来对妻子这样形容。

“怎么样，”她说，“您满意了吗？”

“哦，岂止满意，说不出的欢喜，”职员喊道。“银行得救了！”

===Original===

And then she, so triumphant, buoyant, inspired as she was, sank down upon a chair, and put her head in her hands, and he thought cried; but Rule was not a man to spy upon a lady in the revulsion of her feelings. When she looked up again she said to him quickly﻿—

“In any case, Mr. Rule, we are both sure that my cousin is doing all he can for the bank; if he succeeds or not is in other hands.”

“Oh yes, Miss Vernon, quite sure,” Rule replied promptly. He understood that she meant it to be understood so, and determined within himself that he was ready to go to the stake for the new dogma. And then he related to her his interview with Mrs. John, and her willingness to give him up her twenty pounds to save the bank.

Miss Vernon’s first flush of indignation soon yielded to amusement and sympathy. She laughed and she cried.

“That shall always be remembered to her credit,” she said. “I did not think she had any feeling for the bank. Let us always remember it to her credit. She was ready to give all she had, and who can do any more?”

Mr. Rule was somewhat intoxicated with all these confidences, and with the way in which Miss Vernon said “we”﻿—his head was a little turned by it. She was a woman who understood what it was to have a faithful servant. No doubt, after the sacrifice she was making, she would, in future, have more to do with the business, and Rule could scarcely keep his imagination from straying into a consideration of changes that might be. Instead of merely being head clerk, it was quite possible that a manager might be required; but he pulled himself up, and would not allow his thoughts to carry him so far.

===Chinese===

随后，她——方才那样意气昂扬、神采焕发——跌坐在椅子里，双手捂住脸，他觉得她是哭了；可鲁尔不是那种窥探太太情绪翻覆的人。等她再抬起头来，她很快地对他说：

“无论如何，鲁尔先生，咱们都拿得稳：我表弟正为银行竭尽所能；成与不成，另在天命。”

“哦是的，弗农小姐，拿得稳，”鲁尔立刻应道。他明白她要人这么理解，心里打定主意，为这条新信条上火刑柱也甘愿。接着他向她讲了自己见约翰太太的经过，讲她怎样情愿交出那二十镑来救银行。

弗农小姐最初的义愤很快化作又好笑又怜惜。她笑了，又哭了。

“这一笔要永远记在她的好处上，”她说。“想不到她对银行还有这份心。咱们要永远记着她这一好处。她舍得献出自己的一切，还有谁能做得更多呢？”

鲁尔先生被这一连串知遇之谈熏熏然了，被弗农小姐口口声声的“咱们”熏熏然了——脑袋有点飘飘然。她是一个懂得拥有忠仆之滋味的女人。无疑，经过这番牺牲，她往后与银行业务的干系会多起来，鲁尔的想象力禁不住溜到种种可能的变动上去。与其只当首席职员，说不定要设一个经理呢；可他赶紧勒住，不许自己想那么远。

===Original===

Next day everything happened as had been foreseen. There was a run on the bank, and a moment of great excitement; but when Miss Vernon was seen at the door of the inner office smiling, with her smile of triumphant energy and capability, upon the crowd, and when the Bank of England porters appeared bringing in those heavy boxes, the run and all the excitement subsided as by magic. The bank was saved; but not by John Vernon. The outside world never was aware how the matter was settled. But John did not come back. He would have met nothing but averted looks and biting words, for there could be no doubt that he had abandoned his post, and left Vernon’s to its fate. Messrs. Pounce and Seeling had a good deal to do about the matter, and new deeds were drawn, and old deeds cancelled to a serious extent; but the bank ever after remained in the hands of Miss Vernon, who, it turned out, had more than her grandfather’s steady power of holding on, and was, indeed, the heir of her great-grandfather’s genius for business. The bank throve in her hands as it had done in his days, and everything it touched prospered. She deserved it, to be sure, but everybody who deserves does not get this fine reward. There is something beyond, which we call good luck or good fortune, or the favour of Heaven; but as Heaven does not favour all, or even most of the best people in this way, we have to fall back upon a less pious phraseology. Is it, perhaps, genius for business, as distinct as genius in poetry, which makes everything succeed? But this is more than any man can be expected to understand. Rule attained all the heights of those hopes which had vaguely dawned on him out of the mist on that July evening when his good angel suggested to him Catherine Vernon’s name. He was raised to the dignity of manager as he had foreseen. His salary was doubled, his sons were provided for, and he grew old in such comfort and general esteem as he had never dreamed of. “This is the man that saved the bank,” Miss Vernon would say. And though, of course, he deprecated such high praise, and declared that he was nothing but the humblest instrument, yet there can be no doubt that he came to believe it in the end, as his wife and all his children did from the beginning.

===Chinese===

第二天，一切都如所料。银行遭到挤兑，一时群情汹汹；可是当人们看见弗农小姐站在内间办公室门口，带着那胜利的、精明干练的微笑对着人群，当英格兰银行的脚夫们抬着那些沉重的箱子走进来，挤兑与一切骚动如魔法般平息了。银行得救了；但救它的不是约翰·弗农。外界始终不知道这件事是怎么了结的。可约翰没有回来。他回来只会遇见躲避的目光和刻毒的言语，因为他弃职而逃、听任弗农银行自生自灭，这是没有疑问的。庞斯与西林两律师事务所为此忙了好一阵，新契约订立了，旧契约大批地废止了；但银行从此留在弗农小姐手中——事实证明，她不只有祖父那份咬定不放的韧劲，实在是曾祖父经商天才的继承人。银行在她手中如同在曾祖父当年一样兴旺，它碰到的一切都发达。这是她应得的，这自然没错；可并不是每个应得的人都有这份好报。这里面另有一种东西，我们叫它运气、福分，或上天的眷顾；但上天并不这样眷顾所有人，甚至并不眷顾大多数最好的人，于是我们只好退而用一个不那么虔诚的说法。也许，那是一种经商的天才，如同诗的天才一样分明，叫万事成功？可这就超出任何人所能理解的了。鲁尔得到了那个七月黄昏里从迷雾中依稀闪现的全部希望的极顶——那晚他的守护天使把凯瑟琳·弗农的名字提示给他。他如愿以偿地升到了经理的尊位。薪水翻了一番，儿子们都得了安置，他在前所未有的舒适与普遍的敬重中安度晚年。“这就是救了银行的那个人，”弗农小姐总这么说。当然，他总要谦辞这样的盛赞，声明自己不过是最卑微的工具；但毫无疑问，到头来他自己也信了——他的妻子和儿女们从一开头就深信不疑。

===Original===

Miss Vernon’s was a reign of great benevolence, of great liberality, but of great firmness too. As she got older she became almost the most important person in Redborough. The people spoke of her, as they sometimes do of a very popular man, by her Christian name. Catherine Vernon did this and that, they said. Catherine Vernon was the first thought when anything was wanted either by the poor who needed help, or the philanthropist who wanted to give it. The Vernon Almshouses, which had been established a hundred years before, but had fallen into great decay till she took them in hand, were always known as Catherine Vernon’s Almshouses. Her name was put to everything. Catherine Street, Catherine Square, Catherine places without number. The people who built little houses on the outskirts exhausted their invention in varying the uses of it. Catherine Villas, Catherine Cottage, Catherine Mansion, were on all sides; and when it occurred to the High Church rector to dedicate the new church to St. Catherine of Alexandria, the common people, with one accord, transferred the invocation to their living patroness. She was, at least, a saint more easily within reach, and more certain to lend a favourable ear.

===Chinese===

弗农小姐的当政是一段广施仁惠、广行宽厚的年代，也是一段铁一般的年代。随着年龄增长，她几乎成了雷德伯勒头一号的要人。人们提起她，就像有时候提起一位深得人心的男人那样，直呼她的教名。凯瑟琳·弗农做了这个、办了那个，他们这样说。穷人要救助也好，慈善家要施舍也好，头一个想起的都是凯瑟琳·弗农。弗农济贫院创立于一百年前，到她接手时已败落不堪，此后就一直被叫作凯瑟琳·弗农济贫院。她的名字冠在一切东西上。凯瑟琳街、凯瑟琳广场、数不清的凯瑟琳什么。在城郊盖小宅子的人，把变换这个名号的用法想尽了。凯瑟琳别墅、凯瑟琳小筑、凯瑟琳大厦，四面八方都是；等到高教会派的教区长想起把新教堂献给亚历山德里亚的圣凯瑟琳时，小百姓们便不约而同，把这份祈告转给了他们活着的保护人。至少，这一位圣徒近在身边，更容易亲近，也更肯垂听祈求。

## III / 三
===Original===

The Vernonry

These things all happened a great number of years before the beginning of this history. Catherine Vernon had become an old woman﻿—at least she was sixty-five; you can call that an old woman if you please. Sometimes it may mean the extreme of age, decrepitude and exhaustion: but sometimes also it means a softer and more composed middle age﻿—a lovely autumnal season in which all the faculties retain their force without any of their harshness, and toleration and Christian charity replace all sharpness of criticism or sternness of opinion. Sometimes this beautiful age will fall to the lot of those who have experienced a large share of the miseries of life and learnt its bitterest lessons, but often﻿—and this seems most natural﻿—it is the peaceful souls who have suffered little to whom this crown of continuance is given. Catherine Vernon belonged to the last class. If her youth had not been altogether happy, there had been fewer sorrows and still fewer struggles in her life. She had gone along peacefully, her own mistress, nobody making her afraid, no one to be anxious about, no one dear enough to rend her heart. Most people who have gone through the natural experiences of life are of opinion with the Laureate, that it is

“Better to have loved and lost

Than never to have loved at all.”

===Chinese===

弗农苑

这些事，都发生在本故事开篇之前的许多年。凯瑟琳·弗农已成了老妇人——至少六十五岁了；您乐意，尽可以叫她老妇人。这四个字，有时指年岁的极处、衰朽与枯竭；有时却指一段更温软、更沉静的中年——一段可爱的秋天，一切官能还留着力量，却褪尽了棱角，宽容与基督的仁爱替代了一切批评的刻薄与见解的严峻。这样美的年纪，有时落在饱尝人生苦难、学尽其最苦课程的人头上；可更多的——这也最自然——这顶延续的王冠，加给的是那些受苦不多、心气平和的人。凯瑟琳·弗农属于后一类。她的青春纵然不曾全然快乐，一生里的悲伤却少，争斗更少。她一路安安稳稳走过来，自己做自己的主，没有人叫她惧怕，没有叫她牵挂的人，没有亲到能撕裂她心的人。凡是经历过人生常态的人，多半都同那位桂冠诗人一个意见，说是

“宁可爱过而失去，
胜过从未爱过。”

===Original===

But then we do not allow the other people to speak who know the other side of the question. If love brings great happiness it brings many woes. Catherine Vernon was like Queen Elizabeth, a dry tree﻿—while other women had sons and daughters. But when the hearts of the mothers were torn with anxiety, she went free. She had the good of other people’s children in a wonderful degree, but it was impossible she could have the harm of them﻿—for those whom she took to were the good children, as was natural, the elect of this world. Her life had been full of exertion and occupation since that night when Rule called upon her at the Grange and set all the world of her being in movement. What flagging and loneliness might have been hers﻿—what weariness and longing had ended at that time. Since then how much she had found to do! The work of a successful man of business increased, yet softened by all the countless nothings that make business for a woman, had filled her days. She was an old maid, to be sure, but an old maid who never was alone. Her house had been gay with young friends and tender friendship. She had been the first love of more girls than she could count. By the time she was sixty-five she was a sort of amateur grandmother in numbers of young households. A woman with plenty of money, with a handsome, cheerful house, and a happy disposition, she had﻿—at least since her youth was over﻿—never had occasion to remember the want of those absorbing affections which bind a married woman within her own circle. The children of the barren in her case were more than those of any wife. If ever in her heart she said to herself, like Matthew in the poem﻿—

“Many love me, yet by none

Am I enough beloved,”

===Chinese===

只是我们从不许知道事情另一面的人开口。爱若带来大福，也带来许多灾。凯瑟琳·弗农同伊丽莎白女王一样，是一棵不结子的树——别的女人儿女成行。可当母亲们的心被忧焦撕碎时，她自由自在。旁人的孩子给她带来的好处多得惊人；害处却不可能落到她身上——因为被她看中的，自然都是好孩子，是这世界的选民。自鲁尔那晚到格兰奇登门、把她整个生命的世界搅动起来之后，她的一生便充满了出力与事务。原本可能归她的委顿与孤寂——怎样的疲惫与渴望，都在那时了结了。打那以后，她有多少事可做！一个成功生意人的事业日见其多，又被女人营生里那无数数不清的琐碎软化着，填满了她的时日。她是个老小姐，不假；却是个从不孤单的老小姐。她的宅子里有年轻的朋友、温柔的交情，快快活活。她做过初恋对象的姑娘，多得她自己也数不清。到六十五岁上，她已是许许多多年轻人家里的一个业余祖母。一个钱财充足、宅子漂亮爽朗、性情快乐的女人——至少青春过去之后——从不曾有机会想起自己缺了什么：缺那种把做妻子的拴在小圈子里的、摄人的恩爱。她的孩子——不孕者的孩子——比哪个妻子的都多。倘若她心里也曾像诗里的马修那样对自己说——

“许多人爱我，可是没有一个人
爱我爱到足够”

===Original===

the sentiment never showed, and must have occurred only as Matthew’s did, in moods as evanescent as the clouds. Her face was not without lines, for that would be to say that it was without expression; nor did she look too young for her age: but her eye was not dim, nor her natural force abated. She had a finer colour than in her girlhood, though the red was not so smooth, but a little broken in her soft cheek. Her hair was white and beautiful, her figure ample, but graceful still. At sixty she had given up work, entering upon, she said, the Sabbatical period of her life. For the rest of her days she meant to keep Sunday, resting from her labours﻿—and indeed, with perhaps too close a following of the divine example for any human creature to venture upon, finding them very good.

It follows as a matter of course that she had found somebody to replace her in the bank. There were so many Vernons, that this was not very difficult to do. At least it was not difficult to find candidates for so important a post. Descendants of the brothers and sisters of the great John Vernon, who had first made the bank what it was, were plentiful, and from among them Catherine Vernon selected two hopeful young men to carry on her work. One of them, Harry Vernon, was descended from the daughter of the great John, who had married a relation and continued to bear the family name. The other went further back and traced his descent from a brother of that great John. The parents of these fortunate young men acquiesced with delight in the proposals she made to them. It was a certain fortune﻿—an established living at once﻿—far better than the chances of the Bar, or the Indian Civil Examinations, or Colorado, which had begun to be the alternative for young men. Indeed it was only Edward Vernon who had parents to be consulted. Harry had but a sister, who had come to live with him in the fine house which the last John, the one who had put the bank in such deadly peril, had built. Edward lived with Miss Vernon herself. Five years had passed since their inauguration as partners and managers, with very little change in their feelings towards the old cousin, who had done so much for them, and whom they called Aunt Catherine. She was Aunt Catherine to a great many people, but these three, who were the nearest to her in blood, were disposed to give themselves airs, and to punish intruders who presumed upon a fictitious relationship. They were to all appearance quite satisfactory young people, if perhaps not brilliant; and pious persons said that Miss Vernon had got her reward for her kindness to the poor, and her more than kindness to her poor relations. She was surrounded by those who were to her like children of her own. No mother could have had sons more respectful and devoted. Good and virtuous and kind children﻿—what could a woman have more?

接下来顺理成章：她在银行里找到了接替她的人。弗农家人口众多，这不难办。至少，为这样重要的职位寻候选人不难。老约翰·弗农——银行基业的第一位缔造者——他的兄弟姐妹的后代多得很；凯瑟琳·弗农从中挑了两个有出息的年轻人接她的班。其中一个，哈里·弗农，是老约翰女儿的后人：那位小姐嫁了一位亲戚，照旧姓弗农。另一位溯得更远，是老约翰一位兄弟的后人。这两位幸运青年的父母，喜滋滋地应允了她的提议。那是一份稳稳的家业——一进门就有一份现成的生计——远胜过律师业的前程、印度文官考试，或者科罗拉多——那时这些已渐渐成了年轻人的出路。其实只有爱德华·弗农有父母要商量；哈里只有一个妹妹，已搬来同他一起住在那座漂亮的宅子里——最后那位约翰、险些断送银行的那一位——盖的。爱德华就住在弗农小姐自己家里。他们就任合伙人兼经理至今五年了；对这位恩重如山、被他们唤作凯瑟琳姑妈的老表亲，情分几乎没有变过。凯瑟琳姑妈——许许多多人都这样叫她；可这三个血统上离她最近的人，却摆得起架子，敢惩戒那些偺用假亲假故、前来冒犯的人。外表上看，他们是十分叫人满意的青年，虽说未必才华出众；虔敬的人们说：弗农小姐得了报偿，报偿她待穷人的仁慈，报偿她待穷亲戚的、超出仁慈的厚意。她被一群人围着，于她如同亲生儿女。做母亲的，儿子再恭顺、再尽心也不过如此了。又好、又有德、又仁慈的孩子们——一个女人还能要什么？

Perhaps this was rather a flattering and ideal statement of the case; but at all events one of the young men satisfied all Miss Vernon’s requirements, and they were both steady-going, fine young fellows, paying every attention to business, keeping everything going. Ellen perhaps was not quite so satisfactory. She was young and headstrong, and not sure that Catherine Vernon was all that people made her out to be. There was nothing wonderful in this. To hear one person forever applauded is more likely than anything else to set an impatient mind against that person﻿—and Ellen kept her old cousin at arm’s length, and showed her little affection. Nobody could doubt that this must have vexed Miss Vernon, but she took it with wonderful calm.

“Your sister does not like me,” she said to Harry; “never mind, she is young, and she will know better one day.”

“You must not think so,” Harry said. “Ellen is foolish and headstrong, but she has a very good heart.”

Catherine Vernon nodded a little and shook her head.

“It is not a heart,” she said, “that is disposed towards me. But never mind; she will think better of it one day.”

Thus you will see that Miss Vernon escaped from the worst, and had the best, of motherhood. What a bitterness to her heart would this alienation have been, had Ellen been her child! but as the troublesome girl was not her child in reality, the unkindness vexed her in a very much less degree. She was able to think of the boys, who were so good, without being disturbed by the image of the girl, who was not so good. And so all things went on serenely, and the years went by, gentle, unremarkable, tranquil years.

===Chinese===

这番话说得也许恭维了些、理想了些；可无论如何，两个青年里有一个完全合乎弗农小姐的一切要求，两个也都是脚踏实地的好青年，事事上心，处处照转。埃伦也许不那么叫人满意。她年轻，倔强，拿不准凯瑟琳·弗农是不是真像众人捧的那样。这原不足为奇。一个人听人夸个没完，最容易起不耐烦的反感——埃伦同老表亲保持距离，不露多少亲情。谁都看得出这必定叫弗农小姐恼；可她受下来，平静得出奇。

“你妹妹不喜欢我，”她对哈里说；“不要紧，她还年轻，总有一天会明白。”

“您可别这样想。”哈里说。“埃伦又傻又倔，可她心肠很好。”

凯瑟琳·弗农略点了点头，又摇了摇头。

“那颗心，”她说，“不向我这边偏。不过不要紧；总有一天她会回心转意。”

由此可见，弗农小姐躲过了做母亲的最坏处，得了做母亲的最好处。倘若埃伦是她亲生的，这样的疏远于她的心将是何等苦楚！可这个叫人头疼的姑娘并非她亲生，这点冷淡，恼她的程度便轻得多。她想起那两个好儿子时，不必叫那个不大好的姑娘的影子搅扰。于是一切静静地进行，年复一年——温和的、无声无息的、平静的年头。

Several years before this, before indeed the young people had entered into her life, the old house, called the Heronry, came into Miss Vernon’s hands. It was at some distance on the same side of the Common, but a little further out towards the country than the Grange﻿—a large old redbrick house, in the midst of a thin but lofty group of trees. Though it was so near the town, there was something forlorn in it, standing out against the west, the tall trees dark against the light, the irregular outline of the old house flush against the sky, for it was a flat country, no hills or undulations, but everything that was tall enough showing direct against the horizon in a way that was sometimes very impressive. This great old house Miss Vernon made a curious use of. It contained a multitude of rooms, not any very large except that which occupied the centre of the area, a sort of hall, with a great staircase going out of it. From the moment it came into her hands, she made, everybody thought, a toy of the Heronry. She divided it into about half a dozen compartments, each with a separate entrance. It was very cleverly done, so as not to interfere in any way with the appearance of the place. The doors were not new and unsightly, but adapted with great care, some of them being windows a little enlarged. What was it for? All kinds of rumours ran about the town. It was some sort of a convent which she was going to institute, a community of an apostolical kind, a sisterhood, a hospital, a set of almshouses. Some went so far as to call it Catherine Vernon’s Folly. She spent a great deal of money upon it, elaborating her whim, whatever it might be. It was fitted up with apparatus for warming, which would make the dwellers in it independent of fires, people said, and this looked like a hospital everybody allowed. There was no end to the conveniences, the comforts of the place. The old-fashioned gardens were put in order, and the greatest trouble taken to make the old pool﻿—which had got the place its name, and where it was said that herons had actually been seen in the lifetime of some old inhabitants﻿—wholesome and without prejudice to the health of the house. The pool itself was very weird, and strange to be so near the dwelling of ordinary life.

早在此前好几年——其实还在那两个年轻人进她生活之前——那座叫鹭苑的老宅，落到了弗农小姐手里。它在公地同一侧的稍远处，比格兰奇更朝乡下去一点——一座红砖的老宅子，大，立在一丛稀疏而高拔的树中间。离城这样近，它却有一股荒凉气：朝西峙立，高树衬着天光显得黑，老宅不规则的轮廓平贴着天——这一带是平原，没有山峦起伏，凡是够高的东西都直直衬在天际线上，有时颇具撼人之势。对这座偌大的老宅，弗农小姐的用法很古怪。它有许多房间，都不很大，只中央一间占地居中，像个大厅，一道大楼梯从里面上去。宅子一到她手里，照众人的说法，她就把鹭苑当成了玩具。她把它分作大约六个单元，各有各的门户。分得极巧，全不损那地方的观瞻。门不是新装刺眼的那种，而是精心改制的，有几扇本是窗子，略放大而成。作什么用？满城流言四起。说她要办一座女修道院，一个使徒式的社团，一个修女会，一座医院，一排济贫院。有人索性叫它“凯瑟琳·弗农的荒唐”。她往上面花了许多钱，把她的奇想——不管是什么奇想——琢磨得精益求精。宅里装了暖气设备，据说住的人可以不靠火炉；人人都承认，这像一座医院。那地方的便利、舒适，数不胜数。老式园子收拾停当；又大费周章，把那口老池塘——宅子得名于它，据说有些老居民这辈子还真在塘上见过苍鹭——弄得卫生，于宅中人的健康无害。池塘本身非常奇异：离寻常人家这样近，却有这般荒古之气。

It lay in the centre of the clump of trees which had once been a wood, and which round it had grown tall and bare, with clumps of foliage on the top, and straight, long stems mounting to the sky, and shining in long lines of reflection in the still, dark water. Several gaunt and ghostly old firs were among them, which in the sunset were full of colour, but in twilight stood up black and wild against the clear, pale sky. This pool was about as far from the Grange as Miss Vernon could walk with comfort, and it was a walk she was very fond of taking on summer nights. The Common lay between the house and the town; beyond it spread the long levels of the flat country. In the summer all was golden about, with gorse and patches of purple heather, and the abundant growth of wild, uncultivated nature. What did Catherine Vernon mean to do with this house? That was what all Redborough wanted to know.

By the time at which this story properly begins, Redborough had been acquainted for years with Miss Vernon’s intentions; they were indeed no longer intentions, but had been carried out. The Heronry had changed its name, if not formally, yet in familiar parlance, throughout all the neighbourhood, and was called the Vernonry even by people who did not know why. The six dwellings which had been contrived so cleverly were all occupied by relations and dependents of the family, members of the house of Vernon, or connections of the same. They made a little community among themselves, but not the community of a sisterhood or a hospital. It was said that they had their little internal feuds and squabbles, as people living so close together are always supposed to have, but they were sufficiently well bred, or sufficiently in awe of their cousin and patroness, to keep these quarrels decorously to themselves. How far they were indebted to her for their living, as well as their lodging, nobody knew, which was not for want of many a strenuous investigation on the part of the neighbourhood; but the inmates of the Vernonry were clever enough to keep their own counsel on a matter which involved their own consequence and credit. Disagreeable things were indeed said about “genteel almshouses,” and “poor relations,” when it first became a question in Redborough about calling on the new residents. But, as it turned out, they were all persons of pretensions, expecting to be called upon by the county, and contemptuous of the townspeople. Five of the six apartments into which the old house had been divided were occupied, when Redborough was startled by the extraordinary intelligence that the last and best had been reserved for no less interesting an inmate than Mrs. John Vernon, she who had left the town in circumstances so painful. John Vernon, the unfortunate or the culpable, who had all but ruined the bank, and left it to its ruin, had died abroad. His wife’s marriage settlement had secured their income, but he had spent as much as it was possible to spend of that, and forestalled every penny that he could manage to forestall.

到本故事正式开场的时候，雷德伯勒对弗农小姐的用意已熟知多年；那早已不是用意，而是既成的事实。鹭苑改了名——纵然不是正式改的，在左近的家常话里，它处处被叫作弗农苑；连不知底细的人也这样叫。那巧妙隔出的六套住处，住的全是这一家的亲戚与依附者：弗农家的人，或沾亲带故的人。他们自成一个小社会，却不是修女会或医院的社会。据说他们内部也有小小的宿怨口角——住得这样挤的人家照例被想象成这样；但他们教养够好，或者说对这位表亲兼恩主敬畏够深，把这些争执体体面面地关在自己门里。他们在生计上、不止在住处上受她多少恩惠，没有人知道——这并非左近没有下力气打探；只是弗农苑里的人够精明，在关涉自家体面与信誉的事上守口如瓶。当初雷德伯勒议起该不该拜会这批新住户时，“上流济贫院”“穷亲戚”之类的难听话确实说过。可后来一看，他们个个是有身份的人，等着郡里的乡绅登门，而瞧不起镇上人。老宅隔出的六套宅子占了五套；这时雷德伯勒被一桩惊人的消息震动了：最后也是最好的一套，留给了一位非同小可的住户——约翰·弗农太太，当年在那样难堪的境况里离开本镇的那一位。约翰·弗农——那个不幸的、或者说有罪的、险些毁了银行又撒手任它去毁的人——死在了国外。他妻子的婚产契约保住了他们的进项；可他花掉了那份进项里花得到的每一个子儿，又把预支得到的每一个铜板都预先支尽。

His debts were such that his widow’s income was sadly crippled by the necessity of paying them, which it was said she would not herself have seen so clearly but for the determined way in which it was taken up by her child, a very young girl, born long after the catastrophe, but one who was apparently of the old stock, with a head for business, and a decision of character quite unusual in a child. Mrs. John’s return caused a great sensation in Redborough. She was very well connected, and there could be no question on anybody’s mind as to the propriety of calling on a woman who was aunt to Sir John Southwood, and first cousin to Lady Hartingale. How she could like to come back there, to live within sight of her own beautiful house, and to be indebted for shelter to Catherine Vernon, was a much more difficult matter to understand. But as everybody said, that of course was Mrs. John’s own concern. If she could make up her mind to it, certainly nobody else had any call to interfere.

他欠下的债，使遗孀的进项因偿债之故伤残不堪；据说，若不是她那个孩子毅然担了起来，她自己原看不了这样清楚。那孩子是个很小的姑娘，大祸之后许久才出生，却显然是老弗农家的种：有一副做生意的头脑，有一副孩子里罕见的决断。约翰太太的归来，在雷德伯勒引起大轰动。她姻亲显赫；要不要登门拜会一位约翰·索斯伍德爵士的姨母、哈廷格尔夫人的嫡亲表妹——这体统问题，人人心里都没有疑问。她怎么甘心回这里来，住在一抬眼就望见自己那座漂亮宅子的地方，靠凯瑟琳·弗农遮蔽风雨——这却难懂得多。可正如众人所说：那当然是约翰太太自己的事。她自己拿得定主意，别人自然无权过问。

But what a change it was from the fatal day when poor Mr. Rule, all anxious and miserable, was shown in by the curious servant to the costly drawing-room in which John Vernon’s wife, in her spotted muslin, sat ignorant of business, but confident and satisfied in her good fortune and in the certainty that all would go well with her! Poor lady! she had learned some few things since that day, but never had grasped the mystery of her downfall, nor known how it was that everything had collapsed in a moment, tumbling down like a house of cards. She had not, indeed, tried to understand at that terrible time when it all burst upon her﻿—when the fact that she had to leave her house, and that her furniture was going to be sold in spite of all her indignant protestations, compelled her understanding, such as it was, into the knowledge that her husband was ruined. She had too much to do then, in crying, in packing, in appealing to heaven and earth to know what she had done to be so cruelly used, and in trying to make out how she was to travel, to be able to face the problem how it had all come about. And after she went away the strangeness and novelty of everything swept thought out of her mind, if, indeed, it ever entered there at all. Perhaps it was only after that life was over, and when widowed and growing old she came back to the strange little house which Catherine Vernon had written to offer her, that she remembered once more to ask herself the question. Or, perhaps, even then it was not she who asked it, but Hester, who, greatly excited, with eyes large with curiosity and interest, clinging to her mother’s arm in a way she had, which looked like dependence, and was control, went all over the new-old place with her, drinking in information. Hester led her mother wherever she pleased, holding her arm embraced in her own two clasped hands. It was her way of holding the helm. She was a tall girl of fourteen when she came to the Heronry, outgrowing all her frocks, and all her previous knowledge, and thirsting to understand everything. She had never been in England before, though she prided herself on being an English girl. She knew scarcely anything about her family, why it was they lived abroad, what was their history, or by what means they were so severed from all relationships and friendships.

同那要命的一天相比，何等的变化！那天，可怜的鲁尔先生满心焦灼凄惶，被那好奇的仆人引进那间华贵的客厅；客厅里，约翰·弗农的妻子穿着斑点薄纱裙坐着，生意一窍不通，却对自己的好运、对万事必将顺遂自信而满足。可怜的夫人！那天以后她多少学会了几样事；可她从没有抓住她败落的谜，从没有明白这一切怎么会在一瞬之间塌下来，像纸牌搭的房子一样倒掉。她也不曾真去弄懂——在祸事劈头砸下的可怕时刻，她没有去懂：不得不离开宅子、家具不顾她愤愤抗议仍要拍卖——这些事实把她那份悟性逼着领进“丈夫毁了”这个认识里。那时她要忙的太多：哭啊，收拾行李啊，呼天抢地问自己造了什么孽受这样的刻薄啊，盘算旅途怎么走啊——哪里顾得上面对“这一切怎么来的”这道题。她走之后，样样新奇生疏，把思考从她心里一扫而光——倘若思考进过她心里的话。也许，要等那段生活过完、她孀居而渐老、回到凯瑟琳·弗农来信相赠的这座古怪小宅时，她才又记起问自己这个问题。也许，连那时问的也不是她，而是赫斯特。赫斯特兴奋万分，眼睛因好奇与兴味睁得老大，挽着母亲的胳膊——她挽人有她自己的一套，看似依偎，实为掌舵——同母亲把这新旧的宅子走遍，把种种见闻一口口吸进去。赫斯特要母亲去哪儿，母亲就去哪儿：她双手抱拢，箍着母亲那条胳膊。那是她掌舵的方式。她来鹭苑时是个十四岁的高挑姑娘，个头蹿出了所有的连衣裙，心智蹿出了先前的一切见识，渴着要什么都懂。她从没有到过英国，却自豪自己是个英国姑娘。她对自己的家族几乎一无所知：他们为什么住在国外，他们有过怎样的经历，又怎样同一切亲戚故旧断绝了往来。
