“我是什么年纪都算得的，”老上校说，“因为我什么都记得。明天我要同亚利克去放我的船，快活得像个小孩子（那是只顶好的小船，真的会航行，凯瑟琳，你要是有兴致的话我可以告诉你），回头我再陪一位年轻小姐在公地上散步，谈谈诗，谈谈爱情。”

“呸，上校！”他的老伴说；“不过他那些胡话当不得真，赫斯特。”

“要是爱情是胡话，诗也是胡话，那么她跟我情愿为它们上火刑柱。”上校说。“今晚咱们走远一点，亲爱的，好叫那位老太太明白她错得多厉害。”

“我不能再祝您一件更称心的事了，上校——现在我该走了。”老鲁尔前言不搭后语地说。

凯瑟琳从她插进来救赫斯特的那一刻起——没人道谢，也没人领情——便一直坐着出神；这时趁着老书记员起身，她也站起来，先他一步走出去，她那身华贵的黑绸裙子扫着地，窸窣作响。这些上了年纪的人在一旁一衬，她显得容光焕发，精明干练，年轻。老两口从窗口望着鲁尔满面红光、心满意足地扶她上马车。

“她的样子还年轻，再干一场也够。”摩根上校站在窗前，手里拿着干活用的胶水瓶，说。

“哦，上校！”他的老伴说，“可是钱在哪儿呢？”摇着她苍老的头。

赫斯特在两位老人身后，从两颗苍老的头颅中间张望出去，脸色发白——又是关切，又是敌意，又是着迷。凯瑟琳一在跟前，她就再想不起别人，虽然她浑身的本能都武装起来同她作对。两位老人之间来往的这几句话，在她听来像一门外国话。它们是什么意思，她丝毫也捉摸不出。

这时候，凯瑟琳对她这位卸任比她还晚的老首相叮嘱了一句。

“你险些叫那孩子心疼，”她说。“当着她的面小心，别再说什么。她永远不必知道她父亲丢下职守的事。这孩子荣誉感敏锐，知道了要伤她的。”

“她不像他的女儿，”书记员说，“也不像那位可怜的太太的。她是纯粹的弗农老家血脉。”

===Original===

“Do you think so?” said Catherine, indifferently. “I rather dislike her than otherwise; but I would not do the child any harm.” And then the fat horses put themselves in motion, and she gave a smile and a bow to all her retainers and worshippers﻿—and the Miss Vernon-Ridgways drew away from Mrs. John’s window, where as usual they had been watching Catherine, as she, amid all these visible signs of her wealth and sovereignty, disappeared from their eyes.

“I suppose, Captain Morgan,” said Hester that evening, when she walked out with him as usual, “that Cousin Catherine was young once?”

It seemed an absurd question, but it was put with the utmost gravity; and Hester knew what she meant, as perhaps the reader will too.

“About your age, my dear,” the captain said, promptly, “and not at all unlike you.”

“Like me!”

“You think you are very different now, but there is not much more difference than that of years. She was the same kind of girl as you are﻿—masterful﻿—very sure that her own way was the right one﻿—obstinate as a mule in her mind, but not so difficult to move by the heart.”

“Am I all that?” said Hester, wondering; “not in some things, for I am never sure that I am right﻿—or anyone else﻿—except you, perhaps. No, it is the other way, quite the other way! I am very sure that I am wrong, and everyone else﻿—except you.”

“A large rule and a small exception,” said the old man; “but it is the same thing. Catherine was rich and had everything her own way. You are﻿—in the midst of a poor community where we can have nothing our own way. And at your age you can’t discriminate any more than she could at hers.”

“Then does it come to this, that money is everything?” asked the disciple with some bitterness, but without, as may be supposed, the slightest intention of accepting the master’s teaching on this point.

Captain Morgan made no reply. What he said was﻿—

“I should like to interest you in Catherine, my dear; all that happened, you know, before we came here, while we were busy with our own life, my wife and I; but I have put this and that together since. Catherine was, as people say, crossed in love, notwithstanding her wealth and all her qualities. So far as I can make out, the man preferred a woman that could not hold the candle to her; not so pretty, not so clever, altogether inferior. That must be rather a blow to a woman!”

===Chinese===

“您这样想吗？”凯瑟琳淡然说。“我与其说喜欢她，不如说不喜欢；可我无意伤害这孩子。”于是那几匹肥马迈开步子，她朝她所有的臣仆和崇拜者们微笑颔首——弗农-里奇韦两位小姐从约翰太太的窗前退开，方才她们照例在那里望着凯瑟琳，望着她在这一切财富与威权的明显标记簇拥之下，从她们眼里消失。

“我猜，摩根上校，”当晚赫斯特照例陪他散步时说，“凯瑟琳表姐也有过年轻的时候吧？”

这话问得似乎荒唐，却是板着极正经的面孔问的；赫斯特自己明白这话的意思，说不定读者也明白。

“同你差不多年纪，亲爱的，”上校立刻说，“而且同你并非不像。”

“像我！”

“你如今觉得自己同她天差地远，其实相差也不过就是年岁的相差。她当年同你是同一类的姑娘——专断——十分拿得准自己的路数是对的——脑子犟得像头骡子，可要用感情打动她，倒并不怎样难。”

“我是这样吗？”赫斯特诧异地说；“在某些事上可不是，因为我从来拿不准自己对——也拿不准别人对——除了您，也许。不，正相反，恰恰相反！我十分拿得准自己错了，别人也都错了——除了您。”

“一条大规矩带一个小小的例外，”老人说；“可道理是一样的。凯瑟琳有钱，事事随心。你呢——处在一群穷人中间，我们谁也不能事事随心。而在你这个年纪，你同她在她那个年纪一样，分不出这里的分别。”

“那么归结起来，钱就是一切了？”这位门徒带着几分辛酸问，不过可以想见，她丝毫没有在这一点上接受老师教导的意思。

摩根上校没有回答。他说的是——

“我很想叫你对凯瑟琳发生兴趣，亲爱的；那些事都是在我们来这儿以前发生的，那时我同我太太正忙着过自己的日子；可后来我把这桩那桩拼凑起来了。凯瑟琳，如人们所说，在爱情上失过意——不管她有钱，也不管她有那些长处。照我推断得出的，那个男人挑了一个给她提鞋都不配的女人；没那么俊，没那么聪明，样样不及她。这对一个女人想必是相当重的一击！”

===Original===

“A blow! What sort of a woman would she be that cared for a man who did not care for her?”

This somewhat inarticulate sentiment Hester delivered with an indignant blush and flashing eyes.

“That is all very fine, my dear; but you are too clearheaded to be taken in by it,” said the captain. “A woman might not show it, perhaps. I have no reason to suppose that Catherine showed it. But you must remember that a woman is not a woman in the abstract, but Catherine or Hester as the case may be, and liable to everything that humanity is liable to; and she would be a poor creature indeed if she were incapable of falling in love generously, as a man is supposed to do.”

“I don’t know what you mean by generously!”

“Ah, but you do﻿—none better. Something however occurred after, much worse than his preference of another woman. The man turned out to be an unworthy man.”

Hester had been following every word with breathless interest. She grew quite pale, her lips dropped apart, her eyes blazed out of the whiteness of her face upon her old instructor. He went on without taking note of this change,

“I should think for my part that there cannot be any such blow as that. Don’t you remember we agreed it was the secret of all Hamlet’s tragedy? It is the tragedy of the world, my dear. I told the old woman we were going to talk of love and poetry. You see I was right.”

“But﻿—Catherine?”

Hester was, as became a girl, far too much interested in the individual case to be able to stray to the abstract, and in fact she had only assented to her mentor’s theory in respect to Hamlet, not having begun such investigations for herself.

“Ay, Catherine. Well, that is just what happened to her, my dear. The man first showed that he had no appreciation of herself, which we will allow must have wounded her; and then after, when that was all over, proved himself unworthy, dishonourable﻿—in short, what the young men call a cad.”

“Who was he?” asked Hester, in a low and awestricken tone.

Then Captain Morgan turned to look at her, apparently with some alarm; but his fears were quieted by her face. She had evidently no clue to who it was.

===Chinese===

“一击！一个在乎一个并不在乎她的男人的女人，算得什么女人？”

这句意思含混的话，赫斯特是涨红着脸、目光灼灼地说出来的。

“这话固然漂亮，亲爱的；可你脑子太清楚，骗不过你自己。”上校说。“一个女人也许不露出来。我没有理由设想凯瑟琳露过。可你得记住，女人不是抽象的女人，而是具体的凯瑟琳或赫斯特，凡人性难免的她也一概难免；倘若她不能像一个男人应该的那样豁达地堕入情网，那她倒真是个可怜虫了。”

“我不懂您说的‘豁达’是什么意思！”

“啊，你懂——再没有谁比你更懂了。不过后来又出了一桩事，比他看中另一个女人糟得多。那男人原来是个不肖之徒。”

赫斯特一直屏息听着每一个字。她脸都白了，嘴唇张开，一双眼睛从惨白的脸上灼灼地照着她的老导师。他没有留意这变化，径直说下去——

“要我说，天底下再没有那样的打击了。你可记得我们说好过，那是哈姆雷特全部悲剧的秘密？这是世界的悲剧，亲爱的。我告诉老婆子说，我们要谈爱情和诗来着。你看我说对了吧。”

“可是——凯瑟琳呢？”

赫斯特到底是个女孩子，对具体的这个人太关切，顾不到抽象上去；其实她对导师关于哈姆雷特的理论，也不过是点头认可罢了，她自己还不曾动手做过这一类考究。

“是呀，凯瑟琳。唉，她遭的正是这个，亲爱的。那男人先是露出他全不懂她的好处，这一层我们得承认，必定伤了她的心；随后，等那一段都过去了，他又证实了自己不肖、无耻——总而言之，是年轻人所谓的下流胚。”

“他是谁？”赫斯特问，声音又低又带着敬畏。

摩根上校于是回过头来看她，显出几分惊慌；可她的脸色使他把心放下了。她显然没有猜到那是谁。

===Original===

“I never knew the man,” he said quickly. “One has no wish to know anything about him. The interesting person is the woman in such a case. Here, Hester, you must be the teacher. Tell me, what would that discovery do to a girl, a daring, masterful spirit like you?”

“Oh, captain, I am not daring or masterful,” cried the girl clasping her hands; “don’t you know it is cruel to call me so﻿—I that can do nothing, that am only like a straw tossing on the water, carried the way I would not. If I were masterful, I would go away from here. I would do something for myself.”

“All that is no answer to my question,” the old captain said.

Hester was used to follow his leading at a touch. There was a kind of mesmerism in the effect he had upon her.

“I cannot tell,” she said in a low and hurried voice. “I don’t see: it would turn all the world wrong. It would﻿—But,” she added, collecting herself, “she would throw him away from her like a dead thing. He would be dead. She would think of him no more. Unworthy! One shakes one’s self free﻿—one is done with that!”

“Look again,” said the old man, with a half smile, shaking his head.

“I don’t wish to look again. Is not that enough? I suppose it would make her very unhappy. She would struggle, she would try to find excuses. Oh, Captain Morgan, don’t press me so! I suppose everything would turn round and round. There would seem nothing to stand on, nothing to look up to, the skies would all whirl and the solid ground. It makes my head swim to think of it,” the girl cried, covering her eyes with her hands.

“That was how it was with Catherine, so far as I know. She had to exert herself to save the bank, and that saved her.”

“Had he anything to do with the bank?” she asked quickly.

===Chinese===

“我从来不认识那个人，”他急忙说。“谁也不愿意知道他的事。这样的案子，叫人关心的是女方。来，赫斯特，这回该你当先生了。告诉我，那样的发现，对一个女孩子——一个像你这样大胆、专断的人——会起什么作用？”

“哦，上校，我并不大胆，也不专断，”姑娘扣紧双手喊道；“您不知道这样说多么残忍——我这个人什么都做不成，不过像一根草在水上打转，被冲往我不肯去的方向。我若是专断的，我就离开这儿了。我要自己去成就点什么。”

“这些全都答非所问。”老上校说。

赫斯特素来一点就通，随着他的引导走。他对她的影响里有一种催眠的力量。

“我说不上来，”她声音又低又急促地说。“我看不见：它会叫整个世界都翻转。它会——可是，”她定了定神，又补一句，“她会把他从身边甩开，像甩开一件死物。他就死了。她再也不会想起他。不肖之徒！抖一抖身子就挣脱了——同那个一刀两断了！”

“再想一想。”老人半笑着，摇了摇头。

“我不愿再想。这还不够吗？我想这会叫她非常痛苦。她会挣扎，她会设法替他找借口。哦，摩根上校，别再逼我了！我想一切都会团团地转。会像立脚没有地、仰望没有天，天空打旋，实地也打旋。想一想都叫我头晕。”姑娘喊道，用手捂住了眼睛。

“凯瑟琳的情形，据我所知，正是这样。她不得不振作起来救银行，那件事救了她。”

“他同银行有过牵连吗？”她急忙问。

===Original===

“My dear, I tell you I was not here at the time,” said the wary old man. “I had no knowledge of the circumstances. I never wish to know who he was, lest perhaps I should fail in charity towards him. It is Catherine I want you to think of. The bank troubles came afterwards, and she had to get up and put her shoulder to the wheel, which saved her. But do you think the world ever looked the same after? Hamlet would never have discovered what traitors those young courtiers were, if his mother had not turned out a fraud, and his love a delusion﻿—at least that is my opinion. The wonder is, he did not misdoubt Horatio too. That is what I should have done if it had been me. But there is the good of genius, Hester; the Master who knew everything knew better. Catherine had a sort of honest Horatio in old Rule, and she had that work to do, which was the best thing for her. But you may be sure the world was all dissolving views, and nothing solid in it for years to come.”

Hester, after the shock of the realisation which had been forced upon her, as to what the result of such a calamity would be, felt exhausted and sick at heart, as if all her strength had been worn out.

“Why did you want me to know this?” she said at last. “I see no signs of it in her. She looks so triumphant, as if nothing had ever happened or could happen. She sees through everybody and laughs at them, as if all their lies could never touch her. Oh, she sees very well how they lie, but is never angry, only laughs; is that the way to make one love her? And she does not know the false from the true,” the girl cried with an access of indignation. “She considers us all the same.”

===Chinese===

“亲爱的，我告诉你，那时我不在这里，”机警的老人说。“内情我一概不知。我也从不愿知道他是谁，惟恐自己对他存不了宽厚。我要你想的是凯瑟琳。银行的风波是后来的事，她只得挺身出来，肩膀抵住车轮，那救了她。可你以为世界在她眼里还是从前的世界吗？哈姆雷特倘若不是母亲成了骗局、爱情成了幻影，他永远不会发现那些年轻朝臣是什么奸贼——至少我是这个意见。奇怪的是，他竟没有连霍拉旭也疑上。换了我，我准会。可是天才自有天才的好处，赫斯特；那位无所不知的主知道得更清楚。凯瑟琳有一个老鲁尔，算她忠实的霍拉旭；又有那件工作可做，那是于她最好的事。可你尽可能定，此后多少年里，世界在她眼里全是一幅幅溶化的幻景，再没有一样坚实的东西。”

赫斯特经了这一场——被人硬按着领教了这样一场灾祸会结出什么果子——之后，只觉得心力交瘁，心里发呕，浑身的力气像都用尽了。

“您为什么要我知道这个呢？”她终于说。“我在她身上看不出一点影子。她那副神气那么得意洋洋，仿佛什么都不曾发生过、再没有什么能发生。她看穿每一个人，笑话他们，仿佛他们所有的谎话永远沾不到她身上。哦，人家撒谎她看得清清楚楚，可从不生气，只管笑；这能叫人爱她吗？再说她分不清假和真，”姑娘一阵愤激地喊道。“她把我们大家看成一个样。”

===Original===

“No﻿—no﻿—no﻿—no,” said the old man, patting her arm, but he did not press her any further. He had said as much as he wanted to say. They went further than usual over the Common as he had threatened to his wife, and as they returned the old captain owned himself fatigued and took Hester’s arm. “You must be my great-grandchild in the spirit,” he said. “We had a little girl once, my wife and I. I have often fancied her grown up and married and having children in her turn. Oh, I am a great dreamer and an old fool. You remember Elia’s dream children, and then Tennyson, though he was not old enough to know anything about it, making the unborn faces shine beside the never-lighted fire. These poets make fools of us all, Hester. They know everything without any way to know it. I fancy you are one of little Mary’s grandchildren. She must be as old as Catherine Vernon, though age, we may suppose, doesn’t count where she is.”

“You never told me about *her*.”

“There was nothing to tell,” he said cheerfully. “Her mother cries still if you speak of little Mary, but not I. It would have been a great thing for us if we could have kept her, but she would have married I suppose, and her husband might not have pleased me. I have thought of that. She would have been taken in probably, and brought us some man I could not put up with, though the children might have been an addition. I dare say she would have turned out a soft, innocent creature, taken in all round, something like your mother, Hester. You are tempted to despise that, you clever ones, but it is a great mistake.”

“Oh, Captain Morgan, mother is taken in, as you say, because she thinks everybody true﻿—but she is true always.”

“*Always!*” said the old man with fervour, “and far happier because she does not find it out. My wife is the same. It is such souls as these that keep the world steady. We should all tumble to pieces if the race was made up of people like Catherine Vernon and you.”

“I wish you would not say Catherine Vernon and me!” said Hester passionately; “there is no likeness, none at all﻿—none at all!”

===Chinese===

“不——不——不——不。”老人拍拍她的胳膊说，不再逼她了。他想说的都说到了。他们照他对老伴吓唬的那样，在公地上比平常走得更远；回来时老上校认了输，说乏了，挽起赫斯特的胳膊。“你做我的重孙女，是精神上的，”他说。“我同我太太从前有过一个小女孩。我常常想她长大了、出嫁了、又生儿育女的光景。哦，我是个顶爱做梦的老糊涂。你记得伊利亚梦里的那些孩子吧；还有丁尼生——他那年纪本来还够不上懂得这些——叫那些未出世的笑脸在永不点燃的炉火旁边发亮。这些诗人把我们全都变成傻子，赫斯特。他们没有任何知道的门道，却什么都知道。我设想你就是小玛丽的外孙女中的一个。她如今该同凯瑟琳·弗农一般年纪了，虽说在人家那边，年纪想必是不算数的。”

“您从来没同我讲过*她*。”

“没有什么可讲的。”他愉快地说。“如今一提起小玛丽，她母亲还要哭，我可不。当初若留得住她，对我们自然是件天大的事；可她总归要嫁人的，她丈夫未必中我的意。这一层我想过。多半她要受人哄骗，给我们领回一个我容不下的男人来，虽说孩子们倒是添丁进口。我料想她日后是个软心肠、没心眼的人，四处受人哄，同你母亲差不多，赫斯特。你们这些聪明人禁不住要看不起这个，那就大错特错了。”

“哦，摩根上校，母亲是受人哄，如您所说，因为她把人人都当真的——可她自己永远是真的。”

“*永远！*”老人热烈地说，“而且因为她发现不了这一点，反倒快活得多。我太太也是一样。就是这样的灵魂撑着这世界不倒。世上若全成了凯瑟琳·弗农和你们这样的人，我们早就七零八落了。”

“我求您别再说‘凯瑟琳·弗农和我’了！”赫斯特激动地说；“没有一点相像，一点也没有——一点也没有！”

===Original===

But the old captain only laughed, and turned her attention to the sunset, which was lighting up all the western sky. The pines stood up against it like rigid black shadows, cut out against the golden light which was belted with flaming lines of crimson. Overhead the sky ascended in varying tints of daffodil and faint ethereal greenness up to the deep yet bright summer blue. The last gleams caught the yellow gorse upon the Common and turned every blossom into gold, and all the peaks of the Vernonry rose black against the radiance of the west.

“I wonder if the people *up there* have any hand in it?” said the old man. “I should like to think so. The old landscape painters, perhaps, that never had such colours to work with before. But in that case there would be nothing for me to do,” he added with a laugh, “unless it was some small post about the gunneries. I was always fond of my guns.”

To Hester this light suggestion, and the laugh with which it was accompanied, sounded profane. She shrank from anything which could take away the awe and mystery from death, just as the old man, who was so near the threshold, liked to familiarise himself with the thought of going over it, and still finding himself a recognisable creature there.

===Chinese===

可老上校只是笑，把她的注意力引到落日上去；落日正照亮整片西天。松树衬着天际挺立，像一道道僵直的黑影，剪影在金色光芒上，那金色又束着一道道猩红的火线。头顶上，天空由水仙黄、淡得近乎空灵的绿，一层层升上去，升到深沉而明亮的夏日蔚蓝。最后的光掠过公地上的金雀花，把每一朵都点成金子，弗农苑所有的尖顶都黑黑地立在西方的光焰之前。

“我纳闷，*那上头*的人手可不沾这个？”老人说。“我倒愿意这样想。也许是那些老风景画家，从前从没有过这样好的颜色供他们使唤。不过真那样，就没有什么留给我做的了，”他笑着补一句，“除非炮台上给我留个小差事。我一向喜欢我的炮。”

对赫斯特来说，这一句轻轻的玩笑、连同伴它的笑声，听着都近于亵渎。凡是会夺去死亡的敬畏和神秘的事物，她都畏缩不敢沾；而这位已经站在门槛边的老人，却喜欢把跨过门槛去、并且在那边仍旧做一个认得出来的自己这件事，想得熟熟的。

## X / 十
===Original===

A Lover

It was about this time that Hester became aware of a circumstance the most important that could possibly happen in a young woman’s life. There had been no opportunity for her to become acquainted with the emulations and rivalship of other girls. Girls there were none about the Vernonry, nor did they abound in the neighbourhood, in the class from which alone her mother’s visitors were chosen. Mrs. John, it has been said, belonged to a county family, a fact of which she was as proud as it is natural and becoming a woman should be. She did not altogether frown upon the few callers from the town who thought it only their duty to Miss Vernon, the most hospitable entertainer in the neighbourhood, to take a little notice of the pensioners, as the poor ladies at the Vernonry were called; but she did not encourage these benevolent visitors. “They are all ladies, and as good as any of us,” Mrs. Redfern had been heard to say, who was the mayor’s lady, and considered herself a leader of society; and it was a beautiful sight to see Mrs. John, in her old-fashioned dark room and simplest black gown, receiving with kind condescension, and endeavouring to set at her ease, this very fine lady, who considered herself to be paying the poor widow a quite undeserved honour. Mrs. John returned cards only in acknowledgment of Mrs. Redfern’s visit, and there the acquaintance ended. So that Hester lost altogether the opportunity of knowing how ordinary girls looked and talked, and what was the object of their ambition. She had not even, which may surprise some people, come to any conclusion whatever in respect to her own personal appearance. Sometimes indeed, it cannot be denied, she had looked up in the midst of a novel, where all the young persons in whom the reader was supposed to take any interest were beautiful, and asked herself vaguely, with a blush, feeling ashamed of the question, whether she was pretty. But partly she was ashamed to give the time necessary to the solution of the problem, and partly she had not the data upon which to form her conclusions. There was a beautiful girl in Redborough in a humble position, upon whose claims everybody was agreed, but she was a queenly creature, with dark hair and blue eyes, and features of the most exquisite regularity, to whom Hester could not flatter herself that she bore the slightest resemblance.

===Chinese===

情人

大约就在这个时候，赫斯特觉察到一件对于一个年轻女子的生命来说顶关紧要的大事。她从来没有机会见识别的姑娘们怎样争胜斗奇。弗农苑附近没有姑娘，左近一带、她母亲的访客单从那个阶层里挑——也没有多少。前面说过，约翰太太出身郡里人家，这件事她引以为荣，女人如此也是自然得体的。城里确有少数客人认为，对这一带顶好客的主人弗农小姐手下的食客们——弗农苑的穷太太们是这么被称呼的——多少照拂一下是自己的本分；约翰太太对这班善心的访客也不全然皱眉，可她并不鼓励。雷德芬太太——市长夫人，自命为一方的领袖——曾被人听见说：“她们都是大家闺秀，同我们哪一位都不差”；看着约翰太太，在她那间老式的暗屋子里、穿着顶朴素的黑裙，和颜悦色地接待这位极体面的太太、尽力叫她自在，真是好看的一幕；那位太太自觉是在赏给穷寡妇一份她全然不配的光荣。约翰太太只回拜了雷德芬太太一张名片，这番交情到此为止。于是赫斯特全然错过了知道寻常姑娘们怎样模样、怎样谈吐、她们的志向是什么的机会。她甚至——这也许叫有些人诧异——对自己的容貌也从没有得出过什么结论。的确，无可否认，有时她在一部小说中间抬起头来——书里凡是读者该关切关心的年轻人一概都是美人——红着脸、为这个问题羞愧，模模糊糊地问自己漂亮不漂亮。可她一方面羞于为解决这个问题花费工夫，一方面也没有据以下结论的材料。雷德伯勒有个出身微贱的美女，她的容貌人人公认；可她是位王后一般的人物，深色头发，蓝眼睛，五官端正精致到极处——赫斯特不能自欺，说自己同她有丝毫相像。

===Original===

Nor was she like Ellen Vernon, with her lovely fairness, her look of wax and confectionary. Hester was not ethereal at all. There was no smallness about her, though she was slim as became her age. “The springy motion in her gait,” the swift, light step which never tired, were beautiful in their way, and so was the eager outlook in her eyes, which seemed to contract and expand according to the degree of interest with which outside subjects moved them; but all this rather as exponents of the mind within than as merely physical features. Her hair had never grown long, not much longer indeed than was just necessary to twist into the knot behind which proved her to be grown up, and it remained full of curl and ready to break the smoothness of outline then thought necessary, on the smallest provocation. Her complexion was very variable, sometimes radiant with flutters of sudden colour, sometimes relapsing into a rose-tinted whiteness, more white than pale. Her features were not much to brag of; it was the play of prompt feeling in her face, the interest, the indignation, the pity, the perpetual change and vicissitude, that made it attractive, and on this point of course Hester could not judge. Seeing that her mouth was too large, and her nose too short, and her eyebrows too marked, she concluded that she was not pretty, and regretted it, though in her circumstances it mattered very little; her friends liked her just as well, whether or not; and she was never likely to produce the effect which the heroines in novels﻿—even though comparatively plain﻿—did produce. So she decided, with a little shame to think that she could have been disturbed about the matter, that it was not worth going into it further. All the same it is a pity, for the sake of young readers, that all the girls in novels, with so very rare exceptions﻿—and Jane Eyre, if not pretty, probably was less plain than she thought, and certainly was *agaçante*, which is much more effective﻿—should be beautiful and should have so much admiration and conquest. The girls who read are apt to wonder how it is that they have not the same fortune. Hester, for her part, had a fine scorn of feminine victories in this sort; they had never come within the possibilities of her lot.

她也不像埃伦·弗农那种可爱的白皙，那种蜡与糖果塑造的模样。赫斯特全然不是空灵的一路。她身上没有小巧可言，虽然照她的年纪是苗条的。她步态里那种“富于弹性的轻快”，那种不知疲倦的轻捷急步，自有其美；她眼里那种急切的顾盼也美——那双眼睛似乎随着外界事物打动她的兴味之深浅，一收一放；可这一切之所以美，多半是作为内里心灵的表征，而不是单纯的形貌。她的头发从来没有留长过，实在也就比挽成一个髻——证明她已是成人——所需的长度长不了多少；满头卷曲，一受顶轻微的扰动，就要破掉那时认为必要的轮廓的光滑。她的脸色变化极大，有时一阵突来的红晕光彩焕发，有时又退成一种透红的白，与其说是苍白，不如说是白。她的五官没有什么可夸的；是她脸上那种敏捷感情的流动，那种关切、愤慨、怜惜，那种不停的流转变化，使这张脸动人——而在这一点上赫斯特自然无从评判。她见自己的嘴太大、鼻子太短、眉毛太重，便断定自己不漂亮，并且引以为憾，虽然在她的境况里这实在无关紧要；她的朋友们喜欢她，同她漂亮不漂亮毫不相干；她也不大可能产生小说里的女主人公——哪怕是比较平常的那些——所产生的效果。于是她拿定主意——想到自己竟为这件事心神不宁，还觉着有点羞愧——不值得再深究下去。尽管如此，为了年轻的读者们，这终究是件憾事：小说里的姑娘们，除了绝少的例外——简·爱即使不算漂亮，恐怕也没有她自己想的那么平常，而且她无疑是*磨人*的（*agaçante*），这比漂亮有效得多——一概都美，一概有那么多爱慕与征服。读书的女孩子们免不了纳闷，怎么自己就没有同样的造化。赫斯特呢，她对于这一类的女性胜利抱着高明的轻蔑；那种事从来不曾进入她的命运的可能性之内。

She never went to balls, nor met in society gangs of suitors contending for her smile; she did not believe in such things, and she thought she despised them.

===Chinese===

她从不去舞会，也不在交际场里遇见成群的求婚者为她的一笑争斗；她不信有这样的事，还自以为看不起它们。

===Original===

It was in the very midst of this scepticism that she suddenly became aware of certain facts which, as we have said, were of the kind generally supposed to be most important in a young woman’s life. Harry Vernon had been for some time alone in the splendour of the White House; Ellen, who had inflicted so deep a wound upon Hester’s inexperienced girlhood, had married the previous summer, and in the lack of young ladies worthy to swell her train on that occasion, had selected Hester as one of her bridesmaids. Hester had never forgiven her frivolous kinswoman for that first disenchantment of her youth, but her mother, upon whom her exclusion from society and from all opportunities of distinguishing herself there weighed heavily, had insisted on the acceptance of the invitation, and Hester had figured accordingly in a white muslin frock, much too simple to match the toilette of the other bridesmaids in the pageant, greatly to her own disquiet. She was the only Vernon in it, and thus had been specially put forward, and Ellen, altogether unconscious of previous offence, had exhausted herself in demonstrations of affection to her young relative. It was she whom Harry led out in the morning’s procession, and he had, in the intervals of his duty to his guests, come back again and again to her side. Hester, all inexperienced and unknowing, had paid little attention to these early indications. She did not identify him with his sister’s guilt towards her. He was a weak, good-natured, genial fellow, and no more. If Harry did anything wrong, no doubt it was because of being led astray. In himself he wished nothing but good to anyone. He was not clever, he was steady and stolid, and went through both work and pleasure without much discrimination as to which was which, carrying on both in the same way. When he began to come to the Vernonry evening after evening, Hester paid little attention to him. She would go out to walk with old Captain Morgan in the very face of the young visitor whose “intentions” all the community considered to be of such importance. Hester never thought of his “intentions.” She had none herself in which he was anyhow involved. She was perfectly friendly when they met, but she did not care whether they ever met or not, and repulsed him as much as steady indifference can repulse an obstinate and not very clear-sighted young man.

===Chinese===

正是在这满腹怀疑的时候，她突然觉察到几桩事实——如我们所说，正是一般认为在一个年轻女子生命里顶关紧要的那一类。哈利·弗农独自住在白宅的豪华里已经有些时候；埃伦——曾给赫斯特不谙世事的少女时代留下那样深的一道创伤——去年夏天出嫁了，一时又没有配得上给她增光的年轻小姐，便挑了赫斯特当她的傧相之一。赫斯特从来没有原谅过这个轻浮的亲戚加于她青春的第一次幻灭；可她母亲——被排斥于交际场外、失去一切在那里崭露头角的机会，这事压在她心头——执意要她接受这份邀请，于是赫斯特穿一件白色细麻布衣裳出场了，同那一场面上的其他傧相一比，朴素得过了头，叫她自己好不自在。她是队伍里惟一的弗农家的人，因此被特别推到前头；埃伦全然不觉得从前有什么得罪她的地方，对这位年轻亲戚的亲热简直使不尽。那天早晨的行列里是哈利挽她出场，他在应付宾客的空当里，一次又一次回到她身边。赫斯特全无经验、一无所知，对这些顶初的苗头并不留意。她没有把他同他妹妹对她的亏欠等同起来。他不过是个软弱、和气、好性子的家伙，如此而已。哈利倘若做错了什么，必定是被人带坏的。他本人对谁都没有恶意。他不聪明，可是稳、是钝，做工作也罢、行乐也罢，一律照本宣科，两样用同一个法子办。等他开始一连好几晚到弗农苑来的时候，赫斯特并不大理会他。她照样出门陪老摩根上校散步，全然不避这位年轻访客——他的“来意”，全院的人都看得那么重大。赫斯特从不想到他的“来意”。她自己心里没有任何同他相干的意图。他们见面时她客客气气，可碰不碰得上她全无所谓；她拿一贯的冷淡，把这位执拗而眼光并不怎么亮的年轻人拒之于门外——冷淡所能拒人的，她都用上了。

But this was not saying much. Harry knew as well as anyone that his suit was a wonderful chance for his distant cousin; that Hester had no right to look for such good fortune as that of being the object of his affections. He knew that he was bringing in his hand everything a girl need wish for. And so far as Hester’s course of action was concerned, though he was much irritated by it sometimes, he still felt that it was what she had a right to employ in the circumstances. It “drew a fellow on;” she was right to do what she could to obtain this so desirable consummation. He could not find fault with her even when he was angry. Had she been too ready to meet him, he felt that he would himself have despised what was so easily won. But her coyness, her apparent indifference, her walking out to the old captain from her lover, all helped to rivet his chains. It was excellent policy, and he took it as such; it drew a fellow on.

And it would be impossible to describe the interest of the Vernonry in this new development. Harry made his appearance first when they were all outside enjoying the beauty of the summer evening, Mr. Mildmay Vernon occupying that bench in front of the verandah, which was the most desirable place in the evening, being just clear of the low sunbeams which came into your eyes through the trunks of the pines, penetrating like golden arrows. Mrs. John herself was watering the plants in the verandah, which were a little exhausted by the long, scorching day, and wanted refreshment. The Miss Vernon-Ridgways were walking about with their long sashes extended and their large sleeves flying, the one eagerly talking from a few paces behind her, to the other. Their conversation was on the well-worn subject of “some people who never knew their own place,” and was aimed at the tranquil gentleman on the bench, who when he had secured his own comfort, which was the first thing to be thought of, rather prided himself upon never interfering with his neighbours. When Harry Vernon appeared, there was a universal stir. The sisters made a little flight round him, gazing at him. “I do believe it is Harry. Is it Harry?” they said. Mr. Mildmay Vernon put down his paper in the midst of a paragraph, and came forward with his most genial air. “I hope this is a visit only. I hope there is nothing wrong,” he said.

可这算不得什么。哈利同谁一样清楚：他的求婚对他这位远房表妹是了不起的造化；赫斯特压根儿无福消受被他看中这样的好运。他知道他手里捧来的是一个姑娘所能指望的一切。至于赫斯特的做法，虽说有时叫他着恼，他仍觉得处在她的地位尽可以这样。这叫人“越吊越上”；她理应尽力促成这一桩人人称心的好事。他连恼的时候也挑不出她的错。她倘若太容易接近，他反倒要自己看轻这轻易到手的了。可她的矜持、她表面上的淡漠、她丢下情人去陪老上校散步——这一切都把他锁得更牢。这是绝妙的策略，他也照此领受；这叫人越吊越上。

弗农苑对这一新发展所怀的兴趣，更无法描摹。哈利头一回露面，是大家都在屋外享受夏晚之美的时候：米尔德梅·弗农先生占着游廊前那张长凳——晚上这是顶好的位置，刚刚躲开低低的、从松树干间直射进人眼睛里的落日光，那光像金箭一样穿透过来。约翰太太亲自在游廊里给花草浇水，那些花草叫长长的灼热的一天折腾得有些蔫了，正需要滋润。弗农-里奇韦两位小姐来回踱着，长长的腰带飘着，肥大的袖子飞着，一个落后几步，热切地朝另一个说话。她们谈的是那个说滥了的老题目——“有些人从来不识自己的身份”，矛头对着长凳上那位安闲的先生；他呢，先安置好了自己的舒服——这是第一件要紧事——向来颇为自负的是从不干预邻居。哈利·弗农一出现，全场一阵骚动。姐妹俩绕着他飞了一圈，端详他。“我当真是哈利。是哈利吗？”她们说。米尔德梅·弗农先生在一段文章中间放下报纸，带着顶和气的神气走上前来。“我希望这只是一次拜访。我希望没出什么事。”他说。

===Original===

“Wrong! what should be wrong?” said Harry, turning his fair countenance wonderingly upon the group. “It’s a lovely evening, and I wanted a walk,” he added, with a little reddening of that too fair face; “and besides, I’ve got a message from Ellen to Mrs. John﻿—”

“Dear Ellen! How is Ellen? When is she coming home?” cried Miss Matilda. “When you write to her, give her our love. But I suppose she is too happy to care about anybody’s love save one person’s. Marriage will improve Ellen﻿—marriage will steady her. She used to be a little forgetful, perhaps. Ah! marriage will do her a great deal of good. She had everything too much her own way.”

“But she is missed. It would be pretty to see her again﻿—forgetting,” said Mr. Mildmay, “that she had ever set eyes on you before.”

“Ah, dear Ellen! We should not have known her without her little ways!”

Now Harry was fond of his sister.

“I’ll thank you to leave Ellen alone,” he said, brusquely. “I dare say we’ve all got our little ways. I had something to say to Mrs. John if you’ll let me pass, please.”

“Politeness is characteristic of our family,” said Miss Matilda, drawing her skirts closely round her, and standing ostentatiously, though she was not very near him, out of his way.

Mrs. John stood looking on in the verandah with the watering-can in her hand, not hearing much of what they said, but feeling that it was uncivil, and putting on a little deprecating, anxious smile﻿—

“Come in,” she said, “come in. The parlour, I think, is almost cooler than the garden after this hot day. Shall I make you a cup of tea?”

“These pensioners of Aunt Catherine’s are odious people,” said Harry. “It was you and Hester I came to see.”

“You must not speak of them so﻿—they would not like it,” said Mrs. John, not thinking that she herself might be spoken of in the same way, though rather pleased at the bottom of her heart that Harry should make a distinction between them. He threw himself down in a chair, which creaked under his weight, and looked very large and mannish in the little feminine room﻿—rather, indeed, it must be allowed, out of place there.

“I wonder how you can get on in such a poky little place,” he said. “I should like to see you in handsome big rooms; it would seem much more natural.”

Mrs. John smiled again, a deprecating, half-apologetic smile.

“出事！会出什么事？”哈利说，把他那张白净的脸诧异地转向众人。“今晚天色真好，我想出来走走，”他补一句，那张过分白净的脸上微微一红；“再说，我还带着埃伦带给约翰太太的口信——”

“亲爱的埃伦！她好吗？她什么时候回家？”玛蒂尔达小姐喊道。“你给她写信的时候，替我们致意。不过我料想她太幸福了，除了一个人的爱，谁的爱也不放在心上了。结婚会叫埃伦长进——结婚会叫她沉稳。她从前也许有点健忘。啊！结婚于她大有好处。从前什么都由着她的性子。”

“可大家想她呢。再见到她一定很美——她会忘了，”米尔德梅先生说，“从前见过你们这回事。”

“啊，亲爱的埃伦！要是没有她那些小习性，我们倒要认不得她了！”

哈利是爱他妹妹的。

“请你们别动埃伦。”他粗声说。“我看我们谁都有各人的小习性。我原有一句话要同约翰太太讲——请让我过去。”

“客气是我们家的家风。”玛蒂尔达小姐说，把裙子紧紧裹在身上，夸张地站开——虽然她离他并不很近——给他让路。

约翰太太提着水壶站在游廊里张望，他们说的话她大半没听清，可觉得出话里不客气，便挂上一点赔小心的、焦急的笑——

“进来吧，”她说，“进来吧。这样热的天过罢，客厅里我想比园子还凉快些。我给你沏杯茶好不好？”

“凯瑟琳姨母养的这班食客，真是些可恶的人。”哈利说。“我来为的是看你和赫斯特。”

“你可不能这样讲她们——她们要不乐意的。”约翰太太说，没想到自己也可能被人照这样讲，心里却暗暗高兴哈利把她们分了个彼此。他一屁股坐进一张椅子，椅子给他压得咯吱响；在这间闺阁气的小屋子里，他显得又高又大、一身的男子气——实在得承认，同这屋子不相称。

“我不懂你们在这么个憋屈的小地方怎么过得下去，”他说。“我愿意看你们住上宽绰的大房间；那才像话得多。”

约翰太太又笑了笑，赔小心的、近乎道歉的一笑。

“Oh, I am very glad to be here. I did not expect ever to have to live in such a poor place when I married, it is true; but people’s minds change with their circumstances. I am glad to have it﻿—”

“You oughtn’t to﻿—you should have been provided for in a different way. Ah, Hester! I am so glad to see you,” Harry said, rising with some commotion to his feet. He took Hester’s hand and held it for a moment. “I thought I’d come and tell you about Ellen,” he said, with a blush.

“Hester,” said her mother, giving her a little meaning look, of which she did not understand the signification, “you must give Mr. Harry a cup of tea.”

And there he sat, to her great oppression, for an hour at least. He did not even tell them about Ellen. He said nothing in particular﻿—nothing which it was necessary to say. Hester, who had intended to go out with her old captain, felt herself bound by politeness and her mother’s warning looks. She did not know what these looks meant, but they held her fast. There was not very much conversation. He said a few things over and over, which made it difficult to change the subject; and it was mostly Mrs. John who replied, and who rather liked, also, to repeat the same sentiment. Hester poured out the tea, and when the moment came for that, lighted the candles, and sat down in the background and took her work. She was not very fond of work, but it was better than doing nothing at all. When she took that seat which was beyond his point of vision, Harry turned his chair round so as to face her, and took up one of the candles and arranged it for her, that she might see to work. “You should have a lamp,” he said. “I have a nice little lamp at home just the thing for you; you must let me send it.” What a long time he sat, and how anxious he was to make himself agreeable! After that he came three or four times in succession. Mrs. John began to look for him, brightening up as the hour of his visit approached; and the neighbours kept up a watch which it was impossible to mistake. “If he comes tonight again I shall know what to think,” Miss Matilda said. But when he came that night he met Hester at the gate in her outdoor apparel. Harry’s countenance fell.

“Oh, you are surely not going out,” he said, “not just when I come? You couldn’t be so unkind.”

“哦，你该不是要出去吧，”他说，“偏偏赶着我来？你不会这样狠心。”

“I have been unkind to Captain Morgan very often,” said Hester. “I must not neglect him tonight,” and she passed him quickly with a little bow and smile. It made Harry very angry, but still he felt that it drew a fellow on.

On one of these occasions, when Hester eluded him in this way, Harry spoke his mind to Mrs. John.

“I’m very lonely up there by myself,” he said, “and I have nobody to please but myself. Ellen used to interfere and keep me in order, as she said; but now she’s got somebody else to look after. I’ve thought a great deal of Hester for years back. That time when we came to see you first, you know, when Ellen made so many advances and forgot all about them﻿—that was her way. She’s not a bad sort when you get safe hold of her﻿—but it’s her way. Well, from that time I’ve thought of Hester, though I never liked to say a word as long as Ellen was there.”

“Oh, Mr. Harry,” said Mrs. John, who was fluttered and flattered as if a proposal were being made to herself. “She was only a child in those days.”

“I know; but she isn’t a child now. If she’ll have me﻿—and I can’t see why she shouldn’t have me﻿—we might all make each other very comfortable. I’m not frightened of a mother-in-law as so many fellows are. I believe that’s all bosh. I shouldn’t wish to part you more than for the honeymoon, you know. There is plenty of room for you in the White House, and it would be always nice for her to have you there, when I happened to be engaged. I think we should hit it off very well together. And as for money﻿—I know she has no money﻿—I should never think twice about that. Of course it would be to my own advantage to make as good settlements as possible, which is always a good thing in business when one never knows what may happen. We might have to consult Aunt Catherine just at first, for she always keeps a hold on the funds﻿—”

“And there’s Hester to consult﻿—that is the most important,” said Mrs. John.

“To be sure, that’s the most important; but I can’t see why she should object,” said Harry. “Why, she has never seen anyone, has she? I am the only man that has paid any attention to her. At Ellen’s wedding there were one or two, and that was only once in a way. I don’t say she likes me, but she can’t like anyone else, can she? for she has never seen anybody.”

===Chinese===

“我对摩根上校狠心的时候可多呢。”赫斯特说。“今晚我不能再怠慢他了。”她微微一鞠躬、一笑，很快从他身边走过去。这叫哈利非常生气，可他仍觉得这叫人越吊越上。

有一回，赫斯特又这样躲开他，哈利便对约翰太太吐露了心事。

“我一个人住在那儿，冷清得很，”他说，“除了自己，没有个人可讨喜欢。埃伦从前总要管束我，照她的说法，管着我守规矩；如今她另有要照看的人了。多少年来我把赫斯特想了又想。我们头一回来拜访你们那一回，你知道，埃伦那样亲热了一阵，过后忘了个干净——她就是那个脾气。你稳稳当当地抓住她，她并不坏——可她就是那个脾气。唉，从那时候起我就把赫斯特放在心上，只是埃伦在一天，我不肯说一个字。”

“哦，哈利先生，”约翰太太说，又慌张又受宠若惊，仿佛求婚的是对她本人。“那些日子她还是个孩子。”

“我知道；可她现在不是孩子了。她要是肯要我——我看不出她为什么不肯要我——我们大家可以彼此照应着过得很舒服。我不像许多小伙子那样怕丈母娘。我看那一套全是废话。除了蜜月那阵子，我不想同你分开，你知道。白宅里地方尽够你住；碰巧我有事在外，她有你在那儿总是好的。我想我们准能合得来。至于钱——我知道她没有钱——那个我绝不会想第二遍。当然，产业安排得越优厚，对我自己越有利；生意上这永远是一着好棋，因为谁也保不定日后出什么事。开头恐怕得同凯瑟琳姨母商量一下，钱一向攥在她手里——”

“还有赫斯特要商量——那才是顶要紧的。”约翰太太说。

“可不是，那顶要紧；可我看不出她为什么要反对。”哈利说。“嗐，她从来没见过什么人，是不是？我是惟一注意过她的男人。埃伦的婚礼上有过一两个，那也是难得一回的事。我不说她喜欢我，可她总不能喜欢别人，对不对？她什么人也没见过。”

===Original===

“Not that I know of,” said Mrs. John; “but, Mr. Harry, girls are so fanciful. You cannot be sure of them in that way. They may have some ideal in their heads, though they have never met anyone﻿—”

“Eh?” said Harry, making a large mouthful of the word, and opening wide those blue eyes of his with the light lashes. And, indeed, he did not know much about that sort of thing. He returned to the question without paying any attention to this strange piece of nonsense. “There’s nobody about but the old gentlemen, and Ned at Aunt Catherine’s. Sometimes I’ve felt a little suspicious of Ned. Does he come and see you often? He is a great fellow for books and that sort of thing.”

“Mr. Edward Vernon,” said Mrs. John, a little stiffly, “*never* comes here. Hester, I believe has met him at the Grange or elsewhere; but he never comes here. I scarcely know him, neither of course does she.”

“Then,” said Harry, taking no notice of the offence in her tone, but bringing down his hand vehemently upon his knee, “if it isn’t Ned, there is no one she can have seen, and the field is all clear for me.”

“That is very true,” said Hester’s mother, but her tone was doubtful. “At the same time,” she continued, “perhaps it would be well to let me talk to her a little first, Mr. Harry, just to see, before you said anything.”

“If she doesn’t want to have me, I don’t wish to force her to have me,” said Harry, his pride taking alarm.

“Force﻿—oh, Mr. Harry, do you think I would force my child? And indeed I couldn’t;” cried Mrs. John, shaking her head. “She is far, far stronger than I.”

“She would be the cleverest of us all,” said Harry admiringly. “I believe she is as clever as Aunt Catherine. I dare say she might even find out dodges in the bank, like Aunt Catherine did. Perhaps on the whole it might be better if you would sound her a bit, eh? and find out what she is up to. What she thinks of me, for instance,” said Harry, nodding half with modesty, half with vanity. “Yes, I should like that. I should like to be pretty sure before I committed myself. A man doesn’t like to make a fool of himself for nothing,” the young man said.

“据我所知没有，”约翰太太说；“可是哈利先生，女孩子家心思多虚幻。这种事你拿不准的。她们脑子里说不定有个理想的影子，虽然什么人也没见过——”

“嗯？”哈利说，把这个字囫囵吞了一大口，把他那双浅色睫毛的蓝眼睛睁得老大。说实在的，这一类事他懂得不多。他不理会这句离奇的胡话，径直回到题目上。“这一带除了几个老头子，就剩凯瑟琳姨母那儿的内德了。有时候我对内德有点犯疑。他常来看你们吗？他是个顶喜欢书本那一套的家伙。”

“爱德华·弗农先生，”约翰太太微微板起脸说，“*从来不*到这儿来。赫斯特，我记得在格兰奇还是别处碰见过他；可他从不到这儿来。我几乎不认识他，她自然也一样。”

“那么，”哈利说，全不理会她语气里的见怪，一只手在膝盖上猛地一拍，“只要不是内德，她见过的就没有别人，这场地就全归我了。”

“这话很对，”赫斯特的母亲说，语气却犹疑。“不过，”她接着说，“哈利先生，或许还是让我先同她谈谈的好，先探一探，你再开口。”

“她若是不要我，我也不愿硬叫她要我。”哈利说，自尊心警觉起来。

“硬叫——哦，哈利先生，你以为我会硬逼我的孩子？逼也逼不动呀；”约翰太太喊道，摇着头。“她比我强得多、强得多。”

“那她就是我们大家里头顶聪明的。”哈利赞叹说。“我看她同凯瑟琳姨母一样聪明。说不定银行里的门道她也摸得出来，像凯瑟琳姨母当年那样。这么着，还是你先去探探她的口气，好不好？摸摸她的心思。比如她怎么看我。”哈利说，半个头点得谦虚，半个头点得自得。“对，我愿意这样。拿定主意之前，我愿意先有几分把握。一个男人不愿意白白地出丑。”这年轻人说。

===Original===

Mrs. John thought it was quite natural. And indeed all her feelings were enlisted on Harry’s side, who expressed himself so beautifully. What better could happen to Hester than to be thus uplifted to the heights of luxury and wealth, the White House, and everything else that heart could desire, with a nice husband, so good-looking, so tall, so fair, and so anxious to be kind to her mother? Her imagination, not her strong point on ordinary occasions, was strong enough on this, to jump at all the advantages of the match with a rapidity which would not have disgraced Hester herself. To see her child the mistress of the White House was the very height of Mrs. John’s ambition. She did not feel that the world held anything more desirable. Her mind made a hurried rush through the rooms, all so familiar to her, and which Harry, no doubt, would remodel in preparation for his bride. With what pride and happiness would she see her child at the head of the table, where she herself had once sat! It would be a return more triumphant than any return in her own person. And yet she would be there too, the happy spectator, the witness of it all. She saw in her mind’s eye, the wedding, the beautiful clothes, the phaeton, and the high-stepping horses, and perhaps a pony carriage which Hester herself would drive. All this in a moment, while Harry was telling her that he would like to be pretty sure before he committed himself. Perhaps it was not a lofty sentiment, but she felt it to be quite natural. A man with so much to bestow had a right to see his way before him, and then for Hester’s own sake it was far better that she should not be taken by surprise. She was a perverse girl, and if the young man walked straight up to her without warning, and asked her to marry him, the chances were that she would refuse. That was not a risk to be run when so much was at stake.

“If you will leave it in my hands, I think you will have no cause to regret it,” she said, nodding her head at him with the softest maternal smile. “You may be sure you will have my good wishes.”

They were both quite affected when he took his leave.

===Chinese===

约翰太太觉得这再自然不过。她全部的感情实在都站在哈利一边——他的话说得多漂亮。赫斯特还能遇上什么更好的事呢：这样被抬举到奢华和富足的高处，白宅，外加心所能想望的一切，还有一位好丈夫，那样漂亮、那样高大、那样白净，又那样急切地要对她母亲好。她的想象力——平常场合原不是她的长处——在这件事上却够强的，一纵身就把这桩亲事的好处全数抓住，那份利落连赫斯特本人也不输。看着自己的孩子做白宅的主妇，是约翰太太志向的绝顶。她觉得世上再没有比这个更叫人想要的了。她的心思在那几间屋子里匆匆巡了一遍——她对它们处处熟悉，哈利无疑要为新娘重新装修。看她自己的孩子坐在餐桌的主位上——她自己从前坐过的位子——她要怀着怎样的骄傲和幸福！那将是比她本人任何一次归来都更凯旋的一次归来。而她自己也要在场，做幸福的旁观者，做这一切的见证。她在心目中看见了婚礼、美丽的衣裳、四轮轻马车、昂首阔步的高头大马，兴许还有一辆赫斯特自己会赶的小马车。这一切都在一瞬之间，哈利正对她说，他拿定主意之前愿意先有几分把握。这也许算不得高尚的情操，可她觉得十分自然。一个有这么多可赐予的人，自然有权利看清脚下的路；再说，为赫斯特自己着想，也千万别叫她猝不及防。她是个别扭的姑娘，倘若这年轻人不先打招呼，径直走到她跟前求婚，十有八九要被她回绝。赌注这样大，这个险冒不得。

“这事你交到我手里，包管你不后悔。”她说，朝他点点头，带着顶温柔的做母亲的笑。“你放心，你有我的好意。”

他告辞的时候，两个人都颇为动情。

===Original===

“I feel sure we should hit it off together,” Harry said, warmly grasping her hand; and the water stood in her eyes. She could almost have given him a kiss as he stood before her, a little flushed and agitated with his self-revelation. Indeed, she would have done so but for that doubt about Hester. What would Hester say? That was the one point upon which doubt existed, and unfortunately it was the most important of all. There could not be the least uncertainty as to the many advantages of the match; money, comfort, good position, good connection, everything that can be wished for in marriage, and with no personal defects to be glossed over by these advantages, but a fine young man, a husband any girl might be proud of. Elation and gladness filled Mrs. John’s heart, when she contemplated that side of the question; but when she turned to the other a chill came over her, a cloud that swallowed up the sunshine. What would Hester say? Oh the perverseness of girls that never know what is good for them! If it had been somebody quite ineligible, somebody without a penny, the chances were that Hester would have had no doubt on the subject. Mrs. John could not remain still after this momentous conversation. She went from one window to another, looking out, watching for her daughter’s return. She had been vexed that Hester should have been so uncivil as to go away for no better reason than to walk with old Captain Morgan when Harry was coming, but she felt now that this contradictoriness on the girl’s part had been providential. How full her head was with thoughts and plans how to speak, and what to say, with artful approaches to the subject, and innocent wiles by which to divert all suspicion, and lead Hester unawares towards that goal! She trotted upstairs and down, from one window to another, framing dialogue after dialogue in her mind. She was astonished by her own powers as she did so. If she ever had been so clever in reality as she was in this sudden crisis of imagination, she felt that it might have made a difference in her whole life. And one thing Mrs. John had the wisdom and goodness to do in the midst of her excitement, she kept within her own house, and did not so much as venture down to the verandah, where she might have been seen from outside, and pounced upon by the eager watchers, brimful of curiosity, who wanted to know what it all meant.

===Chinese===

“我拿准我们准合得来。”哈利说，热切地握住她的手；她眼睛里含着泪。他站在她面前，因为这一番自我剖白微微红着脸、心绪不宁，她几乎要吻他一下。真的，若不是对赫斯特那一点疑心，她准会这样做的。赫斯特会说什么呢？惟有这一点存着疑问，而不幸这偏偏是顶要紧的一点。亲事的种种好处不容丝毫怀疑：钱、安逸、好地位、好姻亲，婚姻里所能想望的一切，又没有需要拿这些好处来掩饰的短处，有的是一位漂亮青年，任何一个姑娘都该引以为傲的丈夫。约翰太太一想到问题的这一面，心里便涨满了得意和欢喜；可一转到那一面，一阵寒意就罩下来，一片云吞掉了阳光。赫斯特会说什么呢？哦，女孩子就是别扭，从来不知道什么于自己有益！倘若来的是个全然不合格的人、一个身无分文的人，只怕赫斯特倒干脆。这一番重大谈话之后，约翰太太安坐不住了。她从一扇窗走到另一扇窗，望着外头，守候女儿回来。哈利来的时候赫斯特竟那样失礼，为陪老摩根上校散步就走开了——她原先为此着恼，此刻却觉得姑娘这份别扭是天意安排。她一脑子尽是怎样开口、说什么的盘算：用怎样巧妙的话头引到正题，用怎样天真的巧计岔开一切疑心，引着赫斯特不知不觉走向那个目标！她小步跑上跑下，从一扇窗到另一扇窗，在心里编了一篇又一篇对白。她为自己的本事吃惊。她倘若真有这场想象力的突然危机之中那么聪明，她想，她的一生也许全然是另一个样子。在兴奋当中，约翰太太还有一桩聪明厚道的事：她守住自己家里不出门，连游廊也不敢下去——从外头望得见游廊，会被那些满肚子好奇、急着知道这一切是什么意思的瞭望者们一把逮住。

===Original===

Miss Matilda Vernon-Ridgway, as has been intimated, had been conscious of an internal admonition that something critical, something decisive, something throwing a distinct light upon the “intentions” of young Harry would happen this night. And Mrs. John knew herself, and was aware that she never would be able to stand against the questionings of these curious spectators. Her only safety was in keeping out of their way. Thus not only her imaginations, but her moral faculties, her power of self-control and self-denial, were strengthened by the occurrences of this momentous evening. She had not felt so important before since Hester was born.

===Chinese===

玛蒂尔达·弗农-里奇韦小姐，如前所暗示，心里早得了一种内在的警示：今夜要出事，要出决定性的事，要有一道光把小哈利的“来意”照个分明。约翰太太也知道自己，明白自己决计招架不住这些好奇看客的盘问。惟一的安全是躲开她们。这样，不仅她的想象力，连她的道德力、她的自持和自制之力，都被这个重大夜晚的事变加强了不少。自赫斯特出生以来，她还从不曾觉得自己这样要紧过。

## XI / 十一
===Original===

Mother and Daughter

Mrs. John had a long time to wait. The old captain prolonged his walk, as he was too apt to do, beyond his strength, and came home very slowly, leaning on Hester’s arm; and then as every hindrance, when people are anxious, has a way of doubling itself, Mrs. Morgan sent a polite message to say that she hoped Mrs. John Vernon would not object if she kept Hester to supper. Mrs. John objected greatly, but she was weak, and had never set up her own will in the face of anyone else who made a stand for theirs. She said “Oh yes, with pleasure,” with a pitiful little smile to Mrs. Morgan’s maid. To deny Hester anything (except the power of making a governess of herself and losing caste) was what she had never done in her life. It always gave her a little pang when her child left her to eat her solitary meal in the dark little parlour which nothing would light up, but she had trained herself to feel that this was very wrong, and that young people need change. Hester was entirely unacquainted with the series of little sacrifices which her mother thus made for her. If she thought of them at all, she thought that the poor lady “did not mind.” Her old friends next door were not gay, but they talked as Mrs. John was quite incapable of talking, and lived, though they saw nobody, in a wider atmosphere, a bigger world than any of the others. The old captain’s stories, the people he had seen, the experiences both these old people had gone through, were like another world to Hester. Her mother was small and straitened, had seen without seeing, and lived without living. In the days when Hester had guided her about by the arm, taking her whither she pleased, making new eyes for her in the vividness of her own, it was enough for the girl to have that echo of all her sentiments, that little objection generally ending with agreement, that broken little stream of faint recollections which her mother would give forth. But Hester had long ceased to form part of that sort of dual being which is so often made by a mother and her only daughter. To feel your parent smaller and sillier than yourself is sad. A great many young people do it without any adequate reason, strong in their sense of being the reigning monarchs of the present, while their progenitors belong to the past. Perhaps indeed it is the nature of youth to take a pleasure in such superiority.

===Chinese===

母与女

约翰太太等了许久。老上校散步过了头——他太容易这样，超出自己的体力——回家时一步一步挪得极慢，倚着赫斯特的胳膊；跟着，人一着急，每一样阻碍都会自己翻倍，摩根太太又打发女仆来客气地传话：她想留赫斯特吃晚饭，望约翰·弗农太太不要见怪。约翰太太大大地见怪，可她软弱，凡是别人坚持己见，她从来没有正面坚持过自己的。她对摩根太太的女仆说了声“哦，好的，很乐意”，带着可怜的一小笑。拒绝赫斯特什么（除了不许她去当家庭教师、失了身份），是她一生没有做过的事。孩子丢下她、让她在那间怎么也照不亮的小客厅里独个儿吃饭，总叫她微微一疼；可她已把自己训练得认为这样很不对、年轻人需要换换环境。赫斯特全然不知道母亲为她做出的这一连串小小的牺牲。她若想到它们，也只想这可怜的太太“不在乎”。隔壁她的老朋友家并不热闹，可他们谈的话约翰太太全谈不来；他们虽然谁也不见，却活在一种更宽的空气、一个更大的世界里。老上校的故事、他见过的人物、两位老人经历过的一切，对赫斯特像另一个世界。她母亲窄小而局促，看了等于没看，活了等于没活。当年赫斯特挎着她的胳膊引她到处走、爱去哪儿去哪儿、拿自己眼睛的鲜活给她造一双新眼睛的那些日子里，这女孩子有那样一个应声虫——她的一切感想都得到回声、那一声小小的异议照例以同意收场、那一线时断时续的微弱回忆的小溪——也就够了。可是赫斯特早已不再是母亲和独生女儿常常结成的那种二元生物的一半。觉得自己的父母比自己渺小、比自己傻，是悲哀的。许许多多年轻人毫无足够的理由也这样做，仗着自己身为当今在位的君主，而他们的前辈属于过去。说不定，以这样的优越自娱，正是青春的本性。

===Original===

But that is very different from the fact of actual incapacity on the mother’s part to follow her child’s thoughts or even to know what she meant. Mrs. John was very well aware of it herself, and declared with a smiling countenance that young people liked change, and that she was never so happy as when her child was enjoying herself. And Hester, though she was so much more clever, accepted all this, and believed and thought her mother was quite contented with the evening paper, or a book from the circulating library, and never missed her when she was away. She misunderstood her silly mother, far more than that silly mother did her. The lesser comprehended the bigger, not the bigger the lesser, as in the ordinary course of affairs. Mrs. John had a great many sacrifices to make, of which her daughter was quite unconscious. And tonight the poor lady felt it, as with her mind so full she sat down at her little solitary table, which she had made pretty for Hester. There was nothing on it more luxurious than cold meat and salad, but the crisp greenness of the leaves, the little round loaf, the pat of butter in a small silver dish which was one of her relics, the creaming glass of milk, all set out upon a white cloth and lighted up by the two candles, would, she had flattered herself, call out an admiring exclamation when the girl came in out of the dark, a little dazzled for the first moment by the light. After she had said “Oh, yes, with pleasure,” Mrs. John came in and sat down and cried. Such a pretty table laid out, and oh, for once, so much to say! her mind so overflowing, her news so all important! There could not be anything so exciting to talk about, that was certain, on the other side of the partition, and this provoked and tantalised sense of having herself far better entertainment for Hester than she could be having, gave an insufferableness to the position. At one moment Mrs. John thought she must send for the girl, that she could not put up with the disappointment, but she was much more used to putting up with things, than to asserting herself. She sat down very cheerlessly and ate a mouthful of bread and salad. To eat alone is always miserable. Hester was making the table, where the old Morgans sat, very lively and cheerful, talking as she never talked with her mother. They sat and talked quite late into the night.

===Chinese===

可是这同下面这样的事实全然是两回事：母亲当真跟不上孩子的思想，甚至不知道她说的是什么。约翰太太自己很明白这一点，还满脸堆笑地宣称：年轻人喜欢换换环境，孩子玩得高兴，就是她顶大的快乐。赫斯特虽然聪明得多，也照单全收，相信并以为母亲有晚报、有流通图书馆借来的书就十分满足，她不在家也从不挂念。她误解她那傻母亲，远比那傻母亲误解她厉害。是小的领会大的，不是大的领会小的——同寻常事理正相反。约翰太太有许多牺牲要作，女儿全然不觉。今晚这可怜的太太就觉出来了：她满腹心事地在小小的独桌上坐下——那桌子是她替赫斯特布置得漂漂亮亮的。桌上顶奢侈的不过冷肉和生菜，可是菜叶的脆绿、小小的圆面包、盛在一只银碟里的一小块黄油——那银碟是她的一件遗物——还有那杯泛着奶皮的牛奶，都摆在白桌布上，让两支蜡烛照着；她本来自信，等女孩子从黑地里进来、乍一进门被灯光晃得睁不开眼的一霎，这桌子准会赢得一声喝彩。说完那句“哦，好的，很乐意”，约翰太太进来坐下，哭了。这样一张摆得好看的桌子，而哦，偏偏今晚有这么些话要说！她的心涨得满满的，她的消息这样重大！隔着一堵墙那一边决谈不着这样叫人兴奋的题目——这个又气又痒的感觉：她自己为赫斯特备下的款待远胜过那边可能有的——使这处境不堪忍受。有一霎约翰太太想，必须打发人去把女孩子叫回来，这个失望她受不住；可她一向习惯受，远过于习惯坚持自己。她快快地坐下，吃了一口面包和生菜。一个人吃饭总是凄凉的。赫斯特正把老摩根夫妇的餐桌弄得热热闹闹，谈得同母亲在一起时从来不曾谈过。他们坐着一直谈到深夜。

===Original===

What with the captain’s stories, and Mrs. Morgan’s elucidations and Hester’s questionings, the evening was full of interest. It flew away so quickly that when the clock struck eleven the girl sprang up with a great sense of guilt. “Eleven o’clock! what will mother say? I have never been so late before,” she cried. They were all half proud of it, of having been so mutually entertaining. “The poor little mother must have felt lonely,” Mrs. Morgan said, with a passing compunction when Hester flew round the corner, watched from the door to see that all was safe by the maid; but the captain took no notice. “It is delightful to see how that child enjoys herself,” he said, flattered in spite of himself, “though it’s no very intoxicating amusement we furnish her.” Captain Morgan was very softhearted, and understood by his affections as well as with his understanding, but in this case something beguiled him, perhaps a little complacency, perhaps want of thought.

When Hester ran in, in the dark, locking the door of the verandah behind her, Mrs. John had gone upstairs and was going to bed. She was chilly and “cross” her daughter thought, who ran quickly up to her full of apologies. “We got talking,” she said; “you must forgive me, mother. The captain’s stories run on so, one into another﻿—one forgets how the time runs on too.”

“I wish,” said Mrs. John, with the tears very near the surface, “that your mother was sometimes as amusing as the captain.” It was the greatest reproach she had addressed to her daughter for years.

“Oh, mother! If I had thought you minded,” cried Hester, with wondering eyes.

Mrs. John was penitent at once, and did her best to make things up. “I ought not to speak,” she said, “after all﻿—for I was not so very lonely. Harry stayed a long time and kept me company. It is only when you have him to yourself that you see how nice he is.”

“Is he so nice?” said Hester, indifferently. “How lucky for him to find you alone,” she added, with a little laugh.

“Oh, Hester, how can you say so. As if it was me he came for! Whatever you may try to make yourself believe you can’t think that.”

===Chinese===

有上校的故事，有摩根太太的注解，有赫斯特的追问，这个晚上趣味十足。时光飞也似的过去，钟敲十一点时，女孩子猛地跳起来，满心负疚。“十一点了！妈妈会怎么说？我从来没有这样晚过。”她喊道。他们个个都有几分得意，得意彼此这样有谈有笑。“可怜的小妈妈一定觉得冷清了。”赫斯特飞也似的转过拐角时，摩根太太带着一阵转瞬即逝的懊悔说；女仆在门口望着，看她一路平安。可上校没有理会。“看着这孩子玩得这样高兴，真叫人愉快。”他说，不由得有些得意，“虽说我们供给她的，算不得什么醉人的消遣。”摩根上校心肠极软，凭着感情也凭着理智去懂得事情；可这一回有什么迷住了他，许是一点自满，许是欠思索。

赫斯特摸着黑跑进家来，反手锁上游廊的门，约翰太太已经上楼，正要睡下。她身上发冷，又“别扭”——女儿这样想，一路道歉着飞奔上楼。“我们只顾说话了，”她说；“您得饶我，妈妈。上校的故事一个牵一个地讲下去——人也忘了时间是怎么溜的。”

“我但愿，”约翰太太说，眼泪就在眼边上，“你母亲有时候也同上校一样有趣。”这是她多年以来对女儿说过的顶重的一句责备。

“哦，妈妈！我要是想到您在意。”赫斯特喊道，眼睛睁得大大的。

约翰太太立刻悔了，尽力弥缝。“我不该这么说，”她说，“说到底——我也不是那样冷清。哈利坐了好久，陪着我。只有单独同他在一起，才知道他多么好。”

“他这么好吗？”赫斯特淡然说。“他碰巧撞见您一个人，多运气。”她添一句，微微一笑。

“哦，赫斯特，你怎么能这样说。仿佛他是为我来的！随你怎么硬叫自己相信，你总不能真这样想。”

===Original===

Hester made no reply. She slept in a small room within her mother’s, the door of which always stood open. She had taken off her outdoor things and let down her hair to brush it. It hung about her in a cloud, running up into curls as soon as she let it free. Mrs. John, seated in the easiest chair, sat contemplating this operation with a mixture of pleasure and pain. The mass of curls was pretty, but it was not the fashion. It was quite unlike the smooth brown glossy locks that had adorned her own head when she was young. But she said to herself that it suited Hester, and gazed at her child admiringly, yet anxiously, conscious of many things in which she might be improved: her hair for one thing: and her waist, which was not so small as Mrs. John’s had been in her youth: and her nose, which was a little too short. And yet with all these defects she was pretty. When she was Harry’s wife everybody would admire her. Perhaps it was only because she was not sufficiently seen that she had no more admirers now.

“I had a great deal to say to you, dear,” she said. “I don’t grudge you being away when you are enjoying yourself, but I had many things to say. It is not likely that Harry Vernon would sit with me for hours for nothing.”

“I suppose,” said Hester, from the midst of her curls, “that he finds it dull now without Ellen at the White House?”

“I could tell you a great deal about that,” said her mother quickly, eager to seize an opening. But Hester yawned with discouraging demonstrations of fatigue.

“Don’t you think it will keep till tomorrow, mother? We had a long walk, and I am sleepy. I think Harry can’t be very urgent. Tomorrow will be time enough.”

“Oh, Hester, how strange you are,” cried Mrs. John, “so pleased with those old people, ready to listen to all their old stories; but when I begin to talk to you of a thing that is of the greatest importance﻿—”

“Nothing concerning Harry Vernon can be of great importance to me,” cried the perverse girl; and then she tried to turn off her wilfulness with a laugh. “The beauty of the captain’s stories is that they are of no importance, mother. You can have them when you please. It is like going to a theatre, or reading a book.”

“I am not so clever as the captain to interest you,” Mrs. John said.

===Chinese===

赫斯特没有回答。她睡在母亲房间里面的一间小屋里，那扇门永远开着。她已脱掉出门的衣裳，解散头发来梳。头发像一片云披在她身上，一放手就卷成一圈圈的卷。约翰太太坐在顶舒服的椅子里，又是欢喜又是疼地看着这一番功课。那一头浓密的卷发好看，可是不合时式。它同她自己年轻时装点过头颅的那种光滑的棕色发亮的长鬈发全然两样。可她自忖这于赫斯特相宜，又是赞赏又是担心地望着孩子，心里数着她多少可以改进的地方：头发是一桩；腰身也是一桩，不像约翰太太年轻时的腰身那样细；还有鼻子，稍稍太短了些。然而虽有这些缺点，她是好看的。等她做了哈利的妻子，人人都要赞赏她。说不定她如今没有更多爱慕者，不过是因为她抛头露面不够。

“我有许多话要同你说，亲爱的。”她说。“你玩得高兴，我不怪你不在家；可我有许多话要说。哈利·弗农总不至于白白陪我坐上几个钟头。”

“我猜，”赫斯特从一头卷发中间说，“埃伦不在白宅，他如今觉得闷了吧？”

“这方面我可以告诉你许多。”她母亲急忙说，急切地抓住这个口子。可赫斯特打了个哈欠，倦态叫人泄气。

“您不觉得留到明天再谈也一样吗，妈妈？我们走了不少路，我困了。我想哈利总不至于那样急。明天尽来得及。”

“哦，赫斯特，你这人真怪，”约翰太太喊道，“那些老人的话你听得那样乐意，他们那些老故事你句句肯听；可我一开口同你谈一件顶顶要紧的事——”

“凡是关于哈利·弗农的事，没有一件能对我要紧。”这别扭的姑娘喊道；随后又想拿笑把任性岔开。“上校的故事的好处，就在于它们毫不要紧，妈妈。您什么时候要听什么时候有。像上戏园子，像读一本书。”

“我不如上校聪明，引不起你的兴致。”约翰太太说。

===Original===

There was a plaintive tone in her voice with which Hester was very well acquainted, and which betokened an inclination to tears. She came and kissed her mother, and gave her a few of those half-impatient caresses which generally soothed the poor lady. The girl did not in the least know that any consciousness was in Mrs. John’s mind of the superficial character of those kindnesses. She was not without love for the tender domestic creature who had been hers to use at her pleasure since ever she could recollect, but she bestowed these kisses upon her, as she would have given sweetmeats to a child.

“Go to bed, mother. Don’t mind me. I will shut the door; you shall not have the light in your eyes to keep you from sleeping. Go to bed, mammy darling.”

Mrs. John had liked this caressing talk when Hester was a child. She was soothed by it still, though a faint sense that there was something like contempt in it had got into her mind: and she could not struggle against a will which was so much stronger than her own. But she could not sleep, though she allowed herself to be put to bed. She could not help crying in the night, and wondering what she could do to be more respected, to be more important to her child; and then she prayed that she might be able to put Harry before her in the best light, and stopped and wondered whether it were right to pray about a young man. Altogether Mrs. John had not a tranquil night.

But next morning she made a great effort to dismiss her anxiety, to present herself at breakfast with a cheerful aspect, and to get rid of that plaintive tone which she was herself aware of, which she had so often tried to remedy. Instead of it she tried a little jauntiness and gaiety, for extremes are always easy. It is the juste-milieu which it is so difficult to attain.

“I am afraid I scolded you last night, Hester. I was cross when you came back. One can’t help being cross when one has a great many things to say and no audience,” she said with a laugh.

“I am very sorry, mamma. I did not mean to stay so late.”

“Oh, it was nothing, my dear. I had Harry. He sat with me a long time. He is﻿—really﻿—very﻿—entertaining when you have him to yourself.”

“Is he?” said Hester demurely. “I should not have expected that: but I am very glad, mother, for your sake.”

===Chinese===

她声音里那一种哀怨的调子，赫斯特熟极了，那是要哭的先兆。她走过去吻母亲，给她几个半带不耐的抚爱——它们照例能使这可怜的太太平静下来。女孩子丝毫不知道，约翰太太心里明白这些亲热多么浮面。她并非不爱这个温软的、自她记事以来就听她随意使唤的家常人儿，可她把这些吻赏给她，就像把糖果子赏给一个孩子。

“去睡吧，妈妈。别管我。我来关门；不让灯光晃您的眼睛，叫您睡不着。去睡吧，亲爱的妈咪。”

赫斯特小时候说这种撒娇话，约翰太太顶爱听。如今它仍旧能使她平静，虽说有一丝察觉——这里面有点像轻蔑——已经进了她的心里：而她斗不过一个比她强得多的意志。可她虽然被安顿上床，却睡不着。夜里忍不住哭，盘算怎样才能更受尊敬、对孩子更要紧些；又祷告，求上帝叫她能把哈利往顶好里摆；祷告到一半又停住，想为一个年轻男人祷告究竟对不对。总而言之，约翰太太这一夜不宁静。

可是第二天早晨，她竭力甩开焦虑，一脸愉快地出来吃早饭，去掉那自己也察觉、也屡次想改的哀怨调子。她改试一点轻快活泼，因为走极端总是容易的，难的是恰得其宜。

“怕是我昨晚说了你，赫斯特。你回来的时候我在生气。一个人有许多话要说而没有听的人，忍不住要生气。”她笑着说。

“我很对不起，妈妈。我不是有意待那么晚的。”

“哦，没什么，亲爱的。我有哈利呢。他陪我坐了好久。他——真的——非常——有意思，只要你单独同他在一起。”

“是吗？”赫斯特一本正经地说。“我倒想不到：不过我很高兴，妈妈，为了您。”

===Original===

“Because I am likely to see a great deal of him in the future? Oh yes, my dear. I hope so, at least. He is very kind to me. Nobody has spoken so nicely of me for many a year.”

“I like him for that,” said Hester honestly, yet with a blush of self-consciousness; for perhaps though she liked him for it, it did not improve her opinion of Harry’s intellect, that he should find her mother’s company so congenial.

“Oh, you would if you knew him better, Hester. He feels for me in my changed circumstances. You don’t know how different things used to be, what a great deal people used to think of me when I was young. I don’t complain, for perhaps it was silly of them; but it is a great change. But living where he does in my house, you know, Harry feels that: he says it is there I ought to be﻿—in the White House. Even though nothing should ever come of it, it is nice that somebody should think so.”

“Unfortunately nothing can ever come of it,” said Hester. “However nice people may be they do not give up their house to you, or their living; for you would need his money as well, to be able to live in the White House.”

“You say unfortunately, dear,” said her mother, with eagerness. Mrs. John blushed like a girl as she began her attempt to hint out Harry’s love-tale to her daughter. She was innocent and modest, though she was silly. No talk about lovers, no “petty maxims” about marriage, had ever offended Hester’s ears. Her mother blushed and trembled when she felt herself broaching the subject to her child. “Oh, Hester, it would be easy, very easy, to cease to be unfortunate﻿—if you choose, dear. All that part of our life might fly away like a cloud﻿—if you choose. We might be done with poverty and dependence and thinking of what Catherine will say and what people will think. The White House﻿—might be yours if you liked, everything might be yours. You would only have to say the word.”

Mrs. John’s eyes filled with tears. She could not get to the end of a long speech like this without crying; and she was so anxious, that they found their way also into her voice.

===Chinese===

“因为我往后要常见他？哦是的，亲爱的。至少我盼如此。他待我很好。多少年没有人这样好好说起过我了。”

“为这一点我喜欢他。”赫斯特诚心诚意地说，却红了一红脸；因为虽说为这一点喜欢他，他竟觉得她母亲的陪伴这样投契，并不曾抬高她对他智力的评价。

“哦，你要是更了解他，准会的，赫斯特。他体恤我境遇的改变。你不知道从前多么不同，我年轻的时候人家多么看重我。我不抱怨，也许他们本来傻；可这变化很大。他住在那儿、住在我的宅子里，你知道，哈利觉出这一层；他说我本该在那儿——在白宅。哪怕永远成不了什么，有个人这样想，也是好的。”

“可惜永远成不了什么。”赫斯特说。“人再好，也不会把宅子让给你，也不会把进项让给你；因为要住得起白宅，你还得连他的钱也要呢。”

“你说‘可惜’，亲爱的。”她母亲急忙说。约翰太太红着脸、颤着手，开始向女儿把哈利的风流案一点点暗示出来。她虽傻，却天真而端庄。关于情人的谈论、关于婚姻的烦琐格言，从来不曾冒犯过赫斯特的耳朵。此刻自觉向孩子提起这个题目，母亲红着脸、发着抖。“哦，赫斯特，要不再‘可惜’——容易得很，非常容易——只要你自己愿意，亲爱的。我们生活里那一整块，可以像云一样飞走——只要你自己愿意。我们可以同贫穷、同仰人鼻息、同‘凯瑟琳会怎么说、人家会怎么想’一刀两断。白宅——只要你愿意，可以归你，一切都可以归你。你只要点一个头。”

约翰太太眼里充满了泪。这样长的一篇话，不说到哭她讲不完；她又是那样急，眼泪便也进了声音。

===Original===

“Mother!” cried Hester, opening wide her eyes. They were very bright and clear, and when they opened widely looked almost unnatural in their size. She was all the more startled that she had never been subject to any such representation before. “I don’t know what you mean,” she said. “What should we do with the White House? I think it is a vulgar, staring place, and far too big.”

“Don’t speak so, Hester. I can’t bear it. My own married home that your poor papa took me to!”

“I beg your pardon, mother. I had forgotten that. Of course taste was different in those days.”

“Oh, taste! Your poor papa had beautiful taste. There are some things there that just break my heart﻿—the ormolu set that everybody admired so, and the picture of me over the mantelpiece in the little parlour. It used to be in the drawing-room, but you can’t wonder at them changing it. The hair was worn high then, on the top of your head, and short sleeves. It was very becoming to me. And to hear you call it vulgar and staring﻿—”

“It was a mistake, mamma. I did not think what I was saying. Forgive me, mother dear!”

“You know I would forgive you anything,” cried Mrs. John, now fairly launched, and forgetting all prudential restraints. “But oh, Hester, my darling, when he speaks to you don’t be hasty; think of all that is involved. I am not going to tell you what he wants to say﻿—oh no, he would never forgive me. It is he himself that must tell you that. But Hester, oh, don’t speak hastily; don’t answer all in a moment, without thinking. Often, often a girl says what she is sorry for, not being prepared. Think, my darling, what it would be﻿—not only to be rich, but to be independent﻿—to have your own house, all your own, and no charity﻿—to have as much money as you want, to be able to help the poor, and do everything you wish, and to make me happy, so happy, to the end of my days!”

===Chinese===

“妈妈！”赫斯特喊道，眼睛睁得老大。那双眼睛又亮又清，一睁大，大得几乎异样。她格外吃惊，因为从前从没有人向她做过这样的陈说。“我不懂您的意思。”她说。“我们要白宅做什么？我看那是个俗气的、扎眼的地方，也太大了。”

“别这样说，赫斯特。我受不住。我自己成婚的家，你可怜的爸爸娶我进去的家！”

“请您原谅，妈妈。我忘了这一层了。当然，那时候的风气不同。”

“哦，风气！你可怜的爸爸趣味极高雅。那里有几样东西，想想就叫我心碎——那套人人都赞赏的镀金铜钟，小客厅壁炉架上我的那张画像。它原先挂在客厅里，他们把它挪了，也不怪他们。那时候头发梳得高高的，顶在头顶上，袖子短短的。那样打扮对我很相称。听你说它俗气、扎眼——”

“是我说错了，妈妈。我没想一想自己说的是什么。饶了我，亲爱的妈妈！”

“你知道我什么都饶你。”约翰太太喊道，这一下索性放开了，把一切小心谨慎都忘了。“可是哦，赫斯特，我的宝贝，他同你说话的时候，别急躁；把前后左右都想一想。我不打算告诉你他要说什么——哦不，他永远不能饶我。那话得他亲口对你说。可是赫斯特，哦，别随口就答；别想也不想、一霎之间就回绝。多少女孩子事前没有准备，一句话说出口，后悔一辈子。想一想，我的宝贝，那将是怎样——不光是阔绰，而且是独立自主——有自己的宅子，全是自己的，不是人家施舍的——钱要多少有多少，能周济穷人，事事随心愿，还能叫我快活，快活到老，到我闭眼！”

===Original===

It was thus that Mrs. John treated Harry’s secret. She forgot all her precautions and her conviction that from himself only the proposal ought to come. The dialogues she had invented, the long conversations with Hester which she had held in imagination, delicately, diplomatically leading up to the main possibility, had all disappeared when the moment came. When she began to speak she had forgotten them altogether, and gone off impromptu without recollecting a syllable of all that had been so painfully prepared: and her own eloquence, if it did not affect her daughter, affected herself beyond description: her mouth quivered, the tears flowed out of her eyes. Hester, who could no more bear to see her mother cry (though she had seen that sight often enough) than to see the tears of a child, rose from her seat, and coming round hurriedly behind Mrs. John’s chair put her arms caressingly round her, and laid her cheek to that wet one. She was not so entirely unprepared but that she understood well enough what this emotion meant, but she tried to look as if it had a different meaning altogether. She drew her mother’s head to her breast and kissed her.

“Dear mother! Is it really so bitter to you to be dependent? and you never let me know that you felt it.”

“What would have been the good,” said the poor lady, “when we could do nothing? The thing was to put the best face upon it. But now when it is all in your power﻿—”

“It was always in my power,” said Hester, with a mixture of real earnestness and a desire to persuade her mother that she put a different meaning upon all that had been said; “if you had not stopped me, mother; but I have not lost my accent, and if you will only give your consent now﻿—I am older, and people will trust me with their children.”

“Oh, Hester, do not vex me so,” cried Mrs. John. “Do you think that is what I mean? And besides, if I were to give you leave tomorrow, Catherine, you know, would never consent.”

“If you will trust to me,” said Hester, colouring high, “what Catherine pleases shall not be the last word.”

Mrs. John wrung her hands, drawing herself out of Hester’s arms, to gaze into her face.

===Chinese===

约翰太太就这样处置了哈利的秘密。她忘光了一切小心、一切“必须由他本人亲自开口”的信念。她编好的那些对白、她在想象里同赫斯特进行的长谈——婉转地、有板有眼地一步步引到那个正题——到了时刻全都不见了。她一开口就把它们忘个干净，苦心预备好的一字一句都没用上，脱稿讲了起来：她自己的这番口才，若没有感动女儿，可把她自己感动得没法形容：嘴发抖，眼泪直流。赫斯特——她见不得母亲哭（虽然这光景见得够多了），同见不得孩子哭一样——从座位上站起来，急忙绕到约翰太太椅子背后，胳膊亲亲热热地搂住她，把自己的脸贴上那张湿的脸。她也不是毫无准备——母亲这番激动意味着什么，她清楚得很——可她竭力装出这激动全然是另一种意思。她把母亲的头搂到胸前，吻她。

“亲爱的妈妈！仰人鼻息当真这样苦吗？您从来不叫我觉出您有这个感觉。”

“觉出来又有什么用，”可怜的太太说，“我们什么也做不成呀。要紧的是往好里撑着。可是如今，什么都全在你手里了——”

“从来就在我手里，”赫斯特说，一半真心、一半想叫母亲相信她把这一切话做了另一种解释；“要不是您拦我，妈妈；我如今乡音没有丢，只要您肯答应——我年纪大了些，人家肯把孩子托给我了。”

“哦，赫斯特，别这样气我，”约翰太太喊道。“你以为我指的是这个？再说，我明天就是准了你，凯瑟琳，你知道，也永远不肯。”

“您要是肯信得过我，”赫斯特说，脸涨得通红，“凯瑟琳爱怎么断，不做最后一句话。”

约翰太太绞着双手，从赫斯特怀里挣出来，盯住她的脸。

===Original===

“Oh, why will you make such a mistake? It is not *that*. I am not strong to stand out against you, Hester, but for your own sake. And Catherine would never let you do it. Oh, this is quite a different thing, my dear love! Not to work like any poor girl, but to be far above that, to have everything that heart could desire. And all so right and so nice, and so suitable, Hester. If your dear papa had lived and all had gone well I could not have wished for a better match.”

“Match!” said the girl, colouring violently.

She had indeed understood well enough that Harry was behind all her mother’s anxious insinuations, her promises and entreaties, but she had been confident in her power to defeat Mrs. John by aid of her own confused statements always capable of bearing two meanings. This word “match,” however, was one upon which there could be no confusion, and she was immediately driven to bay. She drew herself away from the tender attitude in which she had been standing.

“I never thought,” she said, “that this was a thing that could be discussed between us,” with all the unreasonable indignation of a high-handed girl, determined to crush all attempts to influence her on the spot.

But Mrs. John, though she was conscious she could not stand against Hester, was too sure that she was right, and too deeply convinced of the importance of this great question to give in, as she usually did.

“Oh why should it not be discussed between us?” she said. “Is there anyone so much interested as I am? I have heard people say it was a mother’s duty. And Hester, abroad where we used to live, I should have settled it altogether﻿—you would never have been consulted. I am sure I don’t know that it is not the best way.”

“It is a way﻿—that could never have been taken with me,” Hester said. She walked round to her own side of the table with a very stately aspect and sat down, and made a pretence of resuming her breakfast, but her hand trembled with excitement as she took up her cup. “It may be quite true what you say, that you are interested, mother. I suppose so. People consider a girl a piece of goods to be sold and disposed of.”

===Chinese===

“哦，你怎么偏这样错会？不是*那个*。我拗不过你，赫斯特，可我是为你自己。凯瑟琳也永远不会让你做。哦，这完全是另一回事，我亲爱的宝贝！不是去像随便哪个穷姑娘那样做工，而是远远高过那个，要什么有什么。又这样正当、这样美满、这样门当户对，赫斯特。就是你亲爱的爸爸活着、事事如意，我也再挑不出一门更好的亲事了。”

“亲事！”姑娘喊道，脸涨得通红。

母亲那些焦急的暗示、那些许愿和恳求，后头站着的是哈利——这层她其实清楚得很；可她自信有本事对付约翰太太，靠着那些语焉不详、永远可作两解的话把话头打散。可是“亲事”这两个字是错不了的，她立刻被逼到了墙角。她从方才那副温存的姿势里抽出身来。

“我从没有想到，”她说，“这是可以摆在我们中间谈论的事，”带着一个专横姑娘全然不讲道理的愤慨，决意把一切想左右她的尝试当场压下去。

可是约翰太太虽然明知站不住赫斯特的对面，这一回却自信得太深、这一个大问题看得太重，不肯照例让步。

“哦，为什么不能摆在我们中间谈？”她说。“还有谁比我更关切？我听人说过，这原是做母亲的本分。再说，赫斯特，在我们从前住的国外，这一层我干脆一手办了——压根儿不问你。我说不准那样倒不是顶好的办法。”

“那是个办法——可用不到我身上。”赫斯特说。她绕回桌子自己那一面，仪态十分端庄地坐下，装出继续吃早饭的样子，端起茶杯来手却激动得发抖。“您说您关切，妈妈，这话也许不错。我猜是不错的。人家把姑娘看作一件货色，拿去卖掉、打发掉。”

===Original===

“Oh, Hester, have I ever thought so? I have been wanting in my duty,” cried Mrs. John. “I have never tried to put you forward, to get you invitations, to have you seen and admired as other people do. You are so proud and so fanciful that I have never dared to do it. And when there comes one, without ever being invited, or thought of, or supposed possible﻿—”

It seemed to Hester that the burning blush which she felt go all over her was capable of bursting into flame. It was not the shy shamefacedness with which every girl contemplates this subject on its first introduction, but bitter and scorching shame.

“Invited﻿—thought of; mother!” she cried in a voice of girlish thunder; “is it possible that you could ever think of scheming﻿—matchmaking﻿—for **me**?”

No capitals could represent the fervour of her indignation. She was entirely unconscious of the arrogance of self-opinion that was in all she said. For **me**. That a man should be invited into her presence with that thought, that she should be put forward, taken into society in order to be seen with that view. Heaven and Earth! was it possible that a woman should avow such possibilities and yet live?

“When I tell you that I never did it, Hester! though I know it was my duty,” Mrs. John cried with tears. Never was woman punished more unjustly. She turned like the proverbial worm at the supreme inappropriateness of this judgment against her, and a sudden impulse of anger sustained the gentle little woman. “I know it was my duty,” she cried; “for who is to care for you, to see that you are settled in life, but me? But I was afraid to do it. I was obliged to leave it﻿—to Providence. I just said to myself, it is no use. Hester would never be guided by me. I must leave it﻿—to Providence.”

It did not appear that Mrs. John had much opinion of Providence in such matters, for she announced this with a voice of despair. Then taking courage a little, she said with insinuating gentleness﻿—

“I was just the same when I was a girl. I could not endure to hear about settlements and things. It was all love I thought of﻿—my darling. I was like you﻿—all love.”

“Oh, mother!” cried Hester, jumping to her feet. This was more intolerable than the other. Her face flamed anew with the suggestion that it was “all love.” “For Heaven’s sake don’t say any more about it, unless you want to drive me out of my senses,” she said.

===Chinese===

“哦，赫斯特，我几时这样想过？是我失了本分，”约翰太太喊道。“我从来没有设法把你往前推，替你张罗请帖，叫人家看见你、赞赏你，像别人家那样。你这样骄傲、这样多空想，我一直不敢。如今来了一个人，不请自来、想也没人想到、做梦也想不到——”

赫斯特觉得那一阵烧遍全身的红，简直要腾起火来。这不是女孩子初次接触这个题目时那种羞答答的害臊，而是又苦又灼的羞愤。

“请帖——想到；妈妈！”她带着女孩子的雷霆喊道；“你竟然想到替**我**——做媒——拉纤？”

再大的字母也写不出她愤慨的激烈。她全然不觉自己满口的话里那股自是的傲慢。替**我**。一个男人竟被抱着那种心思请到她面前来，她竟被往前推、带进交际场，好让人家抱着那种眼光来看。天哪地哪！一个女人竟然把这样的可能说出口来，还活得下去？

“我明明告诉你我从来没有做过，赫斯特！虽说我知道那是我的本分。”约翰太太含着泪喊道。再没有哪个女人受罚受得这样冤枉。她被这判决冤得忍无可忍，像谚语里那条被踩急了的虫子，一阵突来的怒气撑住了这温顺的小妇人。“我知道那是我的本分，”她喊道；“因为除了我，还有谁来疼你、来看着你成家立业？可我不敢做呀。我只得撒手——交给天意。我对自己说：没用的，赫斯特决不肯听我引导。我只好撒手——交给天意。”

听口气，约翰太太对这种事上的天意也没有多大信心，因为她是带着绝望的声音宣布这一条的。随后又鼓起一点勇气，婉转温柔地说——

“我做姑娘的时候也一模一样。一听见人家谈财产文书那一套就受不了。我心里想的净是爱情——我的宝贝。我同你一样——净是爱情。”

“哦，妈妈！”赫斯特喊道，跳了起来。这比刚才那句更受不了。这一句“净是爱情”，使她的脸重新烧起来。“看上天的份上，别再说了，除非你要叫我发疯。”她说。

===Original===

Mrs. John stopped crying, she was so astonished, and gazed with open mouth and eyes. She had thought this last tender touch would be irresistible, that the child would fall into her arms, and perhaps breathe forth the sweetest secret aspiration of her heart﻿—perhaps own to her that dark eyes and a moustache had been her dream instead of Harry’s fairness; or that a melting voice or a genius for poetry were absolute requirements of her hero. With all these fancies she would have so tenderly sympathised. She would have liked to discuss everything, to point out that after all a fair complexion was very nice, and a genius for poetry not profitable. She remembered what occupation and delight these same subjects had afforded herself in the interval before John Vernon had proposed to her. She herself had dreamed of a troubadour, a lonely being with a guitar, with long hair and misfortunes; and John Vernon had none of these attractions. She was talked over by her mother and sister and made to see that the Bank and the White House were far better. Hester, perhaps, would have been more difficult, but yet she had felt that, confidence once established, the sweetness of these discussions would have been unspeakable. When she had got over her astonishment, she sank back in a despair which was not unmingled with resentment. Had it come to that, that nothing a mother could say would please a child nowadays﻿—neither the attraction of a great match nor the tenderness of love?

This was how the great question of a young woman’s life was first revealed to Hester. It was not, to be sure, the last word. That would come when she was placed face to face with the aspirant for her favour and have to decide, so to speak, upon the future of two lives. But to say “no” to Harry would not have excited and confused her being, like this previous encounter with all the other powers and influences which were concerned﻿—or which were considered to be concerned, in her fate.

===Chinese===

约翰太太不哭了，她惊得目瞪口呆，张着嘴、睁着眼望着。她本以为这末了一记温柔的招数万无一失，孩子会扑进她怀里，说不定还吐出心底顶甜的一句隐愿——说不定向她招认，她梦里的原是黑眼睛和两撇髭须，不是哈利的白净；或者一副化人的嗓音、一手做诗的天才，才是她英雄的必不可少的条件。这一切痴想她都会顶温柔地体恤。她本想样样都拿出来讨论，指出白净的面包终究也很好，做诗的天才换不来面包。她记得这些题目当年在约翰·弗农开口之前，曾给她自己多少消遣和欢喜。她自己梦里原是一个行吟诗人，一个怀抱吉他的孤独者，长头发，一身坎坷；约翰·弗农这些好处一样也没有。是母亲和姐姐把她劝过来的，劝得她明白银行和白宅好得多。赫斯特也许更难劝，可她总觉得，知心话一旦建立，这种讨论的甜蜜将妙不可言。惊定之后，她颓然往后一倒，灰心里掺着怨气。难道竟到了这个地步，如今做母亲的说什么孩子都不爱听——大亲事的好处也不行，爱情的温柔也不行？

一个年轻女子一生的大问题，就是这样头一回摊到赫斯特面前的。当然，这不是最后一言。那要等到她同她的追求者面对面、必须——可以这样说——对两条性命的前途作决断的时候。可是，对哈利说一个“不”字，决不会像方才这样搅得她周身沸腾、心慌意乱——同这一切别的力量和影响、这一切被认为同她命运相连的力量和影响的一场遭遇。

## XII / 十二
===Original===

An Indignant Spectator

Hester Vernon had been, during the most important years of her existence, a sort of outlaw from life. She had been unacquainted altogether with its course and natural order, out of all its usual habits, separated from every social way of thinking or discipline of mind. She belonged to a little community which thought a great deal of itself, yet had no foundation for so doing; but, strangely enough, though she saw through the fallacy of its general pretensions, she yet kept its tradition in her own person and held her head above the ordinary world in unconscious imitation of the neighbours whom she knew to have no right to do so. She kept the spirit of the Vernons, though she scorned them, and thought them a miserable collection of ungrateful dependents and genteel beggars, less honourable than the real beggars, who said “thank you” at least. And she had no way of correcting the unfortunate estimate of the world she had formed from this group, except through the means of Catherine Vernon, and the society in her house, of which, at long intervals, and on a doubtful footing which set all her pride in arms and brought out every resentful faculty, she and her mother formed a part. If the Vernon-Ridgways and Mr. Mildmay Vernon were bitterly critical of Catherine, missing no opportunity to snarl at the hand that fed them, Catherine, on her part, was so entirely undeceived in respect to them, and treated them with such a cynical indulgence and smiling contempt, as if nothing save ingratitude and malice were to be expected from humanity, that Hester had found no relief on that side from her painful thoughts. She was so conscious in her own person of meanings more high, and impulses more noble, that the scorn with which she contemplated the people about her was almost inevitable. And when, deeply against her will, and always with an uneasy consciousness that her mother’s pleasure in the invitations, and excitement about going, was childish and undignified, Hester found herself in a corner of the Grange drawing-room, her pride, her scornful indignation and high contempt of society, grew and increased.

===Chinese===

愤慨的旁观者
