Catherine left them with the impression that they were in a mood beyond her comprehension. It was a fine, clear, almost warm day, and the roads dry and walking pleasant. She had come on foot, as was not very usual with her, and meant to walk home. She set out on her return waving her hand to Mrs. Morgan, but in no very cheerful frame of mind. She had not been cheerful when she left home. Her mind misgave her as it had not done before for more years than she could count. What was the reason she could scarcely tell. Edward was not really less kind, less observant of her comfort. The change she saw in him was one indescribable, which no one else would have suspected, which in all probability existed in her imagination alone. Why should she suppose evils that had no existence? There was no one like him, no son so dutiful to his mother, no one so ready to make any sacrifice for the pleasure of his home. If his looks had been a little abstracted lately, if he had spent his time away from her, if his work in his own room, which she had made so comfortable for him, which she had been so anxious to assure him the exclusive proprietorship of, had increased of late, perhaps this was merely the natural course of events. Or if he had fallen in love﻿—what then? Did the boy perhaps think that she would be jealous and stand in the way of his happiness? How little he knew! Provided only his choice was a right one; she would open her arms and her heart. She would be ready to do anything for their comfort. There was no sacrifice she would not gladly make. Notwithstanding that somewhat nonsensical mystical flourish of the old captain’s about his understanding of his wife, Catherine believed, and with much show of truth, that men rarely understood women, and never knew how ready they were to arrange everything, to give up everything for the comfort and pleasure of those they loved. What a welcome she would herself give to Edward’s wife, though he was trembling and putting off and afraid to tell her! What a reception that young woman should have! Provided always﻿—but with Edward’s good taste and good sense how could he go wrong in such a choice?

It was at this moment that a shuffling light step became audible, hurrying along the road, and a voice calling “Catherine﻿—is it really Catherine?” followed by another step and another voice, with a fainter sound in the repetition, but also calling upon “Catherine!” Catherine Vernon paused and looked round, her face losing its gravity and brightening into its usual humorous look of half-contemptuous toleration.

“It is Catherine!” cried Miss Vernon-Ridgway; “I told you so. Dear Catherine, isn’t this long walk too much for you, and on such a cold day? Take my arm﻿—please take my arm: or won’t you come back to our little house and rest, and we’ll send for the carriage? It is a long walk for us who are not used to luxury, and what must it be to you?”

It was true that the Miss Vernon-Ridgways were under fifty, and Catherine was sixty-five; but she was far more vigorous than they were, and more capable of exercise. She turned round upon them smiling, but kept her arms close by her side, and refused any support.

“I assure you,” she said, “I am quite capable of walking. You know I have always been accustomed to exercise.”

“Ah yes,” said the sisters, “you were brought up sensibly, dear Catherine, not spoiled darlings as we were. We have never quite got over it, though we should have known better long ago, if experience was all: no one can tell how we miss our carriage; and when we see you on foot, who can command every ease, it quite wounds our feelings,” said Miss Martha, coming in at the end in a little provocation by herself.

“It is very kind of you: but it does not at all hurt my feelings. This is a fine day for a walk, and I hope you are enjoying yours, as I do,” said Catherine, with her laughing look.

They both shook their heads.

“We do what we have to do, and I hope we don’t complain. But I declare I feel hurt that you should have been at the Heronry and not paid us a visit. I wish not to be jealous. You were no doubt talking things over with Mrs. John?”

“I know nothing that there is to talk over with Mrs. John,” said Catherine, tartly. “I was visiting my old uncle, which is a duty I never like to neglect.”

“Oh!” said one sister, and “Ah!” said the other. Then they cried eagerly each to each, “I knew it was a vile story. Of course we have been misinformed.”

“Yes, of course he was with me; he is only too attentive. I could wish he took a little more amusement. So your fine story is at an end, you see. 她虽有防备，这个名字仍旧震了她一下——搭着她臂肘的马蒂尔达小姐兴许觉出来了；纵然觉出，也不过一瞬。“爱德华！”她笑着说。“你们是说哈里吧？爱德华在家忙着呢，忙的是另一路的事。”

姐妹俩闻言又交换眼色，一齐摇头。“唉，凯瑟琳，您正是这样受蒙蔽的。哈里·弗农的嗓子我们熟得很。那是爱德华。”

凯瑟琳朝她们转过脸来，面容晴朗无云，唇边带笑。“我告诉你们，”她说，“他那时在我自己家里！我想他总不能同时待在两处——我的家，他的家——原是一家。他在家——”她顿了片刻，声音沉了下去，“同我在一起。”

“哦！同您在一起！”姐妹俩猛地缩回去，不敢再往下。这急煞煞一收，把马蒂尔达小姐的活泛才情整个浇灭了。接话的是她妹妹，那位务实的角色，抽着气说：“哦，当然，凯瑟琳，他既是同您在一起——”

“是，他自然是同我在一起；他殷勤得过了头才对。我倒情愿他多寻点乐子。瞧，你们这套妙文就这样收了场。换了别人，我兴许还当该查问查问；可我既拿得出凭据，那不是爱德华——话说回来，就算是爱德华，我也看不出多大坏处。”她添一句，又转向那两个告状的。“我并不喜欢赫斯特·弗农，可她到底是他表妹。”

“哦，没坏处！哦，我们从来没那个意思。”两个长舌妇慌慌张张地说。“只是——不过——我们吓着了，想着亲爱的凯瑟琳准病了，要不出了什么事——”

“你们是那么想的？你们亲爱的凯瑟琳若病了，会打发人去请赫斯特·弗农？——当她头一号的心腹，当那满世界的人里头顶爱她的一个？”

===Original===

Catherine paused; the native magnanimity in her, beneath all the pettiness which her laughing cynicism had taught her, would not insult even these heartless women by a reminder in so many words of their dependence. It cost her all her strength to stand up erect before them, and put off their assault. They had got at her heart, but they should never know it. She stood ample and serene between the two slim shabby figures and smiled defiance. Never were talebearers more completely discomfited. They turned upon each other with mutual reproaches in the confusion of the moment. “You need not have made such a fuss, Matilda.” “I told you, Martha, you oughtn’t to be so confident about a voice.”

“Come,” said Catherine, “we had better say nothing more about it; evidently there has been a mistake. Hester, who ought to be more careful if she is to live at the Vernonry, must have another admirer with whose voice you are not acquainted. But it is unwise to form conclusions on no better ground than the sound of a voice, and perhaps not very charitable or kind of you, so much older than she is, to tell anything that is uncomfortable about that girl, who is no favourite of mine already, to me. Don’t you think you would do better if you warned her, or her mother?” Catherine’s countenance was so calm, her eyes so commanding, that the Miss Vernon-Ridgways, altogether defeated in their malicious intention, which was chiefly to wound herself, felt their knees tremble under them, and were genuinely awestricken for perhaps the first time in their lives.

“Oh, as for that﻿—it was not Hester we were thinking of﻿—it was you,” they faltered between them, “that you might not allow﻿—or be exposed﻿—” Their words got incoherent and ran away to nothing, into breaks and frightened lapses. And when Catherine, opening her eyes still wider, said, “For me! to warn me!” and laughed them to scorn, Matilda, who being the most forward was at the same time the most sensitive, was so overcome by anger and alarm and mortification that she began to cry for sheer despite, and felt in her inmost heart that she hated the woman who could humiliate her so.

===Chinese===

凯瑟琳顿住了。她那冷嘲的笑教出的这一身小家气底下，天生的宽宏还在：她不肯拿话提醒这两个无心无肺的女人，提醒她们靠谁过活。站在她们面前挺直了、顶住这一场进攻，耗尽了她全部的力气。她们戳中了她的心，可她们永远休想知道。她立在两个瘦削寒碜的身影之间，雍容而安详，微笑里全是挑战。搬弄是非的人从没败得这样彻底。她们在慌乱中转而互相埋怨。“你也犯不着这样大惊小怪，马蒂尔达。”“我早说了，玛莎，凭一个嗓音你可不该那样咬定。”

“好了，”凯瑟琳说，“这事顶好不再提；显然是弄错了。赫斯特若还要在弗农宅区住下去，就该检点些，想必另有一位爱慕她的人，嗓音你们不熟。不过，光凭一个嗓音就下断语，本就轻率；你们比她年长这许多，把这姑娘的不体面事说给我听——她本来就不讨我喜欢——恐怕也说不上厚道仁慈。你们若去提醒她，或者她母亲，岂不更好？”凯瑟琳的面容那样平静，眼神那样摄人，弗农-里奇韦小姐们那番恶意——那番恶意主要冲着凯瑟琳自己——败得精光，只觉膝头发颤，平生头一回当真心生敬畏。

“哦，那个——我们想的不是赫斯特——是您。”她们结结巴巴地你一言我一语，“怕您不容——或者叫您担待不住——”话越说越不成句，散成一片停顿同惊惶的空白。待到凯瑟琳把眼睛睁得更大，说：“为我！提醒我！”付之一笑，嗤之以鼻，马蒂尔达——她最冒尖也最敏感——又怒又惊又臊，一口气憋不住，当真哭了起来，心底里恨透了那个能这样羞辱她的女人。

===Original===

“You were kindly afraid that I should be tired a few minutes ago: and standing does tire me, though I like a walk,” Catherine said. “I will say goodbye now. Perhaps you meant it kindly; and if so, I’ll thank you too﻿—all the more as it’s a mistake﻿—for that is the best of it,” she said with a laugh, waving her hand: and leaving them, walked on homewards with an alert and energetic step. But it would have been balm to their feelings if they had been able to see how very little like laughter was her face when she had once turned her back upon them. There was nobody to observe her along that quiet road. The nursemaids with their children had all turned townwards some time ago. There was not a soul between her and the gate of the Grange. Catherine’s face lengthened and darkened as if by a sudden effect of years; the sanguine life and confidence and force went out of it. She looked an old woman in that moment, as indeed she had a right to do, but did not, nature interposing for her aid. She said to herself that she would not think, would not ask herself what it meant until she should get home, and could feel the shelter of her own walls about her. She wanted shelter and privacy before she faced the fact which had been dimly shadowing before her, but never in this form. She was a very resolute woman, and had not come so far in life without having to confront and overcome many things that looked terrible enough at the first glance. But never since those early days which were so far off that they were half forgotten had she been called upon to face those troubles which sap the strength out of heart and will, the disappointments and bitterness brought upon us by those we love. She had few of these sufferings for what seems the saddest reason, that she had nobody to love. But it was not so sad as it appears. She had a number of people whom she loved well enough to be delighted by their prosperities, and overcast by their troubles. She had all the advantages of affection without being so closely knit to any as to have its drawbacks too. But this easy position changed when she became, so to speak, the mother of Edward Vernon. It was not the doing of providence, it was her own doing. She had taken it upon herself, and for years past she had said to herself that the boy had made her know, as she had never known before, what happiness was.

===Chinese===

“方才你们还体贴我怕我累：站着确实累我，散步我倒是喜欢的。”凯瑟琳说。“我这就道别了。你们许是一番好意；若是好意，我也谢谢——错会了好意更该谢——这正是妙处。”她笑着挥手告别，撇下她们，脚步轻快有力地往家走。可她们若看得见她一转过背去的那张脸，看得见那上面离笑有多远，心里就舒坦了。那条静路上没有人看她。带孩子的保姆们早就都朝城里去了。从她到格兰奇宅大门之间，一个人影也没有。凯瑟琳的脸拉长了、暗了，仿佛一霎平添了几年；那股血色的生气、自信同力量，从脸上退了出去。那一刻她看上去是个老妇——她原也到了做老妇的年纪，只是天性一直护着她，不让她显出来。她对自己说：不到家不想、不问这是什么意思；要到家，要觉得自家四壁围住了自己。她要遮蔽、要独处，然后才面对那桩事——它一路朦朦胧胧投着影，可从没有这副形状。她是个极有决断的女人，一生走到今天，吓人的事见过、也降服过不少。可是自从那些远得只剩一半记忆的早年之后，她再没有被迫面对过这一类麻烦——把心力同意志一起耗干的那一类，被我们所爱的人带来的失望与苦楚。这一类苦她受得少，缘由听起来顶惨：她没有可爱的人。可这事也不像表面那样惨。她有一批人，爱得足够：他们得意她高兴，他们倒霉她忧心。她享尽了感情的种种好处，又同谁都不曾紧密到连带坏处也领受。这轻松的位置，在她——不妨这样说——做了爱德华·弗农的母亲之后，就变了。这不是上天的安排，是她自己的安排。她自己揽下的；多年来她对自己说：这孩子叫她头一回知道了什么叫幸福。

===Original===

But now here was, swinging round slowly, revealing itself to her in glimpses, the reverse of the medal, the other side of the picture. Was he deceiving her? She had taken up his defence boldly, not caring what she said: but she had believed what she heard all the same, and had known it to be true. Was this why he had not cared to see her, to bid her good night, before he came out to have that meeting with Hester﻿—like a shopgirl and shopboy, she said to herself, her lip quivering with passion, vexation, derision, all bound together by the pain that produced them﻿—at the gate? The commonplace character of the meeting, the look of petty intrigue in it, humbled her pride in her boy. If they had met at Ellen’s dance, or in any legitimate way, she thought it would not have mortified her so much﻿—but like a lady’s maid and a footman, like Jane the scullery-girl and her young man! She laughed to herself at the thought, but the laugh was more painful than tears.

===Chinese===

可如今这枚勋章的背面、这幅画的另一面，缓缓转过来，一鳞半爪地向她显露。他在骗她么？方才她挺身为他辩护，怎样厉害的话都说得出口；可她信了她听见的，也知道那是真的。莫非为着这个，他才不愿来看她、道晚安，再出门去赴赫斯特的那场相会——像铺子里的小伙计同小姑娘，她对自己说，嘴唇因一股混在一起的怒气、懊恼、讥诮而发抖，统被底下那疼痛拴在一处——就在大门口？那场会面的平庸气味，那副偷情的琐屑相，伤了她为孩子撑的骄傲。若是在埃伦的舞会上，或任何正当场合相遇，她想她不至于这样受辱——可这像贴身女仆同跟班，像洗碗丫头简同她的汉子！她想着想着自己笑了，可那笑比眼泪更疼。

===Original===

By and by, however, Catherine came to take a little comfort out of the fact that Edward had not come to bid her good night. Not considering for a moment that any incident of all this might be accidental, though everything was so, she concluded that his heart had failed him, that he had felt himself incapable of the treachery of kissing her cheek in the usual tender way when about to do a thing which he knew would be so displeasing to her. When this occurred to Catherine the whole aspect of the matter changed: her features relaxed, her colour came back. This, no doubt, was how it had been. The girl had met him at Ellen’s folly﻿—how truly a folly had never been proved till now: and she was pretty and clever. Catherine was too proud to deny her her natural advantages; and men were fools, as was well known﻿—the best of them, the wisest of them!﻿—where women were concerned. She had led him into some engagement, some light wager perhaps, some defiance of what he would venture to do. And Edward had been silly enough to be led away. She did not want him to be too wise. If he was silly, it was no more than everybody else had been before him. But he, dear boy, true boy, having involved himself in a piece of folly, had shown that high respect to her, that he would rather let her suppose he had forgotten and neglected her, than come to her with the usual greeting when he knew he was doing something which would seem treachery to Catherine. Thus she, who for the first moment had known no wish but that of pushing homeward and hiding her sudden downfall within her own house where nobody could intrude upon her, had so triumphantly explained all that trouble away before she got home, that she entered the Grange radiant, with no sense of having a downfall to hide. The casuistry of love is more skilful than any device of philosophy. She explained everything to herself. She wondered that she had not read it in his face all the evening. She felt that it had been there, if she had only had eyes to see. A foolish talk carried a trifle too far﻿—a bold girl, not bad, no, not bad﻿—that was not necessary, and Catherine would be just﻿—pleased to get a little triumph when she could over the other side: and a foolish promise, not intended, had drawn him, perhaps against his will.

===Chinese===

可是渐渐地，凯瑟琳又从“爱德华没来道晚安”这件事里榨出一点安慰来。这一切原是桩桩碰巧——她却一刻也没往碰巧上想——她断定：是他心里过不去，是他自觉做不出那样的事——明知有一桩她必不容的事在先，还照平常那亲热样子来吻她的腮。这个念头一到，事情的全副面貌都变了：她眉目松开了，血色回来了。必是如此。是那姑娘在埃伦那场胡闹里缠上他的——那场胡闹有多胡闹，到今天才算坐实：她又有模样又有心眼。凯瑟琳骄傲，不屑否认人家天生的长处；而男人个个是傻子——顶好的、顶聪明的也不例外！——只要沾上女人。她哄着他许下了什么约，兴许一场小小的赌，一次敢不敢的激将。爱德华傻了一阵，被牵走了。她也不要他太精。他若傻，也不过是步了人人走过的后尘。可是他，乖孩子、实心的孩子，一失足卷进一桩傻事，倒对她存了那一份高敬：宁可叫她当他忘了她、慢了她，也不肯明知道要做一件在她看来近于背叛的事，还照例回来亲她。就这样，头一刻她一心只想奔回家、把她这场突然的塌陷藏进自家宅子里、藏得谁也闯不见；还没到家，她已把那场烦恼解释得烟消云散，进格兰奇宅门时光彩焕发，全不觉自己还有什么塌陷要藏。爱的诡辩术精过哲学的一切机巧。样样她都给自己讲通了。她奇怪：那一晚上自己怎么没从他脸上读出来。她觉得那本就写在那儿，只怪自己没长眼睛。一场糊涂话多说了一步——一个胆大的姑娘，不坏，不，不坏——不必那样，凯瑟琳是公道的——巴不得得空压一压对面那一头的气焰：一场糊涂的许诺，非出本心，就把他牵住了，兴许还违背着他自己的心意。

===Original===

By this subtle demonstration﻿—which no faculty less keen than that of love could have made﻿—Catherine proved, to her full satisfaction, the fundamental truth in him which no little trumpery deceit (of a kind so innocent as this!) could undermine. All this fine fabric was raised on the most insignificant foundation of fact. But what did that matter? it was enough. And if Catherine had been told that Edward’s forgetfulness of the good night had been accidental, and that his meeting with Hester was accidental, and that no incident of the night had been planned beforehand, she would have simply and flatly denied the possibility. She knew better; and she preferred the matter as it stood.

===Chinese===

凭这一番精微的推证——非爱的那种利眼做不出——凯瑟琳充分满意地证明了他身上那根本的真：这样一点小小不然的欺瞒（又是这样一种无伤大雅的！）侵蚀不动。这一整座精美的楼阁，起在最细不成话的一点实事上。可那有什么要紧？尽够了。倘有人告诉凯瑟琳：爱德华忘了道晚安原是碰巧，他同赫斯特相遇原是碰巧，这一夜没有一桩是预先安排——她只会一口回绝：不可能。她知道得更清楚；而且她宁可事情就像她讲的这样。

===Original===

The dinner-party was an insignificant affair to her after this. She did full justice to it, and to Roland Ashton, the chief guest, the man whom she delighted to honour, and for whose pleasure and profit the best people in Redborough were called together. He was already known to many of them, and it was Catherine’s pleasure to make her relationship and interest in the young visitor clear. But her mind was eager to get through the commonplace courtesies of the evening﻿—to come to the moment when Edward and she should meet alone. She could not pass her discovery over without note. She would tell him what she had heard, and what she had divined. She would give him the tender warning which such an affection as hers had a right to offer. If it was more than a passing flirtation (which she did not believe), to beg him to reconsider it; if his heart should be touched (which Heaven forbid! but the thought made her smile, it was so profoundly unlikely), to intreat him to reflect, and see how little satisfaction could come to him from such intercourse. She went over and over again the interview that was to come﻿—so often, indeed, that she exhausted it, and when the moment did come, did not remember half of what she intended to say. It came, indeed, in a way entirely contrary to that she had imagined. After the party had dispersed, Edward took Roland into his room to smoke with him﻿—which she ought to have recollected he was in the habit of doing﻿—and then, what was more disappointing still, went out with him to accompany him part of the way. She was going downstairs to Edward’s room, that she might get these explanations off her mind without a moment’s delay, and was taken entirely by surprise when she heard the door close, and two voices continuing outside.

“Has Mr. Edward gone out?” she asked, with a trembling she could scarcely control, of the butler, when he came up to put out the lights.

“I was to say, ma’am, as he’d be back in half an hour,” said the man.

===Chinese===

那场晚宴在这以后于她不过是件小事。她照样把它应酬得尽善尽美，也照样应酬了罗兰·阿什顿——主客，她乐于尊荣的人，为他的乐与利，雷德伯勒的头等人物都被请到一处。他们许多人已认识他；叫自己的亲眷关系同对这位年轻客人的器重人人了然，也是凯瑟琳的乐事。可她的心只急着熬过晚间那些寻常的客套——熬到她同爱德华单独相见的那一刻。这一桩发现她不能不声不响放过。她要把听来的、猜出的都告诉他。她要给他一声温柔的警告——她这样的爱有权给的警告。倘若那不只是一场过眼的调情（她不信是），就求他再思量；倘若他的心真动了（上天不容！可这念头叫她微笑，实在悬得不能再悬），就恳他掂量掂量，看这样的往来能给他多少满足。那场将来的谈话她一遍又一遍排演——排得太多，竟排空了；真到那一刻，要说的话倒忘了一半。那一刻临头的方式，也同她设想的完全两样。客人散后，爱德华带罗兰进自己屋里抽烟——这本该记得是他的老例——随后，更叫人失望的是，又同他一道出去，送他一程。她正下楼要到爱德华屋里去，好把那些剖白片刻不留地卸下心头，忽听得门关上，两个人声在门外延续下去。

“爱德华先生出去了？”管家上来熄灯时，她问，一身压抑不住的战栗。

“他叫小的回话，太太，说他半个钟头就回来。”那人说。

===Original===

Catherine sent her maid to bed, and kept her particular lamp burning on her little table, waiting there in the dimness of the large deserted room, hearing every crackle and rustle of the night. It seemed to her far more than half an hour before she heard Edward’s key in the door; but she was resolved not to be balked now. She had no idea, poor lady, that he thought her suspicious, inquisitive, and watchful, making domiciliary visits in order to find him out in something, which was very far from Catherine’s disposition. She went down accordingly to lose no time, and met him in the hall. He was astonished to see her, as was natural enough; and she had an uneasy tremor upon her, which was natural too, but which looked like cold. He was full of apologies for having kept her up.

“If I had known you would have waited for me, Aunt Catherine﻿—”

“You did not say good night to me last night, Edward. I did not like that to happen two nights running. I will go into your room, not to hurry you upstairs.”

“I can’t think how that happened,” he said, following her into the cosy room, with its red curtains and cheerful fire, and all the conveniences and prettiness she had accumulated for him there. “I had been thinking hard, and my mind was full of balance-sheets and figures. I entirely forgot I had not seen you.”

She turned round upon him, taking his arm between her hands, and looking with a tender smile into his face.

“No, my dear boy, I know better than that. You had a reason﻿—which shows me how well I have divined you, and how true you are, Edward. I have been told where﻿—you went to last night.”

This startled him greatly for the moment. He looked at her with an alarmed expression: but seeing no anger in her face, said quickly﻿—

“That was all quite accidental, Aunt Catherine. You don’t think I went there on purpose, do you?” without shrinking at all from her eyes.

“Yes, Edward, I thought you did. Perhaps I was wrong. I thought there might have been some silly bargain﻿—some promise made without thought: and that you felt a little treacherous﻿—that is a harsh word﻿—deceitful﻿—that is worse﻿—to me, and would not come back and kiss me when you might be supposed to be going against me. I forgave you entirely, Edward, for that good thought.”

He was a little touched in spite of himself.

===Chinese===

凯瑟琳打发女仆去睡，只留她那盏专用的灯在小桌上亮着，在那间空落落的大屋子的昏暗里守着，听着夜里的每一声脆响、每一阵窸窣。仿佛远不止半个钟头，她才听见爱德华的钥匙插进门去；可这一回她打定主意不容再落空。可怜的太太全不知道，他把她想成多疑、好事、爱盯梢，动不动上门查访、好拿住他的什么把柄——这同凯瑟琳的性子隔了十万八千里。她于是一刻也不耽搁地下楼去，在门厅里截住了他。他见到她自然一惊；她身上也有一阵压不住的轻颤，也是自然的，看着倒像受了寒。他满口道歉，说害她熬了夜。

“早知道您会等我，凯瑟琳姑妈——”

“你昨晚没同我道晚安，爱德华。我可不愿这样的事接连两晚。我到你屋里坐坐，免得催你上楼。”

“真不知怎么就会那样，”他说着随她走进那间舒适的小屋——红帘子、旺炉火，还有她为他攒下的种种便利同漂亮什物。“我想事想得太深，满脑子资产负债表同数字。竟忘了还没见您。”

她转过身来，把他的胳膊夹在两手之间，含着温柔的笑望进他脸里。

“不，我的乖孩子，我知道得更清楚。你有你的缘故——这倒叫我看出，我把你猜得多准，你又是多真，爱德华。有人告诉我你昨夜——到哪儿去了。”

这话一时叫他大吃一惊。他带着一点惊惶望着她；可看她脸上并无怒意，便应声说——

“那全是碰巧，凯瑟琳姑妈。您总不至于当我是有意去的吧？”眼睛对她毫不躲闪。

“是，爱德华，我当你是有意的。兴许我错了。我想或许有什么糊涂的赌约——一句没过脑子的许诺：你自觉有点像背叛——这字眼太重——像欺瞒——更重——欺瞒我，就不肯在临做一件我知道你必不赞成的事之前，还回来照例吻我。那一层好意，爱德华，我全饶了你。”

他不由得有些感动。

===Original===

“You are very good, Aunt Catherine﻿—far better to me than I deserve; but, as a matter of fact, it was all purely accidental. I had been very busy, and felt feverish and sleepless. I went out to have a turn in the moonlight: chance took me that way. There was light in Mrs. John’s window. They heard my steps, and looked out in great surprise, and asked me to come in. I could scarcely satisfy her,” he said, with an embarrassed little laugh, “that you were not ill, and had not sent for her to nurse you. It was as good as a play,” he went on, still laughing, followed in every word by her anxious eyes, “to see poor Mrs. John’s struggle between politeness and sleep. She was very sleepy, poor little woman! but dreadfully polite. You may suppose I was surprised enough to find myself there.”

“Yes,” she said, still holding him, still reading his face with her anxious eyes, but feeling the ground cut from under her feet. She was a little breathless with anxiety and excitement. “I wonder﻿—that you did not tell me of it﻿—this morning.”

“Dear Aunt Catherine,” he said, “pardon me, but you have a little prejudice, you know, against these people. And it was so entirely accidental. You might have thought, had I told you, that it had been done on purpose.”

“Did I ever doubt what you said to me, Edward?”

“No,” he said, taking her hands in his tenderly, as she thought; and indeed the action was not without real tenderness, for his heart was touched. “No,” he said, smiling, “but yet you would have had a little doubt﻿—a little wonder whether it was really so.”

“And it *was* really so?” she said, looking into his face, “really﻿—really﻿—no little shadow of a wish for﻿—a little provocation, a little talk, a little fun if you like, Edward? Oh, no, I have no prejudice. I should know it was quite natural. And you mean that there was nothing at all, nothing of this﻿—a mere accident, nothing more?”

He kissed her cheek, and he laughed at her in a filial way.

“Didn’t I tell you, Aunt Catherine? You believe me﻿—oh, yes; but then you ask me if really﻿—really I am saying what is true? Really﻿—really as often as you like; it was accident, and nothing more.”

===Chinese===

“您太好了，凯瑟琳姑妈——好得我受之有愧；可说实话，那真是全然的巧合。我那时忙极了，浑身燥热睡不着。出去到月光里走一圈：碰巧走到那边。约翰太太窗里有灯。她们听见脚步，又惊又疑地探出头，请我进去。我好不容易才叫她信服，”他有点窘地笑着说，“说您没病，没打发人请她来看护。那一晚抵得一出戏，”他接着说，还在笑，她那双焦灼的眼睛逐字逐句跟着，“看可怜的约翰太太在礼貌同瞌睡中间挣扎。她瞌睡极了，可怜的小妇人！可客气得要命。您想，我发觉自己站在她们家，那份吃惊也不小。”

“是，”她说，仍旧挽着他，仍旧用焦灼的眼睛读他的脸，只觉脚底的地被抽走了。焦灼同激动叫她有点透不过气。“我只是纳帘——今天早晨你没告诉我。”

“亲爱的凯瑟琳姑妈，”他说，“恕我直言，您对那家人有一点成见，您知道的。而那又完全是碰巧。若告诉了您，您说不定当我是有意去的。”

“我可曾疑过你对我说的话，爱德华？”

“没有，”他说，温柔地把她两只手握进手里——她是这样感觉；那动作也确实带着真情，他的心是动了。“没有，”他微笑着说，“可您总还会有那么一小点疑——一小点嘀咕，不知到底是不是。”

“那到底*是*不是？”她望着他的脸说，“到底——到底——没有一丝丝盼着——一点点撩拨、一点点闲谈、一点点您要叫它乐子就乐子的意思，爱德华？哦，不，我没有成见。我自会知道那全然人情之常。你是说，什么都没有，这一类什么都没有——纯是意外，再无其他？”

他吻了她的腮，用儿子般的口气笑她。

“我不是说了么，凯瑟琳姑妈？您信我——哦，是；可您又问我，到底——到底我说的可是真话？到底——到底，随您问多少回；是意外，再无其他。”

===Original===

This was how all the eloquent things which Catherine had prepared to say were never said. She went up to bed pleased and happy, yet not so pleased as if he had confessed her version of the story to be the true one. She did not doubt his word﻿—oh no, no﻿—but yet﻿—the other version looked more true to nature. She could have understood it better that way.

===Chinese===

凯瑟琳备下的那许多恳切话，就这样一句也没说出口。她上楼就寝，又欢喜又快活，却不及他若认下她那一版故事做真版时那样欢喜。他的话她不疑——哦，不，不疑——可是——另一版总更像天理。是那样的话，她倒更能懂了。

## XXXVI / 三十六
===Original===

In the Labyrinth

After these events there seemed a lull, in which nothing more seemed to happen. Though time is so short, and our modern pace of living, we flatter ourselves, so much more rapid than of old, how few after all are the periods in which things happen, and with what long stretches of vacant days between! Hester could hardly explain to herself how it was that Edward Vernon’s sudden evening visit, so unexpected, so unprecedented, had made an entire revolution in her life. There had been no mutual confessions of love, no proposal, no acceptance such as are supposed to be necessary. There was nothing to confide to her mother, had it been possible to take anyone into that strait union of two suddenly become one. The effect bewildered her entirely, and she could not tell how it had been produced; but yet it was so. They had been on the eve of this, she felt, for years, and the first time that they met, in a moment of complete freedom, their souls flowed together, flowed into one. Perhaps he had not meant it when he came. The dim parlour and the sleepy mother, trying hard to be polite, quite unconscious how unnecessary her presence was; the young man, with his eager eyes, scarcely keeping himself in﻿—came before her like a curious picture a hundred times in a day: and then the sudden sweep of the torrent after it, the almost involuntary, impetuous, unalterable junction of these two hearts and lives. But the shock even of happiness when it comes so suddenly is great; and Hester was not sure even that she was happy. He seemed to have led her to the edge of some labyrinth, without freedom to leave it, or to advance into its mysteries. There was a clue, indeed, but it was lying in loose coils at her feet, and who could tell if it ever could be sufficiently straightened, sufficiently tightened, to give any real guidance? There was no habit of meeting in their lives, no way of seeing each other even, without attracting suspicion. He sent her a letter next morning, full of love, and of ecstatic realisation that she was his, and that in all his difficulties he was sure of her sympathy, but it was understood that he was not to make such a breach of all his habits as to come to see her; and Hester was too proud to break through hers, as she had done that one morning in order to see him.

===Chinese===

迷宫中

这些事过后，似乎起了一段风平浪静，再没有什么发生似的。时间这样短，我们现代的生活步调——我们自己夸耀——又比古时快得多；可到头来，真正有事情发生的时辰何其少，中间隔着的空落日子又何其长！爱德华·弗农那个突如其来的夜访——那样意外，那样没有先例——竟把她整个的一生翻了个个儿，赫斯特自己也说不清是怎么一回事。没有彼此的爱情表白，没有求婚，没有人们认为必不可少的应允。没有可以讲给母亲听的东西——就算那两个骤然合一的人，容得下第三个人走进那紧窄的结合。这效果把她整个人弄懵了，她说不出它是怎么造成的；可它就是这样。她觉得，他们在这件事的边上已经站了多年；头一回在完全自由的一刻里相遇，他们的灵魂便流到了一处，流成了一个。也许他来的时候并没有这个意思。昏暗的起居室，昏昏欲睡的母亲，竭力地客气着，全不知自己在场是多馀——还有那年轻人，一双急切的眼睛，几乎收不住自己——这一幅奇特的画，一天里在她眼前过上一百遍：随后是那之后洪流的猛一倾泻：两颗心、两条命，几乎是身不由己的、奔腾的、再改不了的合流。可幸福来得这样骤然，连它的震荡也大；赫斯特连自己快活不快活都拿不准了。他仿佛把她领到了一座迷宫的边上：既不得脱身离去，也不得深入它的奥秘。引线倒是有一条，却松松地盘在她脚边；谁能说它几时挣得直、绷得紧，给得出一点真正的指引？他们的生活里没有相见的惯例，甚至连一条见面的路都没有——不招疑心的路没有。第二天早晨他给她来了封信，满是爱，满是他得了她的狂喜，满是在他一切难关里她那份同情稳稳是他的笃定；可有一点彼此默契：他不该把全部习惯破得那样彻底，跑来看她；而赫斯特也太骄傲，不肯破她自己的——虽说为见他，有一天早晨她已经破过一回。

===Original===

So that everything remained a secret between them, and save for the sudden understanding into which they had leaped, the sort of betrothal which both took for granted, there was no difference in their outward lives; which was a state of things infinitely painful to the girl who lived her usual daily life with her mother and her friends in a state of guilty abstraction, thinking of *him* all the time, and feeling herself a domestic traitor. She felt that it was but the shell of her that remained, following mechanically the usual occupations, talking from the lips outward, absorbed in a long perpetual reverie of new consciousness, new hopes and fears. That secret world had need to have been bright to make up to her for the sense of guilt and treachery with which she entered into it: and it was not bright. The air was dark and tremulous as in that sad valley, sad yet sweet, which, in Dante, lies outside of hell. She never could tell at what moment some dark unknown shape of calamity might appear through its twilight coming towards them; for Edward had been driven to her by anxiety and trouble, and the sense of a burden which he could not bear alone. What was it? He did not tell her in his letter. The other little notes he wrote were but appeals to her sympathy﻿—petitions to her to love him, to think of him. Ah! Hester thought to herself, no fear of that﻿—but how? What was she to think? in what way was her imagination to follow him, groping dimly amid scenes she did not understand? His secret was as a germ of fire in her heart﻿—which by times blazed up into hot flames, devouring her with all the anguish of that thirst to know which is one of the tortures of uneasy love. What was it that troubled him so, that alarmed him so, that might ruin and overwhelm him﻿—that might make him fly, which was the most mysterious hint of all? But to all these questions she got no satisfaction. For the first few days she had a little furtive outlet to her anxiety in questioning Roland, which she did with a vague sense of treachery to Edward, as if she were endeavouring to surprise his secrets by a back way, but very little perception of the false impression which her interest in his communications was making upon Roland, who himself became day by day more ready to believe that marriage might become a possible venture, and that the decision of it rested chiefly with himself.

===Chinese===

于是一切仍是两人之间的秘密；除了他们骤然跳进去的那份默契——那份两人都认作当然的婚约——他们外在的生活没有一丝改变。这局面于姑娘苦到没有底：她照旧同母亲、同朋友过平常的日子，人却在一层负罪的恍惚里，时时刻刻想着*他*，觉得自己是家里的一个内奸。她觉得留下来的只是自己的一副空壳，机械地做惯常的事，嘴唇皮子向外说话，整个人泡在一场绵长的白日梦里——新的自觉，新的盼与怕。那个秘密世界，原该亮堂些，才抵得过她踏进去时那份负疚与背叛之感：可它不亮堂。那里的空气昏暗而颤动，像但丁笔下地狱门外那座愁谷——愁，却也甜。她永远说不准，暮色里哪一刻会走出一个黑暗的、不成形状的灾殃，朝他们逼来；因为爱德华是被焦灼与苦难赶到她这里来的，还背着一副他独自扛不动的担子。是什么？信里他不说。他写的另一些小字条，不过是对她同情的呼吁——求她爱他、想他的请愿。啊！赫斯特心里说，这个不怕——可是怎样去想？她该想什么？她的想象该怎样跟着他，在他不懂的场景中间摸索？他的秘密像一粒火种埋在她心里，时而蹿起烈焰，把她烧噬——那份求知若渴的痛楚，正是惴惴之爱的一种刑罚。究竟是什么这样烦他、这样吓他、可能毁他灭他——还可能叫他远走，这暗示最是神秘？可这些问题，她一个也讨不到答案。起初几天，盘问罗兰给了她一点偷偷的出口；她一边问，一边隐隐觉得对不起爱德华，仿佛在抄后路掏他的秘密；却全没觉出，她对他那些“行情”的关切，正在罗兰心里落下一副假象——罗兰本人一天比一天更相信：成家兴许是一桩可为的冒险，而决断大半握在他自己手里。

===Original===

He knew no other reason why she should question him than interest in himself, and it was with a grateful zeal that he attempted to gratify a curiosity which was so legitimate, yet so unusual. He explained his trade with that pleasure which the wisest of men feel in talking about themselves, and never divined that her rapid mind passed everything through one narrow test, i.e. whether it was possible that it could concern Edward. She did not even remark the *attendrissement* with which he received her questions, with eyes that said volumes. These eyes overflowed with pleasure and sentiment as he made his little disquisitions.

“After this,” he said, with a laugh, “you will be armed *cap-à-pied* against any doubtful agency, and able when you like to speculate for yourself.”

“And why should not I speculate,” said Hester, “if I had any money? It is like fighting, I suppose. It feels like living, they say. But after all it is no true life﻿—only figures, as you tell me.”

“Figures,” said Roland, “mean so much; in this elemental way they mean money. And money means﻿—”

“Figures over again,” Hester said, with a certain weary disdain. It was not possible that this alone could be the tragic danger, the burden of the soul that Edward meant. But Roland was thinking his own thoughts, and interpreted her comments in a way of his own.

“It means most things in this world,” he said; “unfortunately, however high-minded we are, we can do nothing without it. It means of course show and luxury, and gaiety, and all the things you despise; but at the same time﻿—It means,” he said, after a little pause, “the house which two people could make into paradise. It means ease of mind, so that a man can rise every day without anxiety, knowing that he has enough for every claim upon him. Ah! how can I say all that it means﻿—you would laugh, or be frightened. It means the right to love, and the right to say it.” Roland was making use of all his well-worn artillery, but of something more besides which he had not quite understood the existence of﻿—something which lent a very eloquent tremor to his voice and doubled the seduction of his eyes.

===Chinese===

她为什么会盘问他，他想不出别的缘故，只能是对他本人的兴趣；于是他怀着感激的热忱，力图饱足这份好奇心——这样名正言顺、又这样不寻常的好奇心。他讲起自己的行当，带着再聪明的人谈自己时也有的那份乐趣；做梦也想不到，她那颗飞快的头脑把一切只过一道窄筛：此事可不可能与爱德华相干。他接她提问时那一副动情——那双千言万语的眼睛——她甚至没有留意。他小施讲章的时候，那双眼睛里的欢喜与情意满得往外溢。

“经过这一课，”他笑着说，“您就从头到脚全副武装，什么样的可疑经手都骗不了您，高兴时还能自己下场投机呢。”

“我为什么不能投机，”赫斯特说，“如果我有钱？那像打仗，我猜。人说，那滋味像活着。可说到底它不是真生活——不过是数字，照你告诉我的。”

“数字，”罗兰说，“有它的分量；往这最根本里说，它意味着钱。而钱意味着——”

“还是数字。”赫斯特说，带着一丝倦怠的轻蔑。单是这个，不可能就是爱德华说的那种悲剧性的险、那种灵魂的重负。可罗兰想的是他自己的心事，把她的话按他自己的路数解了。

“它意味着这世上大多数东西，”他说；“不幸，我们志向再高，没有它也寸步难行。它自然意味着排场与奢华、欢娱，同你鄙薄的一切；可同时——它意味着，”他略停了停，说，“一座两个人可以变成天堂的屋子。它意味着心安，一个男人每天醒来不必发愁，知道每一项该付的都付得起。啊！它意味着的一切，我怎么说得尽——你要么笑，要么吓着。它意味着爱的权利，同把爱说出口的权利。”罗兰搬动着他那些使旧了的炮；还动了一样连他自己也不甚明了的东西——那东西给他嗓音里添了动人的颤，给他眼睛里的诱惑加了一倍。

===Original===

“Oh! I was not thinking of anything half so sentimental,” said Hester. She never looked at him, to be affected by his glances, or paid any attention to his voice. And yet there had been a moment when Roland’s departure made the world itself shrink and look narrow: but she remembered nothing about that now. “To tell the truth, all I was thinking of was buying and selling,” she said; “for business means that, doesn’t it? Of course I suppose, as we must have money to live, you may say that money is the first thing in life, more necessary than bread; but I did not mean that.”

===Chinese===

“哦！我想的远没有这么多情。”赫斯特说。她从不看他，不受他眼波的撩动，也不留神他的嗓音。可是曾经有过一刻，罗兰的离开叫世界本身缩了水、显出窄来：这些她如今一点也想不起。“说实在的，我满脑子只有买进卖出。”她说；“生意不就是那个吗？当然，人活着总得有钱，你尽可以说钱是人生头一件东西，比面包还不可少；可我不是那个意思。”

===Original===

Conversations which ended in this way were, however, very little serviceable to Hester, for how could she tell which of these mysteries of the craft had entangled Edward, or if any of them could justify the seriousness of his excitement, the tragic sense of a possible catastrophe, the wild expedient of flight, which had been in his words! All this talk about the vicissitudes of money was too petty to satisfy her mind as a reason. And still less was that talk calculated to promote Roland’s purpose, who did not care very much what he was saying so long as he could recommend himself to her favourable opinion. What he wanted was to show her that the future had large possibilities of advancement. He wanted, without committing himself or doing anything that could be afterwards commented upon as “behaving badly,” to leave upon Hester’s mind a delicate intimation that he meant to come back, to speak more plainly, to say things more worthy of her attention; and that she might be able to make up her mind in the meantime and not be taken by surprise. Roland was not so romantic as to be unaware that the advantages lay on his own side; he had solid gifts to give, and a position to offer, which could not be carelessly considered by any person of sense. And he was well aware that there was no crowd of candidates contending for Hester’s hand. She had to him the air of a girl neglected, altogether out of the way of forming any satisfactory engagements, almost painfully divested of that “chance” which Emma looked at with such sensible if matter-of-fact eyes. Roland, to do him justice, was all the more willing to show her a romantic devotion on this account, but it kept him free from anxiety about his own hopes. There had been Harry indeed﻿—but she would not have Harry. And Edward he was aware had paid her furtive “attentions” at Ellen Merridew’s parties; but what could Edward do? He could not pay serious addresses to anyone, in his circumstances, far less to Hester: and he was not the fellow to marry a girl without money and under the cold shade of Catherine’s disfavour. This last was one of the things that made Roland himself hesitate﻿—but he thought it might be got over. And there could be no doubt that his mind had made great strides towards making itself up during this Christmas visit.

===Chinese===

不过，这样收场的谈话，于赫斯特几乎没有用处：这一行的种种奥秘，哪一样缠住了爱德华，她无从知道；哪一样配得上他那份亢奋的郑重、那份大祸将临的悲剧感、他话里那种出亡的孤注——她更无从知道！这一套银钱起落的谈论，作为缘由太琐屑，填不满她的心。而这话于罗兰的目的，促进得更少——只要能把自己推销到她的好感里，他说什么倒在其次。他要让她看见：前程里有的是高升的可能。他要——既不承诺自己，也不做任何日后被议论成“行止不端”的事——在赫斯特心里留下一缕精微的暗示：他打算回来，把话说得更明，说些更配她一听的事；她也好趁这个空当打定主意，到时不会措手不及。罗兰没有浪漫到看不见便宜在自己这一边；他有实打实的馈赠可给，有身份可奉——凡有见识的人都不能等闲视之。他也深知，竞逐赫斯特之手的没有一群人。在他眼里，她是一个被冷落的姑娘，全然够不上结什么像样的婚约，几乎惨然地缺着埃玛用那双务实（虽属平淡）的眼睛望着的那种“机会”。凭良心说罗兰，正因这一层，他越发情愿对她献一场浪漫的殷勤；而这也叫他对自己那份指望分外安心。哈里原是有过一个——可她不要哈里。爱德华呢，他知道在埃伦·梅里迪尤家的舞会上对她下过偷偷的“殷勤”；可爱德华能怎样？以他的处境，他不能向任何人正经求婚，更别说向赫斯特：他也不是那样的人——娶一个没有钱的姑娘，还要站在凯瑟琳冷眼的荫翳底下。这最后一层，也是叫罗兰自己踌躇的一样——可他想，总能过得了。不容置疑，这趟圣诞造访里，他的心朝“定下来”迈出了一大截。

===Original===

But it was a short visit on the whole, for he had not much time to spare for pleasure, and his business had been summarily ended. Emma thought it was owing to Hester’s interference that she was left behind, Reginald Merridew having not yet “spoken;” but there was in reality a certain sympathy in Roland’s mind with his sister’s honest desire to be settled, and there would be much convenience in it could it be accomplished, he felt. He went away accordingly, slightly depressed by Hester’s indifferent farewell, and remembering the look of over-clearness in her eyes when he had gone away the first time with a sort of fond regret. He was sure that day that she had shed a few tears over his departure, of which there was no appearance now. But soon he recovered his spirits, asking himself to look the situation in the face. Who else was there? What rival could he have? There was nobody. She was stranded in that old house as if it had been a desolate island. And she could not be content to vegetate there forever, a girl of her spirit. There was a practical element in Roland’s character, notwithstanding his romantic eyes.

===Chinese===

不过总的说来，这趟造访不长：他均不出多少工夫消遣，生意上的事也已干脆了结。埃玛以为自己是被赫斯特搅了局才落下了——雷金纳德·梅里迪尤还没“开口”；其实罗兰心里，倒真有些同情妹妹那点安家的老实心愿；他觉得，这事若成，还有许多便宜。于是他走了，赫斯特那场淡漠的送别叫他稍稍低沉；又带着一种眷恋的怅惆，想起头一回走时她眼里那副过分明亮的神色。那一天他拿得准，她为他的离去落过几滴泪；这一回却毫无迹象。可他很快便回了神，叫自己直面这局面。此外还有谁？他能有什么对手？没有谁。她搁浅在那座老宅里，像搁浅在一座荒岛上。她那样心气的姑娘，总不甘心在那儿一辈子当草木。罗兰这个人，尽管一双浪漫的眼睛，骨子里是有实干的一面的。

===Original===

And Hester was so ungrateful that his departure was almost a relief to her. She forgot altogether that she had cried the first time when he went away, and she was glad to be set free from the hope, which at the same time was a fear, of finding out something about Edward’s troubles from his chance revelations. Her mind turned now with unbroken eagerness to the sole means of intercourse which she had with her lover, which could be calculated upon with any freedom, which were Ellen’s parties﻿—the Thés Dansantes! It seemed incredible that her entire existence should be concentrated in a weekly assembly so frivolous, so thoughtless, and nonsensical, and that all those grave and troublous thoughts should seek interpretation in a dance. But so it was. The first of them brought her only disappointment, and that of a kind that she felt almost maddening﻿—for Edward did not appear. He gave her no warning, which was cruel, and when she found, after hours of waiting, that he was not expected, the shock of resentment and shame and dismay almost stunned her: but pride carried the day. She threw herself into the current with a sort of desperation, and held her place with the gayest: then entered, sombre and silent, upon another week of suspense. The second occasion was not so bad. He was there, and appropriated her as usual, and breathed hints into her ear which kept her in a whirl of excitement.

“How can I explain to you,” he said, “here? And even if I could explain to you, I don’t want to do it, for it is all miserable trade, which you would not understand﻿—which I don’t wish you to understand.”

“But I want to understand it, Edward. You don’t think how cruel it is to me to tell me just so much, then leave me outside.”

“Should I *not* have told you so much?” he said, looking at her. “You are right. I believe you are right, Hester; but my heart was running over, and to no one else could I say a word. I could not put a little bit of my burden upon anyone but you. I know it was selfish, dear.”

“Oh, Edward; it is not that. I will bear your burden; I am glad to help you; I would bear it all for you if I could,” she cried with her bright eyes widening, her cheeks glowing with enthusiasm. “Don’t you *know* that I would bear it all if I could? It is not that. But tell me, only tell me a little more.”

He shook his head.

===Chinese===

而赫斯特这样不知好歹：他的离去于她几乎是一种解脱。她把头一回他走时自己哭过的事忘了个干净，还庆幸得了自由——从那个指望（同时也是那个恐惧）里得了自由：指望从他偶然的漏话里，探出一点爱德华的难处。如今她的心以不歇的热切，转向她同情人之间唯一可指望的交通——埃伦家的聚会——茶舞会！她整个的生存，竟凝聚在一场每礼拜一回、这样轻浮、这样没心没肺、这样胡闹的集会上；那一脑子的沉重与烦乱，竟要到一场舞里去求解——这看着叫人难以置信。可它就是这样。头一场带给她的只有失望，而且失望得她几乎要疯——爱德华没有露面。他连个招呼都不打，真狠心；等了几个钟头，才听说人家根本没盼他来：怨、羞、慌三路齐撞，几乎把她撞懵：可骄傲撑住了场面。她带着一股绝望扎进人流，同最快活的人抢着位子；随后阴沉着、沉默着，走进又一周的悬望。第二回不算太糟。他在，照旧把她据为己有，往她耳朵里吹着话，吹得她整晚晕眩。

“在这儿，我怎么讲给你听？”他说。“就算讲得清，我也不想讲：那全是些可怜的生意经，你不会懂——我也不要你懂。”

“可我要懂，爱德华。你不想想这有多狠：只对我说这么多，又把我关在门外。”

“那这一点也不该说？”他望着她说。“你说得对。我相信你是对的，赫斯特；可我心里的东西满了，往外溢；除了你，我一个字也说不出。这副担子，除了你，我一小片也搁不到别人肩上。我知道这自私，亲爱的。”

“哦，爱德华；不是那个。我愿意担你的担子；帮你我高兴；只要能够，我全替你担了。”她叫道，明亮的眼睁大了，两颊烧着热忱。“你不知道只要能够我全替你担吗？不是那个。只是告诉我，只再多告诉我一点。”

他摇了摇头。

===Original===

“Hester,” he said, “that is not what a man wants in a woman; not to go and explain it all to her with pen and ink, and tables and figures, to make her understand as he would have to do with a man. What he wants, dear, is very different﻿—just to lean upon you﻿—to know that you sympathise, and think of me, and feel for me, and believe in me, and that you will share whatever comes.”

Hester said nothing, but her countenance grew very grave.

“Don’t you think that a woman could do all that﻿—and yet that it would be easier for her if she understood what it was, and why it was?” she said, after a pause.

“Dear,” said Edward, gazing at her with glowing eyes. He was in a hopeful mood, and he allowed himself to indulge the love and pleasure he felt in her, having bound her to him with a chain more fast than iron. “Darling! was it ever known that a woman, a girl like you (if there ever was a girl like my Hester), thought of what would be easiest? And you who would bear it all, you said.”

“So I should﻿—gladly; but then I should understand.”

“My only love! understanding is nothing, it matters nothing; another fellow, any man, a clerk in the office, would understand. I want your sympathy. I want﻿—you.”

“Oh, Edward!” she cried, “you have me and my sympathy﻿—even if you were wrong you should have my sympathy. But is it just, is it good, do you think, that you should ask all that and tell me nothing? I am a woman, but I am not a fool. I can understand most things. Try me﻿—tell me﻿—I will set my mind to it. Sympathy that is ignorant cannot be so good as sympathy that knows.”

He made a little pause, and then he said, looking at her, she felt, severely, with a scoff in his voice﻿—

“And where is this explanation to take place? Will you appoint to meet me somewhere with my balance-sheet and my vouchers? Perhaps you will come to my room at the bank? or appoint an accountant whom you can trust?”

“Edward!” she drew her hand out of his arm and then put it back again after a moment’s hesitation, “do you want me to look a wretch even to myself? Why should you say all this? and why﻿—why be so unjust to me? You forget that when one knows nothing one thinks all sorts of things, and invents a hundred terrors. Tell me how it is in the general not details. You do not want silly sympathy.”

===Chinese===

“赫斯特，”他说，“男人要女人给的，不是这个；不是拿着笔墨、表格同数字去对她讲解，像对一个男人非讲不可那样叫她懂。他要的，亲爱的，完全是另一样——就只是倚着你——知道你同情，想着我，疼着我，信着我，知道无论来什么你都一同担。”

赫斯特没作声，脸色却沉了下来。

“你不想想，这些一个女人全做得到——可她若懂了那是什么、为什么，做起来岂不更容易？”停了一停，她说。

“亲爱的。”爱德华说，一双发亮的眼睛盯着她。他正在有望的心境里，容许自己放胆受用他对她的爱与欢喜——他已拿一条比铁还牢的链子把她拴在了身上。“心肝！几时听说过一个女人——一个像你这样的姑娘（世上可曾有过像我的赫斯特这样的姑娘）——先掂量怎样省力？还是你说过的：你全都担。”

“我担——甘愿担；可那样我就得懂。”

“我唯一的爱！懂算不得什么，顶不了什么；换个家伙，随便哪个男人，衙门里一个文案，都懂。我要的是你的同情。我要的是——你。”

“哦，爱德华！”她叫道，“你已经有我、有我的同情——就算你错了，这同情也是你的。可你要了这一切、却什么也不告诉我——这公道吗？这算好吗？我是女人，可不是傻子。多数事我都懂得了。试我——告诉我——我把心思全用上去。蒙在鼓里的同情，总比不上明白底里的同情。”

他顿了一顿；随后说——她觉得他望她的眼神很严，话音里带着讥诮——

“这番讲解打算在哪儿进行？您要约个地方见我，带着我的资产负债表和单据吗？兴许您要亲临银行我的房间？还是聘一位您信得过的会计师？”

“爱德华！”她把手从他臂弯里抽出来，迟疑片刻又放了回去，“你要叫我在自己眼里也成个可怜虫吗？你说这些做什么？为什么——为什么这样不公道地待我？你忘了：人一无所知，就会什么都想，凭空造出一百样恐怖。只把大势告诉我，不必讲细节。你总不要一份傻同情。”

===Original===

“I want all your sympathy, silly or not. I want you. Hester, if we are to escape notice we must dance like the rest; we cannot stand and talk all night. And I am just in the mood for it!” he cried.

Many people no doubt have waltzed with very little inclination for it, people who were both sad and sorry, disappointed, heartbroken; but few more reluctant than Hester, who felt her position intolerable, and by whom the complacent injustice of it, the calm assertion that such blind adherence was all that was to be looked for from a woman, was more irritating and offensive than can be described. Was it possible that he thought so? that this was what she would have to encounter in the life she should spend with him? Her advice, her intelligent help, her understanding, all ignored, and nothing wanted but a kind of doggish fidelity, an unreasoning belief? Hester felt it cruel to be made to dance even, to be spun through the crowd as if in the merest caprice of gaiety while at such a crisis of her fate.

But neither this nor their subsequent conversations made any difference; the evening passed for her as in a dream. Edward, who was not much of a dancer, and seldom cared to perform these rites with any partner but herself, danced repeatedly with others that night, while Hester stood by looking on with gathering bewilderment. She had a headache, she said. It was her mother’s way of getting free of every embarrassment, and Hester was acquainted with the expedient, though she had not hitherto been tempted to use it. She sat by Mrs. Merridew, the mother of the house, who was a kind woman, and disposed to be good to her. “Just say the word, my dear, and as soon as our carriage comes I will take you home,” this lady said; “for to sit with a racking headache and watch other young folks dancing is more than flesh and blood can bear.” But alas! Mrs. Merridew’s carriage was not ordered till two o’clock, and Hester had to bear her burden. And of course it was not thus that the evening ended. He came to seek her at Mrs. Merridew’s side, and heard the account of her headache with a sympathetic countenance.

===Chinese===

“我要的是你全部的同情，傻不傻都好。我要的是你。赫斯特，要躲人耳目，就得同大家一样跳；我们不能站着说一整夜的话。再说，我正有跳的兴致！”他叫道。

无可疑，许多人跳华尔兹时全无兴致——伤心人、失意人、心碎人；可再没有比赫斯特更不情愿的了。她只觉自己的处境忍无可忍；那其中自满的不公——那份“女人能给的不过这样的盲从”的断言，说得那样心安理得——气人、辱人到了言语形容不出的地步。他当真这样想？她同他过一辈子，要面对的便是这个？她的主意、她的聪明的助力、她的理解，一概不要；要的只是一种狗一样的忠，一种不讲道理的信？连叫她跳舞，赫斯特都觉得狠——在她命运这样的关口上，叫她旋进人群，仿佛全然一场轻狂的欢娱。

可这也好，他们随后的几场谈话也好，都没改变什么；这一晚于她如一场梦。爱德华不算会跳舞，这些仪节除同她之外也少有兴致；那晚却一而再、再而三地同别人跳，赫斯特立在旁边望着，越望越懵。她头疼，她说。这是她母亲摆脱一切窘境的老方子；这方子赫斯特也会，只是从没动过用它的念头。她接着这家的主妇梅里迪尤太太坐下——她是个厚道人，有心待她好。“你只管说一声，亲爱的，我们的车一到我就送你回家，”这位太太说；“顶着裂开的头疼，眼看别的年轻人跳舞，血肉之躯受不了。”可惜呀！梅里迪尤太太的车不到两点叫不来，赫斯特只好担着她的担子。当然，这一晚也不是这样收的。他到梅里迪尤太太身边寻她来了，一脸同情地听着她头疼的陈述。

===Original===

“This was our dance,” he said; “but come into the hall instead, where it is cool, and let me get you some tea.” He placed her there in the shelter of the evergreens, when all the hubbub of the next dance was in full progress. They were quiet, almost alone, and Edward was in a fever of high spirits and excitement. He had said little about love in that strange moment when he had taken possession of her. Now he made up for all deficiencies. She endeavoured at first to bring him back to what she called the more important subject. “Can any subject be more important?” he said with tender reproach. And she was silenced, for what could she say? And the moments flew too fast and were too brief to be lost in any struggle. They parted with a few mysterious words whispered into her ear, which did much however to bring back the painful tension which had relaxed a little in his presence. “If I send to you, you will see me, Hester?” he whispered. “You won’t think of proprieties? I might have to put your love to the test﻿—to ask you﻿—”

“这一场本是我们的。”他说；“不如到门厅去，那边凉快，我去给你弄点茶。”下一场舞闹得正沸时，他把她安置在门厅常青树的荫翳里。那里清静，几乎只有他们两个；爱德华正发着高烧似的兴致与激动。占据她的那个奇特的时刻，他关于爱说得很少。如今他把亏空全补上了。她先还竭力想把他拉回她所谓更要紧的题目。“还有什么题目比这更要紧？”他带着温柔的责备说。她语塞了——她还能说什么？时光又飞得太快、太短，经不起在争执里荒掉。分别时，他往她耳边低语了几句神秘的话——这几句倒把那根松了片刻的痛弦重新绷紧了。“我若打发人叫你，你会见我吧，赫斯特？”他低声说。“你不会去想那些规矩吧？说不定我要考一考你的爱——要请你——”

“What?” she cried with almost a spasm of alarm. He gave her hand a warning clasp as he put her into the fly, and then stooping to arrange the shawls around her, kissed it secretly. And that was all. She drove home in the silence and dark, feeling every word thrill her through, going over it again and again. What was this test of love that might be required of her? What did he expect her to do for him, in ignorance, in blind trust? Hester had too high a spirit to accept this role with ease. She was bewildered﻿—dazzled by the lavish outpouring of his love; but all that did not blind her to the strange injustice of this treatment, the cruelty of her helpless position. For what could she do? She could not desert him in his hour of need; if he made this call upon her which he spoke of so mysteriously, it would no doubt be in his utmost need, when to desert him would be like a traitor. And Hester knew that she could confront any danger with him or for him﻿—but what was it? A dilemma so terrible had never presented itself to her imagination. There was a cruelty in it, a depreciation of all the nobler parts of her, as if only in ignorance could she be trusted. Her mother’s questions about the ball, and whether she had danced much, and who her partners had been, were insupportable, as insupportable as the maunderings of Emma. In short, if there was anything that could have made this mystery and darkness in which her way seemed lost, more hard to bear, it was the background of amusement and supposed lightheartedness against which it was set. “My head ached,” she said. “I scarcely danced at all,” by way of freeing herself; but this opened only another kind of torture, for poor Mrs. John, well used to the feminine indulgence of headaches, had a whole surgery of little remedies, and bathed her child’s forehead, and drew back her hair, and would have administered sal-volatile, tea, eau-de-cologne﻿—there was no telling how many cures﻿—if she had been allowed.

“Let me fan you then, my love: sometimes that does me a great deal of good. Just let me pour a little eau-de-cologne first; you don’t know how cooling it is.”

“Oh, mamma! let me be still; let me be in the dark; go to bed, and don’t mind me,” cried Hester.

===Chinese===

“什么？”她叫道，几乎是一阵惊悸。扶她上马车时，他把她的手告警地一握；随后俯身替她掖围巾，偷偷吻了那只手。就这样，再没有别的。她在寂静与黑暗里坐车回家，每一个字都穿身而过，一遍又一遍地过。这要向她索取的爱的考验，是什么？他要她在无知里、在盲信里，为他做什么？赫斯特心气太高，这个角色她受不安逸。她晕眩——被他倾泻的爱照花了眼；可这一切没有瞒住她：这待遇里的怪的不公，她这无助处境的残忍。因为她能怎样？他危难时她不能弃他；他那样神秘地说的那一次“请你”，必定是他绝境之时，那时弃他，便同叛逆一样。赫斯特知道自己能同他一起、或为他一人，面对任何危险——可危险是什么？这样可怕的困境，她的想象从不曾遇见过。这里面有一种残忍，一种对她一切高贵处的贬损，仿佛唯有蒙昧里她才信得过。母亲关于舞会的问话——跳没跳多、舞伴是谁——她受不住，同埃玛的絮叨一样受不住。总而言之，倘若还有什么能把这场迷失了她道路的幽暗与神秘弄得更难捱，那便是衬在它背后的那片欢娱、那片想当然的轻快。“我头疼。”她说。“几乎没怎么跳。”想这样脱身；谁知这只打开了另一种刑罚：可怜的约翰太太，惯于纵容女人的头疼，备着一整套小药械，给孩子的额头湿敷，把她的头发拢开，还要上嗅盐、茶、古龙水——天知道多少方子——只消容许。

“那让我给你打扇，我的宝贝：有时这一着于我大有用处。先让我给你倒一点古龙水；你不知道它多败火。”

“哦，妈妈！让我静静；让我待在黑里；你去睡吧，别管我。”赫斯特叫道。

===Original===

“My love! how could I do that and leave my child to suffer,” said Mrs. John, heroically﻿—and it was heroic, for the night was cold, the fire burning low, the hour three o’clock. Hester, with her brain throbbing, all inaccessible to eau-de-cologne, did not know how to free her mother from this too generous unnecessary martyrdom. She began to talk to break the spell.

“Emma is very happy,” she said, “she danced with Edward Vernon. She thinks perhaps it may make the other speak, or that even Edward himself﻿—” Hester broke off with a quiver in her lip. “I am becoming malicious like the rest,” she said.

“That is not malicious, dear,” said Mrs. John. “Emma is very amusing, being so frank, but she is right enough when you come to think of it; for what can she do if she does not marry? And I am sure Edward Vernon, though Catherine makes such a fuss about him, is nothing so very great. I wonder what he meant coming here that one night, and so late.”

“It was by accident,” Hester said.

“It was a very odd accident,” cried her mother, “no one else ever did so.”

“He had been sitting late over his work, and his head was very full of﻿—business.”

Mrs. John looked in all the confidence of superior wisdom into her daughter’s face. A smile dawned upon her lips.

“Perhaps you think he was coming to confide his troubles about his business, Hester, to you and me.”

“And why not?” said Hester, raising herself from her bed.

Mrs. John dropped her fan in her surprise, and sat down abruptly upon the little chair by Hester’s bedside, to her daughter’s great relief.

“Why not?” she said. “I think, though you are my own, that you are the strangest girl I ever knew. Do you think a man *ever* talks to women about these things? Oh, perhaps to a woman like Catherine that is the same as a man. But to anybody he cares for﻿—never, oh, never, dear! I suppose he has a respect for you and me; think of any man venturing to bring business into my drawing-room, though it is only a poor little parlour now, not a drawing-room at all. Oh, no, that could never﻿—never be! In all my life I never descended so low as that,” Mrs. John said, with dignity. “I used to be brought into contact with a great many business people when your poor dear papa was living; but they never talked ‘shop,’ as they call it, before me.”

“我的宝贝！这怎么能，丢下我的孩子受苦。”约翰太太说，一副英雄气——也真是英雄气：夜里冷，炉火将熄，时辰三点。赫斯特太阳穴突突地跳，古龙水全然进不去；她不知怎样才能把母亲从这场过分慷慨、全无必要的殉难里解脱出来。她开口说话，来破这道符。

“那不叫促狭，亲爱的。”约翰太太说。“埃玛这样坦白，很逗趣；可仔细想想，她也满对：她不嫁，还能怎样？还有爱德华·弗农，凯瑟琳把他捧得上天，我拿准他也未必那样了不得。我纳闷他那晚到这里来是什么意思，还那么晚。”

“是碰巧。”赫斯特说。

“这‘碰巧’可真怪。”她母亲叫道；“换个人谁也不这么办。”

“他伏案到深夜，满脑子——生意。”

约翰太太带着更高一筹的智慧的自信，望着女儿的脸。一丝微笑在她唇上亮起来。

“为什么不会？”赫斯特说，从床上撑起身。

约翰太太惊得扇子落了地，一屁股坐在床边的小椅上——这倒叫女儿大松一口气。

“为什么不会？”她说。“你虽是我亲生的，我想你是我认得的姑娘里顶怪的一个。你以为男人会同女人谈这些事吗？哦，兴许会同凯瑟琳那样的女人谈——她同男人一样。可对他放在心上的人——绝不会，哦，绝不会，亲爱的！想必是他敬重你我；你想想，哪个男人敢把生意带进我的客厅——如今虽说只是间可怜的小起居室，根本算不得客厅了。哦，不，这绝不会——绝不会有！我一辈子没低就到那一步。”约翰太太端庄地说。“你那可怜的亲爱的爸爸在世时，我倒常同许多生意人打交道；可他们从没当着我谈‘行话’——他们管那叫行话。”

===Original===

“But my father himself?” said Hester, her eyes blazing with the keenest interest; “you knew all his affairs?”

Mrs. John held her delicate little hands clasped for a moment, and then flung them apart, as if throwing the suspicion away.

“Never!” she cried; “he respected me too much. Your poor papa was incautious about money, Hester, and that has done a great deal of harm to both of us, for we are poor, and we ought to have been rich; but he always had too much respect for me to mix me up with business. You are very inexperienced, my dear, or you would know that such a thing could not be.”

Hester followed her mother with her large eyes, with a wondering wide gaze, which answered well enough for that of believing surprise, almost awe, which Mrs. John was very willing to recognise as a suitable expression. And there was indeed a sort of awe in the girl’s perception of her mother’s perfectly innocent, perfectly assured theory of what was right in women. What wonder that a man should think so, when women themselves thought so? This strange discovery composed and stilled her when at last she was left in the dark and in peace.

“从不！”她叫道；“他太敬重我了。你那可怜的爸爸在手面上不谨慎，赫斯特，这一条害了我们俩：我们穷，本该富的；可他对我敬重得很，从不把我揽进生意里。你太不经事，亲爱的；不然你就知道，这样的事不可能有。”

赫斯特睁大眼睛追着母亲，那副惊异的凝望，正可充作信服的吃惊、近乎敬畏——约翰太太也乐得认它作合适的表情。而姑娘窥见母亲那套关于女人本分的、全然天真、全然笃定的理论，心里也确有一种敬畏。女人自己既这样想，男人这样想，又何怪之有？这个奇特的发现，安顿了她、平息了她——当终于只剩她一人，在黑暗里、在安静里。

===Original===

Hester kept gazing through that wintry blackness, with eyes still wide open, and her clear brows puckered with wonder and alarm. Was it natural, then, a thing she could accept as just, that it was enough for her to sympathise, to share the consequences, to stand by the chief actor whatever happened, but never to share in the initiative or have any moral concern in the motive or the means of what was done? A sense of helplessness began to take the place of indignation in her mind. Was that what they called the natural lot of women? to suffer, perhaps to share the blame, but have no share in the plan, to sympathise, but not to know; to move on blindly according to some rule of loyalty and obedience, which to any other creature in the world would be folly and guilt? But her mother knew nothing of such hard words. To her this was not only the right state of affairs, but to suggest any better rule was to fail in respect to the lady whose right it was to be left ignorant. Hester tried to smile when she recalled this, but could not, her heart being too sore, her whole being shaken. *He* thought so too perhaps, everybody thought so, and she alone, an involuntary rebel, would be compelled to accept the yoke which, to other women, was a simple matter, and their natural law. Why, then, was she made unlike others, or why was it so?

Edward had been in great spirits that night. The next time they met was in the afternoon late, when Hester was returning from a visit to Mrs. Morgan. It was nearly dark, and it startled her to see him standing waiting for her under one of the trees past the gate of the Heronry. She went slowly, somewhat reluctantly, to join him on the sign just discernible in the dark which he made her. He caught her hand quickly, as she came up, and drew it within his arm.

“You have been so long with that old woman, and I have wanted you so,” he cried, leading her away along the deserted country road, which struck off at right angles with the Common. “Couldn’t you divine that I wanted you? Didn’t you know by instinct I was longing for consolation?”

“Oh, Edward! what is wrong? What has made so great a change in you?” she cried.

He drew her arm closer and closer through his, and leaned upon her as if his appeal for support was physical too.

赫斯特仍旧睁着眼，穿过那冬夜的黑望出去，清朗的眉心蹙着惊奇与惊惧。那么，这是天经地义、是她可以认作公道的了：她只消同情，只消分担后果，只消不管出什么事都站在主事人身边——却永不分沾筹划，对所行之事的动机与手段永无道义上的一份？一种无助之感开始在她心里顶替义愤。这就是他们说的女人的天命？受苦，兴许还有分受罪责，却不分沾谋划；同情，却不知情；照着某种忠顺的律盲目前行——这律若加给世上任何别的受造物，都是愚妄与罪愆？可母亲全不识这些硬字眼。于她，这不但对的秩序；谁想提出一条更好的规矩，反而是失敬于那位有权利蒙在鼓里的女士。赫斯特回想这话，想笑一笑，笑不出——心太痛，整个人摇擑着。*他*多半也这样想，人人都这样想；唯有她，一个不由自主的叛逆，将不得不接受这副轭——于别的女人，它不过是件寻常事、她们的天法。那么，为什么把她造得同旁人不一样？又为什么，事情偏是这样？

那一晚爱德华兴致极高。他们再见面，是在一个下午的黄昏，赫斯特从摩根太太家探望回来。天差不多黑了；她一惊——他立在弗农院大门外一棵树下等她。他在暗里朝她做了个刚能认出的手势，她慢慢走过去，带着几分勉强，去到他身边。她一走近，他迅速抓住她的手，拉进自己臂弯。

“你在那老太太那里待了这么久，我这样需要你。”他叫道，领着她走上那条无人的乡路——路同荒原成直角岔开。“你难道没算出我要你？你难道没有凭本能知道，我正渴着安慰？”

“哦，爱德华！怎么了？什么把你变大了这样？”她叫道。

他把她的手臂越拢越紧，整个人倚向她，仿佛他求援的，连身体也在内。

“I told you it was too long to explain,” he said; “it is all the worry of business. Oh, if you only belonged to me, Hester, and we had a home somewhere where I could go in to you and say ‘Console me!’ ”

“But Edward, your business never used to be a fever and an excitement like this.”

“How do you know? I did not dare to come to you; and you were a child then. Ah, but you are quite right, Hester; it was different. But a man cannot vegetate forever. I endured it as long as I could. Now it is all on a turn of the cards, and I may be able to face the world tomorrow, and have my own way.”

“On a turn of the cards! Edward, you cannot mean it is play? You are not a﻿—gambler?” Hester gave a little convulsive cry, clutching him by the arm with both her hands.

He laughed. “Not with cards, certainly,” he said. “I am a respectable banker, my darling, and very knowing in my investments, with perhaps a taste for speculation﻿—but that nobody has brought home to me yet. “Do you mean speculation, Edward?”

“Something of that sort; a capital horse when it carries you over the ford﻿—and everything that is bad when you lose.”

“But do you mean﻿—tell me﻿—that it is simple speculation﻿—that this is all that makes you anxious?” Hester had never heard that speculation was immoral, and her mind was relieved in spite of herself.

“Only﻿—simple speculation! Good Lord! what would she have?” he cried, in a sort of unconscious aside, with a strange laugh; then added, with mock gravity, “that’s all, my darling; not much, is it? You don’t think it is worth making such a fuss about?”

“I did not say that,” said Hester, gravely, “for I don’t understand it, nor what may be involved; but it cannot touch the heart. I was afraid﻿—”

“Of something much worse,” he said, with the same strange laugh. “What were you afraid of?﻿—tell me. You did not think I was robbing the bank, or killing Catherine?”

“Edward!”﻿—she did not like these pleasantries﻿—“why do you talk so wildly? Come in with me, and my mother will give you some tea.”

“We ought to go and hand in the banns, perhaps,” he said, with sudden bitterness, “like two﻿—honest shopkeepers, as you say. Catherine Vernon would give me away. I will come back in two or three days; but Hester, another time, if it should be for good, would you come?﻿—you would come?﻿—with me?”

“Elope!” she said, breathless, her eyes large in the darkness, straining upon the face which was too near her own to be very clear.

He laughed. “If you like the word; it is an innocent word. Yes, elope then,” he said.

“But why?﻿—but why? It would wound them all﻿—it would break their hearts; and for what reason?” Hester cried.

===Chinese===

“兴许我们还该去教堂登记结婚预告。”他忽然刻毒起来，“像两个——照你的说法——诚实的店主。凯瑟琳·弗农好来把我当场交出去。你对爱的全部见识，就这些吗，赫斯特？——想来这就是女人的路数——道喜，贺礼，压倒一切人的全面凯旋。我说带着我的爱一起失踪、一起迷路、甚至一起死掉——这你怎么懂？”

两人静了一静：赫斯特伤了，也动了，两样都到了心口。过了一刻，她几乎气声地说：“那个我也懂。”她声音的颤、头的低垂，连同他对她的需要——比这两样更急——把爱德华的讥诮变了。他把她拉近，把脸凑到她耳边。

“我们不能吵。”他说，“我唯一的爱。我要走了，不能同你吵，我唯一的爱！我又是你唯一的爱。我们中间从来不曾有过别人。过两三天我就回来；可是赫斯特，下一回，倘若那一回是一去不回，你肯来吗？——你肯来吗？——同我一起？”

“私奔！”她说，气都屏住了；黑暗里她的眼睛睁得大大的，竭力望着那张脸——贴得太近，反而望不真切。

他笑了。“你爱用这个词；它本是个无辜的词。好，就私奔。”他说。

“可是为什么？——到底为什么？那要伤尽他们所有的人——要碎尽他们的心；又为着什么呢？”赫斯特叫道。

## XXXVII / 三十七
===Original===

Alarms

Edward was about a week away from home. He had often been away before, and his absence had caused no particular commotion: but now it affected a good many people. To Catherine, if it were possible, it might be said to have been a certain relief. He and she had got over that explanation when she had intended to say so many things to him, and had found the words taken out of her mouth. All things had gone on again in their usual way. But the suspicion which he had supposed to exist so long without any reason now had actually arisen in her mind. She showed it less than he had supposed her to show it when she had no such feeling. She was on her guard. She did not worry him any longer by her old affectionate way of going to the window to watch him when he went out; that had been simple love, admiration of his orderly, regular ways, pleasure in the sight of him: but somehow instinctively since she had begun to doubt she came to perceive the interpretation he had put upon it, and she did it no longer. But at night when all was still in the house and Edward downstairs at work in his room, or supposed to be at work, if any sound of the door closing echoed upwards, Catherine would steal behind the curtains and watch if it was he who was going out, and which way he took. She believed him, of course; but yet there was always in her soul a wish to ask﻿—was he really, really sure that he was true? Doubts like these are beyond the power of any but the sternest self-command to crush, and Catherine was capable of that in his presence. She would not betray her anxiety to him: but when he was not there no such effort was necessary, and she betrayed it freely, to the silence, to the night, when there was nobody to see.

===Chinese===

警讯

爱德华离家约莫一个星期。他从前也常出门，他不在从来不曾引起什么风波：如今却牵动了许多人。对凯瑟琳来说，这若有可能，倒可算是一点松快。那场剖白——她本预备了满肚子话要对他说的，却被人把话头从嘴里夺了去——他们俩已经熬过去了。一切照旧运转。可那桩他以为无端存在了许久的猜疑，如今当真在她心里生出来了。她露出来的，反倒比他原先料想的、她无所疑心时会露出的还少。她存了戒心。她不再用她那套旧日慈爱的做派，赶他出门时到窗前目送——那本来纯粹是爱，是欣赏他井然有序的规矩日子，是一见他眼里就高兴：可自从起了疑，她本能地觉出了他给这套做派的注解，便不再做了。可夜里，宅子全静下来，爱德华在楼下他屋里办事——或想必在办事——只要门响一声往上传，凯瑟琳就悄悄躲到帘子后面，看他是不是又要出门，往哪边走。她当然是信他的；可她灵魂里总有一句要问——他当真、当真拿得准自己是真的么？这样的疑心，非最严酷的自制压不下去；而当着他的面，凯瑟琳拿得出这份自制。她不肯叫他看见她的焦灼：可他不在时，就用不着这份力气了，她放任它——对着寂静、对着黑夜，反正没人看见。

===Original===

And her thoughts had travelled fast and far since that evening. She had no longer any doubt that he loved somebody, and she had made up her mind that it was Hester who was the object of his love. This had caused her perhaps the greatest mental conflict she had ever known in her life﻿—for her life had this good thing in it, that it had been wonderfully free from struggle. She had been the arbiter of all things in her little world, and nobody had made any actual stand against her will. Many pretences had surrounded her, feigned assents and furtive oppositions, but nobody had stood out against her. It was a great wonder to her that he or anyone should do so now (though he did not: he had opposed her in nothing, nor ever said a word from which it could be inferred that he rejected or questioned Catherine’s sway), but with all her natural strength of mind she set herself to reconsider the question. If she disliked Hester before, if for all these years the bright-eyed, all-observant girl, mutely defiant of her, had been a sort of Mordecai to Catherine, it is not to be supposed that she could easily receive her into favour now. Her parentage, her looks, her mind, her daring setting up of her own personality as a child, as if she were something important, had all exasperated Catherine. Even the consciousness of her own prejudice, of the folly of remembering against a girl the follies of her childhood, helped to aggravate this sentiment; nor was it likely that the fact that this girl was Edward’s chosen love should make her heart softer. She said to herself that she could not endure Hester; but yet she prepared herself for the inevitable from the first day. Perhaps she thought it well to propitiate fate by going to the very furthest length at once, and forecasting all that the most evil fortune could bring her.

===Chinese===

自那晚起，她的念头跑得又快又远。他爱着什么人，她再无怀疑；她也认定了，他爱的那个就是赫斯特。这给她带来的是她平生所未有的一场大交战——她这一生有个好处：出奇地不识争斗。她那个小世界里，一切由她裁断，没人真正违拗过她的意志。她身边尽是假意：假意的附和、偷偷的作梗，可没人挺身出来同她作对。如今他也好、谁也好，竟会这样（其实他并没有：他事事没顶过她一句，从没吐露过半个字，可据以推断他拒绝或质疑凯瑟琳的权威），这在她简直是奇事一桩；可她凭着天生的心力，沉下身来把问题重新想过。从前她就嫌赫斯特；这些年，这个眼睛亮亮、什么都看在眼里、默默同她较劲的姑娘，于凯瑟琳一直像她的末底改；如今再要把她收作心腹，谈何容易。她的出身、她的相貌、她的心思、她从小敢把自己一个人立起来、俨然一尊要紧人物的做派，样样叫凯瑟琳光火。连自己也知道这是成见、也知道拿小孩子家的傻气记一个大姑娘的账是愚蠢——这份自觉，反倒火上浇油；何况这姑娘如今是爱德华选中的爱，心肠就更软不下来。她对自己说，赫斯特她受不住；可打头一天起，她就为那不可避免的结局作起了准备。兴许她想得是：索性一步让到底，把厄运能送来的全数预演一遍，也算给命运上个供。

===Original===

It cost her a sharp and painful struggle. No one knew what was going on in her mind in those wintry days of the early year: her preoccupation was attributed to other things: afterwards, when events seemed to account for it, her wonderful prevision was admired and wondered at. But in reality the previsions in Catherine’s mind were all of one kind. She saw a series of events happen in succession, as to which she was as confident as if they were past already; and in her imagination she did the only thing that nobody expected of her, the thing which fate did not demand of her﻿—she made up her mind that she would make no stand against this hateful thing. What was the use of it? If the young but held out, even the most unwise and the most cruel, they must win in the end. It would not be for her dignity, she said to herself, to stand out. She would make no opposition to Edward’s choice. The separation that must ensue she would bear as she could﻿—with dignity at least if nothing else. The elevation of her enemy and her enemy’s house she must submit to. She would withdraw, she would have no hand in it; but at least she would not oppose. This, by dint of a hard fight, Catherine obtained of herself. She would say nothing, forestall nothing, but at the same time oppose nothing. All the long hours which a lonely woman must spend by herself she appropriated to this. She must lose Edward; had she not lost him now? He had been her sole weakness, her one delusion; and it was not, she said to herself, a delusion﻿—the boy had loved her and been true to her. He had made her happy like a mother with a true son. But when that vagrant sentiment comes in which is called love (the fools! as if the appropriation of the name to one kind of affection, and that the most selfish of all, was not a scorn to love, the real, the all-enduring!) what was previous virtue, what was truth, and gratitude, and everything else in life, in comparison? Of course they must all give place to the fascination of a pair of shining eyes. Father and mother, and home and duty, what were they in comparison? Everybody was aware of that, and the old people struggled often enough as was well known. Sometimes they appealed to heaven and earth, sometimes were hysterical and made vows and uttered curses. But in the long run the battle was to the young ones.

===Chinese===

这一场交战又利又疼。年初那些冬日的日子里，没人知道她心里进行着什么：她的心事被归到旁的头上；后来事态仿佛恰好作了注解，人们又惊叹她那份神奇的先见。其实凯瑟琳心里的先见只有一种。她看见一串事情接连发生，看得同既成往事一样确凿；在想象里，她做了唯一一件没人指望她做的事、命运也没索取的事——她拿定主意：这桩可憎的事，她绝不抵抗。抵抗有什么用？年轻人只要熬得住——哪怕顶不明智、顶狠心的人——末了赢的总是他们。她说，负隅顽抗，有失她的身份。爱德华的选择，她不作任何反对。随之而来的离散，她能怎样便怎样受——至少受得有个身份。仇人高升、仇人一家高升，她只好顺受。她抽身，她不插一手；可至少她不反对。这一条，凯瑟琳是凭一场苦战才从自己身上挣到的。她不说破，不抢先，可也不反对。一个孤身的女人独坐的漫漫长时辰，全叫她挪作这一桩用途。她要失去爱德华了；如今岂不已经失去了？他是她唯一的软处、独一个的自欺；而这又不是自欺——她对自己说——孩子爱过她，真过。他叫她幸福，像有真儿子的母亲那样。可是当那股叫作爱情的浪子情绪一来（这班傻子！仿佛把这个名号派给一种感情、还偏是顶自私的那一种，就是对爱——真的爱、担荷一切的爱——的褒奖似的！），先前的德性算什么，真、感恩、人世一切算什么？当然全得让位给一双亮眼睛的蛊惑。爹娘、家宅、本分，比起来算什么？这个谁都懂；老人家的挣扎，也有的是人见过。他们有时呼天抢地，有时发癔症、赌咒、咒人。可长远看，胜仗总归年轻人打。

===Original===

They had time and passion, and universal human sympathy, on their side, whereas the old people had none of all these, neither time to wait, nor passion to inspire, nor sympathy anywhere in heaven or earth. Catherine said to herself proudly that she would not expose herself to the pity which attends the vanquished. She would retire from the fray. She would clothe herself in double armour of stoicism, and teach herself to see the humour in this as in so many things. Was not seeing the humour of it the last thing that remained to the noble soul amid the wonder of life?

===Chinese===

年轻人有的是时间同热情，还有普天下人的同情；老人呢，这些一样没有：没时间等，没热情鼓动，天上地下没一份同情。凯瑟琳骄傲地对自己说：她不肯把自己摆到败军之将那份受人怜悯的位置上。她要退出战团。她要给自己披上双层的坚忍铠甲，教自己把这桩事、同许多事一样，看成一笑。把这桩事看成一笑，岂不正是高贵的灵魂在这人生奇观里剩下的最后一招么？

===Original===

Her sense, however, of this great downfall which was approaching, and in which she meant to enact so proud and magnanimous a part, was so strong and bitter that Edward’s absence was a relief to her. She expected every day that he would present himself before her, and burst forth into some agitated statement﻿—a statement which she would not help out with a word, but which she would receive, not as he would expect her to receive it, with opposition and wrath, but with the calm of one who knew all about it, and had made up her mind to it long ago. But when he was absent she felt that here was a respite. She was freed from the eager desire she had, against her will, to know what he was doing, where he went, who he was with, which tormented her, but which she could not subdue. All this ferment of feeling was stilled when he was away. She did not ask why he should go away so often, what the business was that called him to London. For the first time in her life she was overmastered by a conflict of individual feeling; and she was glad when there came a lull in it, and when the evil day was postponed. She went on seeing her friends, visiting and being visited, keeping a fair face to the world all the time. But it began to be whispered in Redborough that Catherine Vernon was beginning to fail, that there were signs in her of breaking up, that she began to show her age. People began to ask each other about her. “Have you seen Catherine Vernon lately? How did you think she was looking?” and to shake their heads. Some said she had been so strong a woman always, and had taken so much out of herself, that probably the breakup would be speedy if it was true that she was beginning to break up; while others held more hopefully that with her wonderful constitution she might yet rally, and see twenty-years of comfort yet. The fact was that she was not ill at all. It seemed to herself that she was more keenly alive, more highly strung to every use of existence than ever. She saw better, heard more quickly, having every sense on the alert. Nothing had so quickened her and stimulated her powers for years. She was eager for every new day which might carry some new crisis in it. She did not even feel the deadly chill of Edward’s desertion for the intense occupation which the whole matter brought her.

然而，这场眼看要来、而她预备在其中扮演这样高傲宽宏一角的塌陷，感觉太强、太苦，所以爱德华出门，于她竟成了解脱。她天天等他到她面前来，激动地摊牌——那摊牌她一个字也不会接济，却会照她的方式、不是他料想的反对与震怒，而是以一个早知底细、早拿定主意的人的平静去领受。可他不在，她便觉得是缓刑。她这才从那股逆着自己心意、偏要知道他在做什么、去了哪儿、同谁在一起的渴望里脱出身来——那渴望磨她，可她压不服。他一走，这满腔翻腾便平了。他为什么这样频频出门、什么生意唤他去伦敦，她一概不问。平生头一遭，她被一场私情的交战压倒了；交战暂歇、凶日延期，她就欢喜。她照旧会客、拜客、受拜，始终给世人一副体面脸面。可雷德伯勒已开始交头接耳：凯瑟琳·弗农开始撑不住了，她身上有了败象，她开始见老了。人们开始互相打听：“近来见过凯瑟琳·弗农么？气色你看怎样？”说罢摇头。有人说她向来那样要强、把自己用得太狠，败象若是真的，崩起来多半也快；另一些人抱着指望，说凭她那副顶好的体质，兴许还缓得过来，再享二十年清福。其实她一点病也没有。她自己倒觉得，比往常更清醒、生命的每一样机能绷得更紧。她看得更清，听得更捷，五官全在戒备。多少年来没有一件事这样催过她、鼓过她的劲。她巴望每一个新日子，说不定带着新的关口。爱德华撇下她的那阵死寒，她竟不觉得——整桩事给她的占领太满了。

In this way the spring went on. It had appeared to Edward himself as certain that some great coup must have settled his fate long before. It was his inexperience, perhaps, and the excitement of his determination to act for himself, which had made everything appear so imminent; but after all it did not turn out so. The course of events went on in that leisurely current which is far more deadly in its sweep than any sudden cataract. He did not lose or gain anything in a moment, his ventures either did not turn out so vast as he imagined, or they were partial failures, partial successes. Step by step he went on, sacrificing, jeopardising, gradually, slowly, without being himself aware of what he was doing, the funds he had under his control. He had been ready in the first passion of his desire for wealth to risk everything and finish the whole matter at one swoop; but that passed over, and he was not really aware how one by one his counters were being swept out of his hands. It went on through all the awakening time of the year, as it might have gone on for half a life time, and he was impatient of the delay. Besides, this new accompaniment, this love which he would not have suffered himself to indulge had he not believed everything on the eve of a crisis, became a great addition to his difficulties when the crisis did not come. The habit of resorting to Hester was one which grew upon him. But the opportunities of indulging in it were few, for he was as anxious not to betray himself nor to let Catherine suspect what was going on, as at the beginning, when he believed that all would be over in a week or two. And Hester herself was not a girl with whom it was easy to carry on a clandestine intercourse. The situation chafed her beyond endurance. She had almost ceased now to think of the mystery in which he hid his proceedings, or to rebel against the interest and sympathy which he demanded from her blindly, out of the keen humiliation and distress which it cost her to feel that she was deceiving her friends and the world, conspiring with him to deceive Catherine. This consciousness made Hester disagreeable to live with, an angry, resentful, impatient woman, absorbed in her own affairs, little accessible to the world.

===Chinese===

春天就这样过去。在爱德华自己看来，也原以为早在多日前，一场豪赌总该把他的命定下来了。兴许是他的没历练，兴许是自作主张的那股兴奋，把一切都显得近在眉睫；可到底没有如此。事势沿着那道散漫的缓流走下去——那种缓流，扫荡起来比任何骤发的瀑布更毒。他没有在一瞬间输光或赢得什么；他的冒险，或是不如他想的那样大，或是半败半成。他一步一步往前走，把他手里掌管的资金，一点点地押上、赔上——渐渐地、慢慢地、连他自己也不觉察。起初求财心最热那阵，他原打算孤注一掷、一挥手了结全局；那阵热过去了，他也就不曾真觉出：他手里的筹码，正一枚一枚叫人扫走。事情贯穿了全年苏醒的时节，仿佛可以再走半辈子；他嫌这场拖延磨人。再说，这路新的伴奏——这份爱情，他原以为大局已在一两周内见分晓，才容许自己沉溺——大局迟迟不来，它就成了他重重困难上头又一大宗。投奔赫斯特，成了他戒不掉的习惯。可沉溺的机会寥寥，因为他还同起初一样，急切不肯露形迹、不肯叫凯瑟琳起疑——起初他以为一切一两个礼拜就完。而赫斯特又不是那种容易同她私相往来的姑娘。这处境磨她磨得超出忍耐。如今她几乎不再去想他把行藏裹得那样严的那层秘，也不再抗拒他盲目向她索取的兴趣与同情；磨她的，是那尖锐的羞辱与苦楚：自觉在欺骗亲友、欺骗世人，同他合谋欺骗凯瑟琳。这份知觉叫赫斯特变得难于相处：一个愠怒的、怀恨的、没有耐性的女人，一头扎在自己的事里，旁的世界进不去。

Her mother could not understand what had come to her, and still less could the old Morgans, who loved and had understood her so completely, understand. She avoided them now, she cared for nobody. Week by week with a joyless regularity she went to Ellen Merridew’s dances, where half the evening at least was spent with Edward in a curious duel of mingled love and dislike﻿—yes, sometimes hatred almost. It seemed to her that her distaste for everything that was going on was more than her love could balance, that she so hated the expedients he drove her to, that he himself took another aspect in her eyes. Sometimes she felt that she must make the crisis which he had so often anticipated, and instead of consenting to fly with him must fly by herself, and cut the tie between them with a sharp stroke. It was all pain, trouble, misery﻿—and what was worse, falsehood, wherever she turned. As the year slid round into sunshine, and the days grew longer, everything became intolerable to Hester. His absence was no relief to her. And though it was now nearly six months after Christmas, Emma Ashton still lived with the old Morgans, and pursued her adventures with her bow and spear in the dances and entertainments of the neighbourhood. She was going home at last, to Roland, in the beginning of June, and the old people were looking forward to their deliverance with no small impatience. Emma never failed at the Thés Dansantes. Catherine, who did not sleep very well on these nights, got to recognise the sound, and would sometimes look out from her window and wonder bitterly whether *that girl* too was glancing out, perhaps with triumph in her eyes as she passed the shut-up house, thinking of the day when it would be her own. It gave her a little pleasure on the first of June when she heard the slow vehicle creeping by to think that Edward had been called away that afternoon, and that if Hester had expected to meet him she would be disappointed. That was a little consolation to her. She heard it creeping back again about one in the morning, earlier than usual, with a satisfied smile. There had been no billing and cooing that evening, no advance made towards the final triumph. She thought there was a sound of disappointment even in the rumble of the fly; and so indeed there might have been, for Emma was sobbing, and discoursing among her tears upon the sadness of her prospects. It was the last Thé Dansante to which Emma could hope to go. “And here I’m going just as I came,” Emma said, “though I had such a good opening, and everybody has been so kind to me. I can’t say here that it has been for want of having my chance.
