而这印象也并非全错：那屋里聚议的人，几乎无一例外，都这样想。人们在田庄爱德华的屋里发现了一束文书——他从银行保险库里提走的证券。大头已被抽走，剩下的寥寥几张，却把他用的手段显示得太清楚了。银行本身值得搭救。它的令名还几乎没沾着尘；可这些亏空怎么补？没有钱怎么运转？它的信用又怎么恢复？凯瑟琳如今已没有当年那份独立的家财——那次她把它掷进公账，怀着对弗农银行骄傲的信心。全数后来都还了她，却一直留在生意里；弗农银行今日若一倒了之，那笔钱也随之而去。这撼不动这位骄傲的老妇的心。她把自己、把自己的钱财看得分文不值。她不知疲倦地坐着，一个接一个地见人——这些人一两个礼拜前还对她毕恭毕敬——不皱一下眉，听他们一切的疑虑，受他们的摇头，受他们对“把一切交在一个人手里的罪责疏忽”的指摘——受他们对爱德华的痛诋，受他们对那股急切劲头的享用：每逢人有求于人，挑剔与责难之权便到了他手里。起初，当凯瑟琳发现要救爱德华的名声、抹平他的罪、替他开脱已不可能时，她也虚了一虚。这些怒气冲冲的人一句辩白也不要听。于他们，他就是个骗子，仅此而已。“恕我直言，亲爱的弗农小姐，您对那个年轻人表现的信任，我始终觉得过了头。”“就不该容他握有他那权力的十分之一。这对别的远更相称的人不公道。”“若说我，我同爱德华相提并论，就像乌龟同兔子。”哈里说。凯瑟琳在桌子底下伸出手，把他那只手一握——她那只手那样纤秀，这一握几乎叫这强壮的年轻人叫出声；可同时又一眼止住了他，把这一切受了下去。她受下了一切——长长时辰的争执、解说、指摘、辩白，一次又一次焦灼地指出她这案子里的强处。

===Original===

She argued it all out with every individual, and again with every combination of them, when two or three together would return to the old objections, the difficulties they had originally started, and which again and again had been argued away, with no doubt the natural special pleading of all who speak in their own defence. During this continually repeated process Harry would stand behind her with his face of trouble, watching the countenances of the speakers, now and then blurting out something (the reverse of judicious in most cases), shuffling with uneasy feet upon the floor; sometimes, poor fellow, there being nothing else in his power, holding her elbow with the idea of supporting her, kneeling down to put her footstool straight; while old Mr. Rule, sitting at a little distance, equally anxious, equally eager, not of importance enough to speak, would come in with a quavering “Miss Vernon explained all that, sir﻿—” “As Miss Vernon has already said, sir﻿—”

===Chinese===

她同每一个人逐一辩明；又同他们的每一种组合再辩一遍——两三个人凑在一处，又会绕回那些老异议、起初提的那些难题，那些已被一遍遍驳倒的东西——驳的时候自然带着所有自辩者天生的偏护之词。在这一遍遍重演的过程里，哈里立在她身后，一脸愁苦，盯着说话人的脸，时不时冒出一句（多半并不相宜），两只脚在地上不安地蹭来蹭去；有时，可怜的人，别无能为力了，就扶着她的肘，心想是攙她，或者跪下去替她摆正脚凳；而老鲁尔先生坐在稍远处，一样焦急，一样热切，分量又不够开口，只能颤巍巍地插进一句“弗农小姐都说明过了，先生——”“正如弗农小姐方才说的，先生——”

===Original===

She alone showed little anxiety and no distress. She was as dignified as if she had been entertaining them at her table, as she had done so often. She bore those repetitions of the old objections with composure. She did not get impatient, twisting and turning in her chair like Mr. Rule, or crushing her impatience under foot like Harry. She was like an Indian at the stake: or rather like a prime minister in his place in Parliament. The hundred times repeated argument, the old doubt brought up again, all afresh with shakings of the head, the stolid little compliments to her as a woman so much superior to her sex, her masculine understanding (good lack! wonderful, though not equal to those whom she had convinced over and over again, yet who began again next moment where they had left off), all this she put up with without shrinking. Oh, the dullness of them, the unconvinceableness, the opaque vision, the impotent hearts! But she made no sign that she perceived. She sat still and held her own. She had the best of the argument in logic, but not, alas, in power. Ten mortal hours had struck by the time the last of her visitors hastened away to his dinner, promising to think of it, yet shaking his head. Catherine leant her head upon the back of her high chair and closed her eyes; the tears came to them in the relief of having no more to say. She was so pallid and so worn now that they both rushed to her in silent terror. She opened her eyes with an astonished look. “I hope you do not think I am going to faint; I never faint,” she said.

Ten hours! She walked to her carriage with a foot lighter and firmer than that of Harry, upon whose fine physique and troubled soul this day had wrought more havoc than the severest football. She would not allow her old friend and servant to come to the door with her.

“Don’t tire yourself,” she said. “You have so much to do for us yet. I think we shall pull through.”

“God bless you, Miss Catherine,” said the old man; “if we pull through it will be your doing.”

“What merit is that?” she said quickly. “Why should God bless me for that? It is for myself.”

“Oh, my dear lady,” cried the old clerk. “I know you better than you do yourself. It is for Vernon’s and not for you. And Vernon’s means the honest living of many a family. It means﻿—”

===Chinese===

唯独她，不大见焦灼，也全无苦相。她端坐得如同在自己席上待客——从前她常这样待客。那些老异议的重弹，她从容受着。她不烦躁——不像鲁尔先生在椅子里拧来拧去，也不像哈里把烦躁往脚底下踩。她像火刑柱上的印第安人：或者说，像国会座席上的首相。重复过一百遍的论调，重新抬出的旧疑，配上新一遍的摇头；那些木木的小恭维——夸她是远超同性之上的女人，夸她男子般的头脑（天可怜见！真是奇迹——却还是比不上那些被她一遍又一遍说服了的人，他们下一刻又从原处重新开始）——这一切她都受了，不缩一下。哦，他们的钝，他们的说不服，他们浑浊的眼，他们无力的心！可她不露一点察觉。她端坐，寸步不让。论道理，她占尽了上风；论势力，唉，没有。致命的十个钟头敲过去，最后一位来客才匆匆赶回家用饭，许诺考虑考虑，头还在摇。凯瑟琳把头靠上高背椅，合了眼；再无一语可说的松弛里，眼泪涌了上来。她此刻那样苍白、那样耗竭，两个人无声地惊骇着扑向她。她睁开眼，一脸诧异。“你们别当我要晕；我从不晕。”她说。

十个钟头！她走向马车，脚步比哈里的还轻、还稳——这一天在那副好身板和那颗烦恼的灵魂上造的破坏，比最狠的一场橄榄球还重。她不许她的老友、老仆送到门口。

“别累着自己。”她说。“你为我们还有那么多事要做。我想我们熬得过。”

“上帝保佑您，凯瑟琳小姐。”老人说；“我们若熬得过去，那是您的功。”

“这算什么功德？”她很快地说。“为这个上帝保佑我做什么？我是为我自己。”

“哦，我亲爱的夫人。”老文案叫道。“我比您自己还知道您。您是为弗农银行，不是为您自己。而弗农银行，意味着多少人家干净的饭碗。它意味着——”

===Original===

“Don’t tell me what it means,” she cried, putting up her hands. “It means downfall and shame now. It means a broken heart, Mr. Rule.”

“No, no,” he cried. “No, no, we’ll get through. I’ll come back if you’ll let me, and Mr. Harry will work like a hero.”

She gave Harry a strange glance. There was in it a gleam of repugnance, an air of asking pardon. She could not endure the contrast which it was not possible to refrain from making. He, standing by her, so dutiful, so kind, while the other who had ruined her, fled away. She could have struck him with her nervous hand, which now was trembling; she could have made a humble confession to him of the injuries she had done him in her heart. She could bear the old town dignitaries, the men of money, better than this.

“May I go with you?” he said, supporting her with his arm, bending over her with his fair countenance full of trouble and sympathy.

She could have struck him for being so good and true. Why was he true, and the other﻿—Better, better if they had both been alike, both traitors, and left her to bear it by herself.

“No, Harry,” she said; “no, Harry, let me be alone.”

He kissed her hand, poor boy, with a piteous look, and she felt it wet with a tear. Nor did she misunderstand him. She knew it was for her he was sorry. She knew even that he was the one alone who would stand up for the absent, and excuse him and pity him. All this she knew, and it was intolerable to her, and yet the best and sweetest thing that was in her lot.

===Chinese===

“别同我说它意味着什么。”她叫道，举起双手。“它如今意味着倾覆与耻辱。它意味着一颗碎掉的心，鲁尔先生。”

“不，不。”他叫道。“不，不，我们熬得过去。您若容许，我回来做事；哈里先生会像英雄一样干。”

她给了哈里奇怪的一瞥。里面有厌，有近乎求恕。那层对照忍不住要摆出来，而她受不住这对照。他，立在她身边，这样恭顺，这样好；而另一个，毁了她的人，正逃得远远的。她真想拿她那只此刻发抖的、神经质的手打他一下；她真想对他卑声忏悔——忏悔她心里一向对他的那些亏负。镇上的老先生们、那些钱袋子，她倒受得住；这个她受不住。

“我陪您走吗？”他说，用手臂攙着她，俯下那张写满愁苦与怜惜的白净的脸。

他这样好、这样真，真叫她想打他。为什么偏偏他是真的，而另一个——倒不如两个一样，都是叛徒，撙下她一个人扛，倒好些，倒好些。

“不，哈里。”她说；“不，哈里，让我一个人待着。”

他吻了她的手，可怜的孩子，一脸哀恳；她觉出那手背上湿了一滴泪。她也没有误会他。她知道他是心疼她。她甚至知道：唯有他一个，肯为那个不在场的人辩护，替他开脱、怜他。这一切她都知道；这一切于她难忍——却又正是她命里最好、最甜的那样东西。

## XLII / 四十二
===Original===

Afterwards

Hester woke next morning in an unfamiliar room with a consciousness of something strange and terrible that had happened, she could not tell what, that first sensation before memory awakens which is one of the most bitter indications of having entered upon the world of evil. So the guilty pair in Paradise, in the morning of the world, must have woke out of their sleep, and felt, before remembrance came, the sense of ill. She scarcely remembered how she had been transported to that bed. She had slept for sorrow, calamity crushing all her unused faculties, and her first waking sensation was one of trouble and wonder what it was. She had not long to wait before the whole came rushing back upon her mind. She gave a low cry, and all her wounds began to bleed anew﻿—nay, she felt them as for the first time, for last night’s terror and commotion and misery were like a dream to her. When she uttered that cry, there was a soft stir in the room, and a little, noiseless figure, and anxious face appeared at her bedside.

“Mother!” Hester cried, with a voice of dismay.

“Yes, my darling, I am here. Catherine was so good as to send for me. She said you had received a great shock. She went out herself very early, so that you need not be afraid of being disturbed, Hester. And what is it, my dear? She would not give me any satisfaction. She said you had behaved very well, and had been the means of giving her valuable information. I am very glad of that anyhow, Hester. I always told you she was kind in the main. If you and she should be better friends after this it would be a great pleasure to me.”

There was anxiety in Mrs. John’s plaintive face, but it was confined to the fear lest her daughter’s health should be affected, and to a little uncertainty whether the relations with Catherine might be improved or injured by this mysterious event, whatever it was.

“She has been very kind, mamma.”

===Chinese===

后来

第二天早晨赫斯特在一间陌生的屋里醒来，只觉出了一件又古怪又可怕的事发生了，却想不起是什么——记忆醒来之前的那第一阵感觉，是人踏进了恶的世界最苦的征兆之一。开天辟地那个早晨，乐园里那对罪人从睡中醒来，想起还没回来时，感到的大约也是这一股凶。她几乎不记得自己怎样被送上了那张床。她是因悲伤睡去的，灾祸把她未经调用的官能全压垮了；初醒的第一阵感觉只有烦乱，同“到底是什么”的疑惑。她没有等多久，一切便涌回心里。她低低叫了一声，所有的伤口重新流血——不，她像头一回觉出它们，昨夜的恐怖、骚乱同悲惨，于她已像一场梦。那一声叫出口，屋里一阵轻轻的骚动，一个小小的、无声的身影同一张焦虑的脸出现在她床边。

“妈妈！”赫斯特惶然喊道。

“是，我的宝贝，我在这儿。凯瑟琳好心打发人接了我来。她说你受了一场大惊吓。她一早就自己出门了，省得你怕人搅扰，赫斯特。到底是怎么回事，亲爱的？她什么也不肯对我讲。只说你表现很好，给她送去了要紧的消息。这一层我总是高兴的，赫斯特。我一向对你说，她大体上是和气的。经过这一场，你同她若能亲近些，我真是求之不得。”

约翰太太那张哀婉的脸上全是焦灼，可焦灼只限于两桩：怕女儿的身体受了影响；再有，这场说不清的事变，同凯瑟琳的关系究竟会变好还是变坏，她拿不准。

“她一直很和气，妈妈。”

===Original===

“I was sure of it, my dear. Catherine has a way with her that is not very﻿—*nice*﻿—sometimes. But then we all have some fault. I was to ring for tea as soon as you were awake. That maid, after all, though I have always had a prejudice against her, is kind too, in her way. She has made me most comfortable. I have always observed in my life, Hester, that when you get to know people you so often think better of them than when﻿—That has been my experience. Do you feel able to take some breakfast, dear? or will you get up first? You are to do exactly as you please.”

Hester lay still with a little moan, and made no reply. She would have liked to turn her face to the wall, to beg that the light of day might be shut out, that she might be left to make acquaintance with her trouble. But none of these things were possible. Her mother’s gentle face shining upon her with so much easy anxiety, and so little conception of anything under the surface, brought her to herself as nothing else could have done. Why should she be troubled with these anguishes that were beyond her? The girl raised herself with that heroism of necessity which is more effectual than mere will. Mrs. John would weep with her, and make up to her with a thousand caresses for the loss of her lover, when she came to understand it; but she would never understand the burden that was on Hester’s soul. The girl said to herself that it must be borne silently, that there must be no further betrayal. She begged her mother to leave her a little, while she got up.

“I have had a long sleep. I am quite myself again,” she said.

“You look pale,” said Mrs. John, kissing her. “You have had a shock, and you have never told me yet what it was. But perhaps, on the whole, the best thing you can do is to get up; breakfast in bed is not very comfortable. I will go and have a good look at Catherine’s pretty things in the drawing-room﻿—she has some nice china﻿—and come back in half an hour or so. Don’t hurry, my darling, but it is such a lovely morning; it will do you good to have some fresh air.”

===Chinese===

“我本来就料到，亲爱的。凯瑟琳的做派，有时候不算很——*可爱*。可谁没有几分短处。她嘱咐过，你一醒就摇铃上茶。那个女仆，我从前一直对她存着成见，如今看来，她那一道里也和气。她招呼得我舒舒服服。赫斯特，我一辈子看下来：人同你处熟了，你常会把他看得比先前好——我的阅历就是这样。你能吃点早饭么，亲爱的？还是先起来？一切随你的意。”

赫斯特躺着不动，低低呻吟了一声，没有答话。她原想脸朝着墙，求人挡掉天光，让她独自同她的祸事相识。可这些一样也办不到。母亲那张温良的脸照着她，那份安闲的焦虑、那份对水面以下一无所知的浑然，把她拉回了自己，别什么都不奏效。何必拿这些她受不住的苦去搅她？姑娘凭着一种出于必要的英雄气立起身来——那比单凭意志顶事得多。约翰太太等弄明白了，会陪她哭，会拿一千种爱抚补偿她失去的情人；可压在赫斯特灵魂上的那副担子，她永远不会懂。姑娘对自己说：这担子必须默然担着，再不许走漏。她求母亲让她独自待一会儿，好起身。

“我睡足了。我全缓过来了。”她说。

“你脸色白。”约翰太太吻着她说。“你受了一场惊，到今天还没告诉我是什么。不过呢，总的看来，顶好的办法还是起身；床上用早饭不自在。我去客厅里好好看看凯瑟琳那些漂亮玩意儿——她有几件好瓷器——半个来钟头就回来。别急，宝贝；今早天气这样好；透点新鲜空气于你有好处。”

===Original===

When Hester was left alone she tried to think, but could not. Scenes came back to her as in a theatre﻿—the meeting at the gate, and all that passed there; Catherine’s appearance, and the force with which Edward flung her away from him, and set out into the dark, into the unknown. Why﻿—why had he done it? Was it in a sudden fit of passion, which he had repented of? Was it in the terror of being discovered﻿—and out of that suspicion and opposition, and gloomy distrust which had always been in his mind towards Catherine? And then the railway would rise before her mind﻿—the crowd and noise, and wild unnaturalness of everything, the disappointment which to her at heart was a relief. Had he not gone after all? What if a better thought had struck him? What if, when they all went to the bank, thinking him a traitor, they should find him there, throwing light on everything, putting the wrong right? Hester raised her head again when this thought came into her mind. Was it not after all the most likely, the most natural thought? A man does wrong by temptation, by evil companions, by the leading on of one wrong thing after another; but when he is brought to a pause, when there is a distinct call upon him, when he is made to see beyond dispute what his duty is, is it not natural, certain, that he must do it? So she said to herself. For a moment all the clouds flew away, a warm exhilaration took possession of her. Then there floated up before her eyes another scene﻿—the table round which they had sat in the dead of night; Harry with his troubled face opposite to her; Catherine paramount in her energy and rapidity; she herself putting down upon paper, so quickly that her fingers alone moved and her mind had no share but the most broken and imperfect one, what she was told to write. If he had come back, if he was working now at the reestablishment of everything, could Edward ever forgive them? What matter, what matter, she cried, so long as he set himself right, so long as Vernon’s stood by his help and did not fall? From all this it will be seen that nothing of the despair which in reality and in reflection had overwhelmed all the other chief actors in the drama, had touched Hester. To her everything was still possible, and Edward’s vindication, Edward’s repentance, the chief, the most natural event of all.

===Chinese===

只剩她一人时，赫斯特试着想，想不动。一幕幕像在戏台上回到她眼前——门口的相会，同那里经过的一切；凯瑟琳的出现；爱德华把她从身边甩开的那股狠劲，同他投进黑暗、投进未知的那一去。为什么——他为什么那样？是一时情急、事后又悔了？是怕被撞破——出于他对凯瑟琳素来怀着的那份猜忌、那股对着干的劲、那种阴沉沉的不信？随后火车站又浮上心头——人群同喧嚣，样样东西那种狂乱的不自然；那场落空，在她心底其实是一阵松快。他到底没走成？万一他转了一个更好的念头呢？万一等他们全到银行、把他当叛徒的时候，却在那儿撞见他，正把一切照亮、把错处扳正呢？这个念头一进心里，赫斯特又抬起了头。这岂不终究是最顺理成章、最自然的念头？人行错，是由于引诱、由于恶伴、由于一件错事牵着一件错事；可他一旦被拦停下来，一旦有一声明白的呼唤，一旦叫他无可置疑地看清本分，他自然而然、必然地就得去尽它——她这样对自己说。有一刻，乌云全飞散了，一股暖热的振奋占了她的心。随后另一幕又浮上眼前——他们深夜围坐的那张桌子；对面哈里那张愁苦的脸；凯瑟琳以她的精力同迅捷君临一切；她自己在纸上飞快地记，快得只有手指在动、心思只余最碎最残的一星——记的全是叫她记的话。他若回来了，他若此刻正为重整一切奔忙，爱德华可还肯饶他们？有什么要紧，有什么要紧，她喊道，只要他自己归了正，只要弗农银行靠他的手撑住、没有倒——由此可以看出：那场实际上、也照情理压倒了剧中一切主角的绝望，一丝也没有沾到赫斯特。于她，样样仍有可能；爱德华的自辩、爱德华的悔悟，是头一件、也最自然的一件。

===Original===

“Well, my dear, are you ready?” said Mrs. John. “There is quite a nice breakfast waiting for you downstairs. Catherine’s maid (whom I really was unjust to, Hester, for she is a very nice woman when you come to know her) insisted upon making you some chocolate instead of tea: for it would be more sustaining, she said, in case you should not be disposed to eat. I don’t know why she should think you would not be disposed to eat. I told her you always liked your breakfast. But come, my dear, come, I am sure you must want something. Did you find the clean things I brought you? Oh I thought you would be better in a nice clean print, instead of that dark thing; but you have put on the old one all the same.”

“It is best for me today,” Hester said.

She thought to herself if it all turned out as she hoped, with what joy she would return to her summer garments in the evening, even if it might be that Edward had broken with her forever. She thought this almost certain, for had she not turned against him? but this was not the question paramount in her mind. There was but one thing all important, that he should have returned to his post. Mrs. John was greatly surprised at the wisdom of that prevision on the part of Catherine’s maid. How could she have foreseen that Hester, a healthy girl, with generally a healthy appetite, would turn away almost with loathing from the dainty food, the pretty tray, the careful provision made for her? She swallowed the chocolate hastily at her mother’s entreaty: the very air of the house, those stairs and passages, all flooded with light, which had painted themselves on her recollection in the darkness, filled Hester with a sense of the intolerable. She made haste to get out, to get away, to take her mother home.

===Chinese===

“怎么样，亲爱的，好了么？”约翰太太说。“楼下给你备好了一顿像样的早饭。凯瑟琳的女仆（赫斯特，我先前真委屈她了，处下来才知道她是个顶好的女人）非要给你做可可，不上茶：她说万一你没胃口，可可更养人。我不懂她凭什么当你没胃口。我对她说了，你一向早饭吃得好。来吧，亲爱的，来吧，你准是饿了。我给你带来的干净衣裳见了没有？哦，我想你换件漂亮清爽的花布裙好，别穿那件深色的；可你还是穿了这件旧的。”

“今天穿它顶合适。”赫斯特说。

她心里想：若一切照她盼的成了，晚上她会怀着怎样的欢喜换回夏装——哪怕爱德华同她也许已恩断义绝。这一点她几乎拿得准：她不是同他决裂了么？可这不是她心上第一位的题目。要紧的只有一件：他已回到他的岗位。约翰太太对凯瑟琳那位女仆的先见之明大为叹服。她怎么会料到：赫斯特，一个健旺的姑娘、一向胃口健旺，竟会几乎带着憎恶，从精美的食物、漂亮的托盘、那份细心的供奉前掉头？她经母亲夾告，匆匆咽下了可可；这宅子的空气本身，那些楼梯同过道——在黑暗里印上她记忆时是那样，如今全淹在光里——叫赫斯特满心一股不可忍。她急着出去、急着离开、急着把母亲送回家。

===Original===

“Don’t you think it will only be polite to wait till Catherine comes back?” Mrs. John said. “You must remember, dear, that she has been very kind to you; and nothing could be kinder than her note, and sending the carriage for me this morning, and all. I think we ought to wait and thank her for her kindness. She will think it strange that we should go away without a word. Well, if you think it really will be better to come back in the afternoon, Hester﻿—Has Catherine gone out to spend the day? That is quite unusual, surely for her﻿—but however, of course it is not our business. Lean on my arm, my dear. I am sure, as you say, the air will do you good.”

===Chinese===

“你不觉得等凯瑟琳回来才是礼数么？”约翰太太说。“你要记得，亲爱的，她待你极好；她的便条，今早打发马车接我，桩桩都再和气不过。我想我们该等一等，谢过她的好意才是。咱们一句话不留就走，她要奇怪的。唉，你若当真觉得下午再来好，赫斯特——凯瑟琳出门过一天去了？她可不常这样——不过，当然，不关我们的事。挽着我，亲爱的。我信你的话，透透气于你有好处。”

===Original===

The air did not do Hester good: the shade of the holly-tree lying motionless upon the road, the half open gate at which Catherine had appeared in the darkness, the strange intelligence that seemed to be in every bush, as if these inanimate things knew and remembered what had been done and said in secret, seemed to bring conviction, and force back upon her all the scenes she had gone through of which her innocent mother knew nothing. And every inch of the way recalled her own proud, eager thoughts of the night before, the desperation with which she had gone to that meeting, determined upon her protest and refusal, yet never sure that she would ever retrace these steps again. To retrace them now as she was doing, with her mother’s gentle talk in her ears, the occasional mild question which it was so easy to elude, the praises of Catherine which her supposed kindness called forth so easily, seemed an incredible thing. Mrs. John enjoyed the walk. It was seldom she went out in the morning, and the excitement of her daughter’s absence all night, of Catherine’s explanations, of the drawing together of some new and closer bond between Hester and the head of the Vernon society﻿—the most important person of all the kindred﻿—gave her a secret exhilaration. There had not been such a sensation in the Vernonry for months as that which had been caused that morning by the sight of Catherine’s well-known brougham, sent for Mrs. John! It might be that in future this would be no rare sight: it might be﻿—but the poor lady scarcely knew how to contain the satisfaction with which she saw the vista opening up before her of Hester’s promotion and favour with Catherine. Valuable information! She was proud of what seemed to her like the highest praise. She always knew that her Hester, so much superior as she was to other girls﻿—if Catherine but knew her as she deserved to be known. And then she asked with pleasant expectation﻿—

===Chinese===

那口气并没有叫赫斯特好过：冬青树的影子一动不动伏在路上；那扇半开的大门，凯瑟琳就是在那儿的黑暗里现身的；还有每一丛灌木里仿佛都有的那股灵觉，仿佛这些无知无识的东西全知道、全记得暗地里做过的说过的——这一切像是把定谳送回来，把她经过的、她无辜的母亲一无所知的那些场面，尽数逼回她身上。一寸一寸的路，都唤回她前一夜那骄傲急切的心绪、她奔赴那场相会的决绝——拿定了要抗辩、要回绝，却从没拿得稳还能不能再走回这条路。如今当真走回来了，耳边是母亲温软的谈话，间或一句轻轻的问话——轻易就躲得开——还有对凯瑟琳的称许，那“好意”一引就出来；这一切于她恍如不可思议。约翰太太倒是走得受用。她早晨难得出门；女儿彻夜未归的惊动、凯瑟琳的解说、赫斯特同弗农一族之首——全族顶要紧的人物——之间一条新的、更近的纽带仿佛正结起来——这一切给了她一种暗中的兴奋。弗农宅区好几个月没出过这天早晨那样的轰动：人人认得的凯瑟琳那辆四轮马车，竟是为接约翰太太来的！往后这兴许不再是稀罕景：兴许——可怜的太太简直不知道怎样安放那份满足：她眼前展开的前景，是赫斯特的高升、是凯瑟琳的恩宠。要紧的消息！她为这句在她听来无以复加的夸奖骄傲。她一向知道她的赫斯特比旁的姑娘高出那样一头——只消凯瑟琳像她该被认识的那样认识她。于是她带着愉快的指望问——

===Original===

“What was the information, Hester, that you gave Catherine? I am so glad that you were able to tell her something she didn’t know. I was quite in a flutter when I got her note last night; but of course it was perfectly right for you to stay when she wished it. I shall tell her I am so much obliged to her for having taken such good care of you. It gave me quite a fright for the moment, but I soon got over it. And Emma, you know, went away at last by the night train.”

Thus Mrs. John diverted her own attention and never pressed a question. But it is impossible to tell how deserted, how silent, how far out of the world and life the little rooms at the Vernonry looked after the agitation of the night. Hester could not rest in them: the summer forenoon seemed a twelvemonth long. She could not take up any of her usual occupations. She was afraid to meet anyone, to be questioned perhaps more closely than her mother had questioned her. Her heart was away, it was not in this place. In the pauses of Mrs. John’s gentle talk she felt her own thoughts thronging upon her almost audibly. It seemed impossible that other people, that even her mother, unsuspicious as she was, should not find her out. And how slow, how slow were those sunshiny minutes, sixty of them in an hour! The time of the early dinner came, and again Hester turned from the food. Mrs. John began to be alarmed. “If it goes on like this I shall have to send for the doctor,” she said.

===Chinese===

“你给凯瑟琳送的是什么消息，赫斯特？你能告诉她一点她不知道的事，我真高兴。昨夜接了她那条子，我心里好一阵慌；可她既然要你留，你留下自然千妥万妥。我要告诉她，我多谢她把你照看得这样好。当下真吓了我一跳，一会儿也就过去了。还有埃玛，你知道，到底搭夜车走了。”

约翰太太就这样自行岔开，从不追问。可是无法形容，经过那一夜的激荡之后，弗农宅区那几间小屋显得怎样冷落、怎样静、怎样远在人世之外。赫斯特在里面安不下身：夏日的前晌长得像一年。她拿不起任何一件惯常的活计。她怕见人，怕人问起来——问得只怕比母亲还紧。她的心不在此地，在别处。约翰太太温软的谈话一停，她便觉得自己的念头几乎有声地涌上来。旁人、连她母亲那样不疑心的人，竟没看破她，简直不可想象。那些洒满阳光的分针走得又多慢、多慢，一个钟头六十下！早午饭的时候到了，赫斯特又从饭食前掉头。约翰太太着了慌。“再这样下去，我就得请大夫了。”她说。

===Original===

Hester hastened out as soon as the meal was over to escape from her mother’s comments. It seemed to her that she recognised some new knowledge in the keen glances of the sisters, and in Mr. Mildmay Vernon’s grin as he sat over his newspaper in the summerhouse. And she was afraid of the old Morgans, who had more insight. The surroundings of the house altogether were odious to her﻿—unnecessary things that had nothing to do with those real affairs and mysteries of living which were being solved elsewhere. She asked herself wistfully, whether it was not time for her to go back: though if Catherine had not returned, what could she do but cause suspicion if she went to the empty house? To be even in the empty house would be something﻿—it would be so much nearer the scene in which everything was going on. While she stood with her hand curved over her forehead looking out upon the road, with her eyes “busy in the distance shaping things that made her heart beat quick,” the old captain came up to her. She thought he was paler than usual, and his eyes were troubled. He had laid his hand on her shoulder before she heard his approach, so absorbed was she in her own thoughts. He took her by the arm in his fatherly way﻿—

“Come with me, Hester, and talk to my old woman,” he said.

It was with a great start that she turned to him, trembling with nervousness all unknown to the Hester of yesterday.

“Is she ill?” she cried, scarcely knowing what she said; and then with a vague smile, “I forgot. Emma is gone, and she is missing﻿—”

“It is not Emma we are thinking of. Hester, tell me,” said the old man, leading her away with her arm in his, “what is this about Catherine? What has happened? Your mother told us you were there all night, and now today﻿—”

“What do they say has happened?” cried Hester with a gasp of suspense.

“I cannot make head nor tail of it. I hear that one of the young men has gone wrong; that Catherine is at the bank; that there are great defalcations; that he went off last night﻿—I can testify,” cried Captain Morgan, querulously, “that he did not go away last night, for I was there.”

Hester looked up at him with a face from which all colour had fled.

“Is it known who it is? are you sure he has not come back? Oh, I have a feeling,” she cried, “a feeling in my heart that he has come back!”

===Chinese===

一用完饭，赫斯特便急着躲出母亲絮叨的范围。她仿佛从姐妹俩尖利的瞟视里、从避暑亭里对着报纸的米尔德梅·弗农先生的龇牙里，认出了一点新的知情。而她怕的是老摩根夫妇，他们眼力更透。宅子周遭的一切于她都可憎——都是多余的物事，同正在外头了结的那些真正的生计大事、那些秘密毫不相干。她怅然自问：是不是该回去了？——可凯瑟琳若还没回来，她到那座空宅去，除了惹疑心还能做什么？可哪怕待在空宅里也是一点安慰——离那一切正在进行的场面，总要近些。她正弯手遮额、望着大路出神，眼睛“在远处忙着描画那些叫她心跳的东西”，老上校来到她跟前。她觉得他比平日苍白，眼里含着乱。她全神想着心事，他把手搭上她肩头她才听见。他用他那父亲般的方式挽起她的胳膊——

“跟我来，赫斯特，陪我的老婆子说说话。”他说。

她大大一惊，转向他，浑身发着昨天的赫斯特全然不识的那种紧张的颤。

“她病了？”她喊，几乎不知自己在说什么；随后茫然一笑，“我忘了。埃玛走了，她想她——”

“我们想的不是埃玛。赫斯特，告诉我，”老人挽着她的胳膊引开她，“凯瑟琳那边是怎么回事？出了什么？你母亲说你在那儿待了一整夜，今天又——”

“他们说出了什么？”赫斯特屏着气喊。

“我摸不着头尾。听说一个年轻人出了岔子；说凯瑟琳在银行里；说亏空很大；说他昨夜走了——我可以作证，”摩根上校急赤白脸地喊，“他昨夜没有走，因为我就在场。”

赫斯特抬头望他，脸上的血色褪尽。

“知道是谁了么？你拿得准他没有回来？哦，我有一种感觉，”她喊，“心里的一种感觉：他回来了！”

===Original===

“My child,” said the old captain, “you may trust her and me. Whatever it is, it is safe with her and me.”

Mrs. Morgan was sitting at the window in her summer place; her placid brow had a cloud upon it, but was not agitated like her husband’s.

“Have you come back to us, Hester?” she said. “We thought we had lost you. If you can satisfy his mind with anything you can say, do it, my dear.”

“What can I say?” Hester cried. “We are all in great trouble. I don’t know which is the greatest, but I cannot tell you secrets that are not mine. Dear Mrs. Morgan, tell the captain so. Whatever I know it is by accident. I think I shall die with anxiety and suspense, but there is nothing I can say.”

“My dear, you will not die, you will live to be anxious many another day. Rowley, my old man, you hear the child. We must not ask her another question. Wait, as you have waited many a time before. It is all in the Lord’s hands.”

The old man was wiping the moisture from his forehead: he had seated himself as soon as he came in, his old limbs were shaking under him. His large, colourless hands shook, holding his handkerchief.

“Mary,” he said, “if it is my flesh and blood that has brought this disturbance into the place, that has seduced her boy, and brought down ruin on her house, how am I ever to lift my head again?”

The old lady looked at him with pathetic eyes, in which there was a suffering as acute as his own, softened and made almost bright by the patience and calm that were habitual to her.

“Rowley, we are not thinking of Catherine, we are thinking of ourselves,” she said.

And then there was a pause. It seemed to Hester that her own brokenheartedness was a sort of child’s passion in comparison. She said humbly﻿—

“Will you tell me what you are afraid of? There is nobody blamed but one. There is not a name spoken of but one. I don’t know if that is any comfort to you, Captain Morgan.”

“And the one is her boy, the apple of her eye, the only one that she has trusted, her choice out of all the world,” the old lady said. “Oh be silent, be silent, my old man! What is your pride to that? I would rather I had a share of the burden﻿—I would like to be suffering with her.” The tears stood in the deep wells of those old eyes, which had wept so much. She was past weeping now. “The Lord forgive him and bring him back,” she said.

===Chinese===

“孩子，”老上校说，“你可以信她，也可以信我。不管是什么，她同我都守得住。”

摩根太太坐在窗前她夏天的位置上；安详的眉宇间罩着一层云，却不像她丈夫那样激动。

“你回到我们这儿来了，赫斯特？”她说。“我们只当你丢了。你能拿话安一安他的心，就安一安，亲爱的。”

“我能说什么呢？”赫斯特喊。“咱们都在大难里。哪一桩最重我说不上，可我不能说不是我的秘密。亲爱的摩根太太，请同上校这样说。我知道的一切，全是碰巧知道的。我怕我要焦心悬念到死，可我一个字也说不得。”

“亲爱的，你死不了；往后要焦心的日子还多着呢。罗利，我的老头子，你听见孩子的话了。咱们不能再问她一句。等罢，像你从前多少回等过的那样。一切在主手里。”

老人正抹着额头上的潮气：他一进门就坐下了，老迈的四肢在身子底下发颤。一双苍白的大手抖着，握不住手帕。

“玛丽，”他说，“若把这场乱子带进这地方、勾走了她的孩子、把塌天大祸压到她宅子上的，是我的骨血，我往后还怎样抬得起头？”

老太太望着他，一双眼睛里含着同他自己一样尖锐的苦，只是被她惯常的忍耐同平静软化得几乎发亮。

“罗利，咱们想的不是凯瑟琳，是咱们自己。”她说。

随后是一阵沉默。赫斯特觉得，比起眼前这一对，她自己那颗碎掉的心简直像孩子使性子。她谦卑地说——

“你们肯告诉我怕的是什么么？遭怪罪的只有一个人。大家嘴里说的只有一个名字。我不知道这于你们算不算一点安慰，摩根上校。”

“那一个却是她的孩子，她的眼珠，她唯一信过的，她从全世界里挑出来的。”老太太说。“哦，住口，住口，我的老头子！你的骄傲同这个比算什么？我倒情愿担子有我一份——我巴不得同她一道受。”泪水蓄在那双哭过太多的老眼深井里。她如今已哭不出了。“愿主饶恕他，领他回来。”她说。

===Original===

“You mean punish him, you mean give him over to the powers of darkness that he belongs to! What does he deserve, a man that has used a woman like that?”

“I am not asking what he deserves. I will tell you what he would get if he would come back. Pardon!” said the old woman with a sob, instinctively putting out her old soft hands.

“I am not for pardon,” said the captain vehemently, his head moving in his agitation, his hands shaking. “I am for every soul bearing its own burden. Here is a woman that has spread prosperity around her. She has been kind, even when she has not been merciful. The grateful and the ungrateful, she has been good to them all. She has been like the sun shining and the rain raining upon both just and unjust. And here is the end of her, stung to her heart by the child of her bosom. For it will be the end of her. She is a grand woman. She won’t bear being deceived.”

“Do not say that,” said Hester; “she is so strong, stronger than any of us﻿—if you had seen her last night!”

“Where could I have seen her last night?” he said quickly; then, with a smile, “that is all you know, you children. Yes, stronger than any one of you, able to do everything. Do you remember the French boy in Browning’s ballad, Hester, that could not bear it when his Emperor asked if he were wounded? ‘I’m killed, sire!’ That is like Catherine. She stands like a tower. I can see her in my mind’s eye. She needs no sleep, no rest: but she is killed for all that.”

Hester rose to her feet as he spoke in an excitement she could not control.

“I must go,” she said. “I must go﻿—I might be wanted.”

The old man rose and hobbled out after her. He followed her to the gate.

“I will wait while you get your hat. I am coming with you,” he said. “We cannot rest, Hester, neither you nor I.”

===Chinese===

“你是说惩办他，把他交给他本属的黑暗权势！”是上校的声音。“他那样作践了一个女人，还配得什么？”

“我不是问他配什么。他若肯回来，得什么，我倒能告诉你：饶恕！”老妇人抽噎着说，本能地伸出她两只柔软的老手。

“我不干饶恕这一套，”上校激烈地说，头激动地晃着，手抖着。“我主张各人担各人的担子。眼前这个女人，把兴旺撒满周身。她就是不和气的时候，也算得上仁厚。感恩的、忘恩的，她一律待他们好。她像日头，照好人也照歹人；像雨水，淋义人也淋不义的人。如今她的结局却是这样：叫她怀里的孩子戳中心口。这就是她的结局。她是位了不起的女人。她受不了人骗。”

“别说这话，”赫斯特说；“她那样坚强，比咱们谁都坚强——您昨夜要是见了她！”

“我昨夜上哪儿见她去？”他急急地说；随即一笑，“你们这些孩子，懂什么。是，比你们谁都强，什么都办得来。赫斯特，你还记得布朗宁歌谣里那个法国孩子么？皇帝问他伤了没有，他受不住那个。‘我死了，陛下！’凯瑟琳就是那样。她像一座塔站着。我闭眼就看得见她。她不要睡眠，不要歇息：可她照样是死了。”

赫斯特听他说着，在一阵按不住的激动里站起来。

“我得去，”她说。“我得去——兴许用得着我。”

老人起身，一瘸一拐跟出来，送她到门口。

“你去取帽子，我等着。我同你一道去。”他说。“咱们安不下心，赫斯特，你也是，我也是。”

===Original===

Mrs. John was dozing in her chair as she generally did in the afternoon. She opened her eyes and said, “Are you going for a walk, dear?” then closed them tranquilly again. The very atmosphere in the brown wainscotted parlour breathed of peace and quiet uncongenial with any such throbbings as those in Hester’s heart. She joined the old man, who was waiting for her at the door, and they went on together, saying little. The great window in the Grange where Catherine usually sat commanding the road was vacant. There was a certain deserted air about the place. They knew without a word that Catherine was still out of it.

“It is too far for you to go,” Hester said.

Though they had not spoken for a long time they understood each other *à demi-mot*.

“It is too far for me,” said he, “but what does that matter? everything will soon be too far for me. Let me go on while I can.”

They walked as far as the bank, where their anxious eyes made out the people lingering about, the air of curiosity and excitement. Old Captain Morgan hobbled up to Mr. Merridew, who was making his way out with a serious face. “You will excuse me for my anxiety, sir,” he said, “but will you tell me if Miss Vernon is there, and what is going on?”

“That is an easy question you are asking me,” said Mr. Merridew, eying him closely; “certainly Miss Vernon is there.”

“I am her near relation,” said the old man, “and you are connected with her by marriage.”

“I know very well who you are, Captain Morgan: a distinguished officer, though people have not found it out here. If you can lend Miss Vernon substantial help I advise you to do it at once.”

Captain Morgan drew back a little: he gave Hester a pathetic glance. They retired slowly with lingering steps from the vicinity of Vernon’s. They understood all without knowing anything.

===Chinese===

约翰太太在椅子里打盹，午饭后她惯常如此。她睁开眼说：“去散步么，亲爱的？”又安然阖上。棕色护壁板小客厅里的整个空气都吐着安宁清静，同赫斯特心口那阵阵搏动格格不入。她同候在门口的老人会合，两人一道走，话不多。格兰奇宅那扇凯瑟琳惯坐的大窗——正瞰着大路——空着。那地方有一种人去楼空的气象。不须一句话，两人都知道：凯瑟琳还不在家。

“这路对您太远。”赫斯特说。

虽然两人多时不曾开口，彼此却一点就透。

“对我是太远，”他说，“可那有什么要紧？再过不久，样样对我都要嫌远。趁还能走，让我走罢。”

他们走到银行，焦急的眼睛辨出了逗留的人群、那种好奇同兴奋的空气。老摩根上校一瘸一拐迎上正板着脸出来的梅里迪尤先生。“您恕我性急，先生，”他说，“可否告诉我，弗农小姐在不在里头，事情怎样了？”

“您这问题问得倒轻巧。”梅里迪尤先生细细打量他说，“弗农小姐自然在。”

“我是她的近亲，”老人说，“您同她也沾着姻亲。”

“你是谁我知道得很清楚，摩根上校：一位有战功的军官，只是此地人还没认出来。您若能助弗农小姐一臂实在之力，我劝您立刻出手。”

摩根上校退了半步，朝赫斯特投去凄然的一瞥。他们放慢脚步，恋恋地、迟迟地退出弗农银行的地界。他们什么都明白了，又一无所知。

===Original===

“There is the bitterness of having nothing,” said the old captain, “and that man knew it, Hester. I would coin myself if I could, for her, and yet I cannot help her.” Neither of them knew about business, nor how men like Mr. Merridew, who had been listening all day long to Catherine’s explanations and arguments without being moved, could save the bank still if they would. But they felt in their hearts the dull opposition of his face, the shake of his head, the nature of his advice to one whom he knew to be a poor man, to help her now. “Money is a wonderful thing,” said Captain Morgan; “it can do so much and yet so little. If you or I were rich as we are poor, we could make Catherine think for half an hour that she had surmounted everything.”

“Why for half an hour, Captain Morgan?” said Hester.

“Because, my dear, at the end of that time Vernon’s being safe, there would come back upon her that from which neither heaven nor earth can deliver her.”

“Oh, Captain Morgan, do not say so. Cannot Heaven, cannot God, deliver from everything?” cried Hester, with a sense of horror.

“Ay, in a way that He uses always at the end﻿—by death. At least we think death will do that for us; but it is only a guess even then. How otherwise?” said the old man, raising his dim old eyes beneath their heavy lids. “What is done cannot be undone. If the boy were to be touched with compunction too late and come back, even that would not restore the past.”

“Why not?” she said, “why not? We could forgive him.” It was the first acknowledgment she had made of any share in the catastrophe.

“Forgive him! You speak as if that could change anything! What is your forgiveness? You seem to think it is a thing, not so many words.” Then after they had gone a little while in silence the old man burst forth again. “You could forgive him! A man wants not forgiveness, but to make up for his sins. You think it is like giving him a fortune to give him your pardon, as if he could set up again, and make a new beginning upon that. Forgiveness may save a man’s soul, but it does not save his honour or his life. You could have him back and let him live upon you, and eat out your hearts with his baseness trying to make it show like virtue. But Catherine is too noble a creature for that,” cried the old captain. “Thank God she has never been broken down to that.”

===Chinese===

“‘两手空空’的苦就苦在这里，”老上校说，“那个人心里明白，赫斯特。只要办得到，我肯把自己铸成钱给她，可我帮不了她。”他们两个都不懂生意，也不懂梅里迪尤先生那样的人——听了一整天凯瑟琳的解说同陈情、不为所动——只要肯，本来怎样还能救下银行。可他们心里觉出了他那副面孔的沉沉的抵拒、那一下摇头、他给一个他明知穷人的那句忠告里头的意思：现在帮她。“钱是个奇妙的东西，”摩根上校说；“它能做那么多，又那么少。你我若富得像如今这样穷，就能叫凯瑟琳有半个钟头觉得一切都翻过去了。”

“为什么只有半个钟头，摩根上校？”赫斯特说。

“因为，亲爱的，半个钟头一到，弗农银行稳了，那件天地都救她不得的事，还是要回到她身上。”

“哦，摩根上校，别这样说。上天不能么，上帝不能救一切么？”赫斯特喊，一股恐怖。

“能，用他永远用在末尾的那一手——死。至少我们当死能替我们办到；其实连那时也只是猜想。不然还能怎样？”老人抬起沉重的眼皮底下那双昏花的老眼。“做了的抹不掉。那孩子就算太晚动了悔心、回来，过去的也回不来。”

“为什么不能？”她说，“为什么？我们可以饶他。”这是她头一回认自己在这一场大祸里的份。

“饶他！你说得好像那能改变什么！你的饶恕算什么？你当它是一件东西，不是几句话。”默默走了一阵，老人又爆发了。“你饶得了他！男人要的不是饶恕，是赔他的罪。你当你饶他，就是给了他一笔家私，他好靠那个重新起家、重新开头。饶恕救得了人的灵魂，救不了人的名誉同性命。你可以领他回来，养着他，看他的卑劣拿你们的心一口口吃空，还得替他把卑劣装点成德行。可凯瑟琳不是那样的人，”老上校喊道。“感谢上帝，她从没被作践到那一步。”

===Original===

This torrent of words overwhelmed Hester; they had turned into the quiet road again, and the girl fell into a low sobbing and weeping as she went. She was too much overstrained to be able to control herself. Yet her heart struggled against this sentence.

“If you love anyone is it only while he is good?” she said. “Is it noble to cast him from you because he has gone wrong? Then what is love or faithfulness? Are they nothing﻿—nothing?”

She knew now that he had not come back. Honour had not moved him, nor love, nor any nobler impulse. She could have flung herself upon the earth in her misery. She felt that a touch now would be too much﻿—that she could bear nothing further. And her companion saw that she was beyond the reach of any argument. He was silent, and they moved slowly along together, he tottering on his aged limbs, scarcely able to get along.

“Soon everything will be too far for me,” he said with a half-pleased, almost satisfied nodding of his head. It took them a long time to get home, and the old captain was so worn out that he could not rise from his chair again that evening. He and his old wife sat sadly, saying something to each other once in half an hour. They could think of nothing but Catherine. They kept up their broken musing discussion upon her and her fate as the slow summer evening again crept silently by.

But Hester could not rest. She satisfied her mother easily that it was right she should go back to the Grange and find out if she could be of use.

===Chinese===

这一番倾泻压倒了赫斯特；他们已转回那条静路，姑娘一路低低地抽噎、落泪。她绷得太满，管不住自己了。可她的心还在抗拒这句判词。

“你若爱一个人，难道只在他好的时候爱？”她说。“他走了岔道就把他甩开，这算高贵？那还叫什么爱、什么忠贞？它们什么都不是——什么都不是？”

她如今知道了：他没有回来。名誉没有动他，爱也没有，任何更高贵的冲动都没有。她苦得恨不能扑倒在地。她觉得此刻再碰她一下都是多余——她再也受不住什么了。她的同伴看出她已到了一切道理够不着的地方。他不言语了，两人缓缓同行，他在老迈的腿上打晃，几乎挪不动。

“再过不久，样样都要嫌我远了。”他说，点着头，那样子半是欢喜、几乎满足。他们走了很久才到家，老上校累得当晚再没能从椅子里起来。他同老妻哀哀地对坐，隔半个钟头才交谈一两句。他们想不出别的，只想凯瑟琳。夏日的黄昏又一次悄悄爬过，他们把那场断断续续的沉思谈论续下去，谈她，谈她的命。

可赫斯特安不下来。她轻而易举地说服了母亲：她该回格兰奇宅去，看看用得着她不。

===Original===

“It is what I was going to suggest, my dear,” said Mrs. John. “If Edward Vernon is away, as you say, and nobody with her, she must be lonely. And if there is any trouble besides﻿—though you have never rightly explained to me what it was. No no, dear, I don’t mean to say it is your fault. No doubt you have told me, and I have not taken it up. To be sure, Hester, you must go; and though I cannot bear to be without you, yet if Catherine wants you, and she is in trouble, stay. I am sure she would do as much for me,” said the simple soul, without any cold breathings of doubt. She went to the gate with Hester, and when she came back could not help giving her neighbours a little sketch of the state of affairs. “My Hester has gone back to the Grange,” she said, “she will probably stay there all night. Catherine Vernon wrote me the nicest note to tell me my child had been of so much use to her; that is always gratifying to a mother.”

“Of use!” cried the ladies both together. “Gracious goodness, what can be going to happen? Hester of use!” cried one sister. “And to Catherine!” said the other. “Dear Catherine, she tells you so to please you﻿—when probably she is thinking you the greatest bore﻿—”

“She likes something new to experiment upon,” said Mr. Mildmay Vernon with a snarl. Mrs. John was much discouraged by this reception of her news. She said﻿—

“You little know my child if you think she will be experimented upon,” holding her head high; but when she got indoors she cried a little over their ill-nature. If it had been one of them who had been chosen how different would have been their tone. Had the brougham been sent express for Miss Matilda or Miss Martha, what airs they would have given themselves! and Mrs. John knew that she had given herself no airs: she had not said a word. But she could not be silent about the promotion of her child.

===Chinese===

“这正是我要提议的，亲爱的。”约翰太太说。“爱德华·弗农既像你说的那样不在家，又没人陪她，她准寂寞。再说若还有什么难处——虽然你始终没对我讲明白到底是什么。不不，亲爱的，我不是说是你的错。不用说你对我说过了，只是我没接住。当然，赫斯特，你一定去；我虽舍不得离了你，可凯瑟琳既用得着你、她又在难处里，就留下。我拿得准，她待我也会一样。”这个单纯的灵魂说，没有一丝凉气疑云。她送赫斯特到大门口，回来忍不住给邻舍们小小勾画一番现状。“我家赫斯特回格兰奇宅去了，”她说，“多半要在那儿过夜。凯瑟琳·弗农给我写了顶客气的条子，说我孩子于她大有用处；做母亲的听了总是得意的。”

“有用处！”两位小姐一齐喊。“老天爷，要出什么事？赫斯特有用处！”一个喊。“还是对凯瑟琳！”另一个说。“亲爱的凯瑟琳那是哄你——她心里没准正当你是个天大的腻烦——”

“她不过是又找了个新鲜人做试验。”米尔德梅·弗农先生嗤了一声说。这番待遇把约翰太太气得够呛。她说——

“你们当我孩子是随人做试验的，就太不认识她了。”头昂得高高的；可一进家门，还是为她们的坏心肠掉了几滴泪。挑中的若是她们里的哪一个，那口气又该怎样不同。那辆马车若专程去接的是马蒂尔达小姐或玛莎小姐，她们要摆出多大的架子！约翰太太知道自己没摆架子：她一个字没夸。可孩子的高升，她到底憋不住。

## XLIII / 四十三
===Original===

An Interruption

Catherine was in her usual chair in the familiar room where she had lived for so many years. These walls had witnessed most of the pleasantnesses and disappointments of her life; within them she had grown into that amused spectatorship of all the pranks of human creatures which it had pleased her to think was her characteristic attitude, indulgent to everybody, seeing through everybody. They had never seen her in the aspect which she bore now, beaten down under the stroke of fate. She was too far gone even to be conscious of the extraordinary irony of life which had made of the one only creature to whom she had been consciously unjust, whom she had considered from her childhood as an enemy, her sole ministrant and sympathiser now. But she was not conscious even of Hester’s presence, who, overpowered by a great awe of the suffering which she shared, kept herself in the background, recognising, as so few watchers do, that she was there for the sake of the sorrowful woman whom she watched, and not at all for her own. Catherine lay back in her chair, her head thrown back, her eyelids half closed. She did not move, except now and then to put up her hand and dry the moisture which collected slowly under her eyelids. It could not be called tears. It was that extorted dew of pain which comes when the heart seems pressed and crushed in some giant grasp. She was not thinking, any more than it is inevitable to think as long as life remains. She was only suffering, nothing more. She could not make any head against it. Her last stronghold had fallen. This it is which makes calamity so terrible to the old. She could not get beyond it. There was nothing, nothing in her path but this, blocking it across with a darkness that would never be dispersed. If he had died she would have known she could not remain long behind him, and the gloom would have been but a mist between; but he had not died. The thought of searching for him through the world, of holding out succour to him when he came to need, of forgiving, that last prerogative of love, was scarcely in her nature. It was hers rather to feel that deep impossibility of re-beginning, the misery and pain of any struggle to make the base seem noble, which is as true a sentiment as the other. She could not have done it.

===Chinese===

一场打搅

凯瑟琳坐在她惯坐的椅子里，在那间住了多年的、熟得不能再熟的屋子。这几面墙，见证过她一生大半的快意与失望；在这四面里，她长成了那副观戏者的姿态——饶有兴味地看世人的一切把戏，还乐于把它认作自己的本色：对人人宽容，把人人看穿。可它们从没见过她如今这副模样——被命运的打击压伏在地。她已经沉得太深，连命运那层奇异的讽刺都意识不到了：她平生唯一自觉亏待过的人、她自幼当作仇人的那一个，如今成了她唯一的侍奉者与同情者。她甚至意识不到赫斯特在场；赫斯特怀着对这场她有份的苦难的大敬畏，退在一旁，认得清清楚楚——守望着的人很少有认得清的——她在这里，是为了她守望的那个悲伤的女人，全不为自己。凯瑟琳仰在椅中，头向后靠着，眼皮半阁。她不动，只是偶尔抬手，拭去眼皮下慢慢积起的那点湿。那算不得泪。那是痛楚被逼出的露水，在心仿佛被一只巨掌攒紧压碎时渗出来。她不在想什么——只要生命还在，想什么原由不得人。她只是在受苦，仅此而已。她无从再挣扎。她最后一座堡垒陷落了。灾难之于老人所以这样可怕，正为此。她越不过去。路上没有别的，只有这个，横着一段永不开散的黑。他若死了，她会知道自己跟随他去的日子不远，那片阴翳不过是中间一层雾；可他没有死。走遍天下寻他，等他困厄时援他，饶恕他——爱到末了的那宗特权——这样的心思，同她的天性几乎不相干。她天性里更深的，是那份无从重新来过的绝境感，是把卑污硬撑成高贵的挣扎里的苦与痛——这情感同那一种一样真。她是做不到的。

===Original===

To many women it is the highest form of self-abnegation as it is the bitterest lot that can be borne on earth; but to Catherine it would not have been possible. The blow to her was final. There was but one thing﻿—to fight for Vernon’s to the last gasp, to ward off disgrace and failure from the name, to keep the ground it had occupied so long, against possibility, against hope; but after that no more﻿—no more. She had borne herself bravely as long as any eye was upon her, betraying nothing; and had sat down to table and tried to eat, with that utter self-mastery which will sustain the life it loathes with sedulous care so long as it is necessary﻿—talking to Hester at intervals, giving Marshall directions as if nothing had happened. She had been first impatient, then satisfied to find the girl there. Her presence was a help in that needful struggle.

Catherine went upstairs after dinner as usual. Nothing was changed; but when she had attained to that shelter, she could do no more. She put back her head and closed her eyes, and gave herself up to the endurance of her deathblow. At the other end of the room Hester sat motionless. A keen-sighted spectator would have seen the outline of her figure in her dark dress, but nothing more. She was watching, forgetting her own share, intent upon the other. Her mind was full of what the old captain had said, “I’m killed, sire.” Hester watched with a great awe, wondering if even thus, in the silence, without any more demonstration, a woman might die. She thought in her heart it would be well; but being so young she was afraid. And the silence was so deep, more deep than life could tolerate. She watched eagerly for that sole movement, the lifting of Catherine’s hand to dry away the moisture from her eyes.

===Chinese===

对许多女人，那是克己的最高形式，也是人间能担的最苦的命；可对凯瑟琳，它不可能。这一击于她是终局的。只剩一件事——为弗农银行战到最后一口气，替这个姓氏挡开耻辱与败亡，守住它占据了这么久的地盘，逆着可能，逆着指望；此后再没有——再没有别的。只要有眼睛望着她，她便挺得住，不露分毫；她入了席，试着进食，凭着那份彻底的自制——那自制会殷勤地供养着它厌弃的性命，只要还有必要——间或同赫斯特说句话，给马歇尔吩咐事情，仿佛什么都没发生。起初她嫌姑娘在场，随后又觉出她在场的好处。这份在场，是那场必要之战里的一个帮手。

正餐后凯瑟琳照常上了楼。什么都没变；可一抵达那处庇荫，她便再也做不动什么了。她头向后一靠，阁上眼，把自己交给那致命一击去消受。屋子另一头，赫斯特一动不动地坐着。眼尖的人能辨出她深色衣裙里的身形轮廓，仅此而已。她在守望，忘了自己的一份，一心只在另一人身上。她满脑子是老上校那句话：“陛下，我阵亡了。”赫斯特怀着大敬畏望着，暗想：人会不会就这样——在寂静里，再无一点动静——死过去？她心里想，那样倒好；可她太年轻，怕。寂静又那样深，深得生命受不住。她急切地守着那唯一的动作：凯瑟琳抬手、拭去眼底湿意的那个动作。

===Original===

This stillness was broken suddenly by a loud knocking at the door﻿—a continued volley of knocks, accompanied by the sound of voices outside. Then this sound surged inwards, and hasty steps were heard rushing upstairs. Hester’s heart leaped to her mouth. It could not be that *he* would come back with such a noise and outcry; but yet a sort of frantic hope took possession of her as she rose to her feet. Catherine had raised herself too, and sat with her eyes widely open fixed upon the door. They had not long to wait. The door was flung open, dashing against a cabinet which stood near, with a superfluity of noise and emphasis; and, sweeping away the silence before her, and every possibility of calm, Ellen Merridew burst into the room, her eyes inflamed with crying, her fair countenance streaked with red, her light locks standing up round her face. She was followed by her husband, trying to hold her back, and by Marshall in the rear, eager﻿—under a respectable semblance of attending the hasty visitors﻿—to give accuracy to the floating suspicions of the servants’ hall, and find out what it was all about. Ellen rushed in, and gazed about her wildly.

“Where is he?” she cried. “Oh, Aunt Catherine, where is he? You are hiding him, I said you would hide him, whatever he did. Oh, is it nothing to you if he goes and ruins people that never did him any harm?﻿—young people like us that have all our life before us, and a dear baby to be turned out upon the world. Oh, Aunt Catherine, if you have any heart at all, where is he, where is he? I’ll have him to justice!” cried Ellen. “I’ll not sit under it. I won’t﻿—not if he should kill me! I want Edward. Where is Edward? I shan’t go out of this till you give him up to me. He has ruined us, he has ruined us!” cried the excited creature, bursting into a transport of passionate tears.

There had been a moment of bewildered struggle in Catherine’s face; then she rose up with what seemed to the excited newcomers her usual composure.

“What does all this mean?” she said, in her quiet voice.

Hester had shut the door upon the servant’s curiosity; Ellen crying violently, and poor Algernon, endeavouring vainly to console her, stood between the two, in the centre of the room. It was all that poor young Merridew could do not to weep too.

===Chinese===

这份寂静，猛然被一阵擑门打破——敲门声连珠炮似的一串，还夹着门外的人声。随后那声浪向里涌，急促的脚步冲上楼来。赫斯特的心跳到了嗓子眼。总不会是*他*带着这样的吵嚷叫喊回来；可她站起身时，一种狂乱的希望还是攫住了她。凯瑟琳也直起了身，坐着，双眼大睁，钉在门上。没等多久。门被猛地推开，撞在近旁的一口柜上，声音与气势都过了分；埃伦·梅里迪尤扫开身前的寂静、扫开一切安宁的可能，冲进屋来——一双眼哭得通红，白净的脸上一道道红痕，浅色的发丝在脸旁炸着。她丈夫跟着，一路想拽住她；马歇尔殿后——顶着一份体面的、照料急客的表象，急切地想替下人房里那些飘忽的猜测寻个准头，看看究竟出了什么事。埃伦冲进来，狂乱地四下张望。

“他在哪儿？”她嚷道。“哦，凯瑟琳姑姑，他在哪儿？你把他藏起来了——我就说你准会藏他，不管他干了什么。哦，他跑出去毁掉从来没害过他的人，你全不当回事？——毁我们这样的年轻人，一辈子还在前头，还有个亲亲的娃娃要被撂到世上。哦，凯瑟琳姑姑，你要还有半点心肝，他在哪儿，他在哪儿？我要送他上法庭！”埃伦嚷道。“这口气我咽不下。我不咽——他杀了我也不咽！我要爱德华。爱德华在哪儿？你不把他交出来，我就不出这个门。他毁了我们也，他毁了我们也！”这激动的人嚷着，迸出一阵狂风暴雨般的泪。

凯瑟琳脸上有一瞬慌乱的挣扎；随后她站起身，在那两个激动的来客看来，还带着她惯常的镇定。

“这都是什么意思？”她用她安静的嗓音说。

赫斯特已把仆人的好奇心关在了门外；埃伦哭得凶，可怜的阿尔杰农徒劳地劝慰着，两人立在她们中间、屋子中央。可怜的年轻梅里迪尤勉力撑着的，只是不陪着她一起哭。

===Original===

“I am sure you will forgive her, Miss Vernon,” he said, in faltering tones. “We are nearly out of our senses. Oh, don’t cry, my dearest; whatever they do they can’t part us, and I’ll work for you and baby. I’ll work till I drop. Miss Vernon, if Edward’s here﻿—she doesn’t mean any harm. She is just off her head, poor girl! and baby not a month old yet. If you will only let us see him, I’ll pledge my word﻿—”

“Algy, hold your tongue!” cried Ellen amidst her sobs, stamping her foot. “Hold your tongue, I tell you. She’ll never, never give him up﻿—never till she’s forced, I know that. She has always liked that fellow better than the whole of us put together. And we’ve every one kowtowed to him for her sake. He’s been the head of everything, though he was nothing but a poor﻿—And as frightened of her as a dog, and hated her all the time. Oh yes, Aunt Catherine, you may believe me or not, but whenever there was a word about you, Edward was always the worst. Of course we all had our remarks to make, I don’t say anything different; but he was always the worst. And now he’s gone, and led Algy to his ruin,” she cried, with another wild outburst. “We have lost every penny. Do you hear me, Aunt Catherine, do you hear me? We’re ruined, with a dear baby not a month old, and I that have never got up my strength. Oh yes, Algy, yes, dear. I know you’ll work till you drop. But what good will that do to me, to have you work yourself to death, and to be left a widow at my age, with a baby to support? And, Aunt Catherine, it will all be your fault,” cried Ellen. “Yes, it will be your fault. If you hadn’t made such a fuss about him, who would have ever trusted him? It was because of you I gave my consent. I said Aunt Catherine will never let him come to harm. And now here it has all come to smash, and me and Algy are ruined. Oh, how can you have the heart? and a dear innocent baby without a word to say for himself! And me at my age﻿—and poor Algy that thought he was making so good a marriage when he got one of the Vernons﻿—”

“Nelly, Nelly, darling!” cried the poor young fellow, “I married you because I loved you, not because you were one of the Vernons.”

===Chinese===

“您千万担待她，弗农小姐。”他颤着声说。“我们差不多疯了。哦，别哭，我最亲的；他们随怎样也拆不散我们；我养你同宝宝。我干到倒下为止。弗农小姐，爱德华若在这儿——她没有坏心。她只是失了神，可怜的人！宝宝还不满一个月。您只消让我们见见他，我拿人格担保——”

“阿尔吉，闭嘴！”埃伦哭着跺脚叫道。“闭嘴，我说。她永远不会、永远不会交出他——不逼到头她不交，我知道。她喜欢那家伙，一向胜过我们全部加在一起。我们一个个都为着她的缘故向他磕头。什么都归他当头，其实他不过是个穷——还怕她怕得像条狗，心里又一直恨她。哦是，凯瑟琳姑姑，你信也罢不信也罢：但凡提起你，爱德华回回话最毒。当然我们个个都说过闲话，我不说旁的；可他回回最毒。如今他跑了，还把阿尔吉拖下水。”她又一阵狂风暴雨般地哭喊。“我们一个便士也不剩了。你听见没有，凯瑟琳姑姑，听见没有？我们毁了，抱着个还不满月的亲亲的娃娃，我又一直没养回元气。哦是，阿尔吉，是，亲爱的。我知道你会干到倒下。可那于我有什么好——看你活活累死，叫我这样年纪守寡，抱着个娃娃？还有，凯瑟琳姑姑，这全是你的错。”埃伦叫道。“是，全是你的错。你若不曾把他捧成那样，谁会信他？我当初点头，就因为你。我说：凯瑟琳姑姑永远不会叫他吃亏。如今全砸了，我同阿尔吉全毁了。哦，你怎么忍心？一个亲亲的无辜娃娃，连一句自辩的话都不会说！我又这样的年纪——可怜的阿尔吉，娶到一个弗农家的人，还当自己结了多好的一门亲——”

“内莉，内莉，心肝！”可怜的年轻人叫道，“我娶你，是因为我爱你，不是因为你姓弗农。”

===Original===

“And he had a good right to think so,” said Ellen pushing away his caressing arm. “And they all thought so﻿—everyone; and now they’ve turned against me, and say I’m extravagant, and that I’ve ruined him. Oh! me to have ruined him that thought I was making a man of him! Aunt Catherine! Will you let us all be sacrificed, every one, only to keep Edward from harm?”

Catherine Vernon had sunk into her chair, but there was something of the old look of the spectator at a comedy again upon her face. The evening was beginning to fall, and they did not see the almost ghastly colour which had replaced the wonderful complexion of which everybody once spoke.

“Make her sit down, Algernon, and stop this raving,” she said. “What has happened? I know nothing of it. If you have any claims upon Vernon’s you will be paid with the rest﻿—if we stand, till the last penny, if we fall, to the utmost that can be paid. I cannot say any more.”

They both sat down and gazed at her with consternation on their faces; even Ellen’s tears dried up as by magic. After she had stopped, they sat staring as if stupefied. Then Ellen got up, and threw herself at Catherine’s feet with a cry of wild dismay.

“Aunt Catherine! you don’t mean to say that you cannot help us, that you cannot save us? Oh, Aunt Catherine! don’t be angry with me. I did not mean to make you angry. I was always silly, you know. You will help us, you will save Algy, you will pay the money, won’t you?” She crept close to Catherine, and took her hand and kissed it, looking up piteously, with tears streaming down her face. “You’ll do it for me, Aunt Catherine? Oh, though I am silly I am fond of my husband. And he’s so good; he’s never said it was my fault. And I always knew you would put it right. Aunt Catherine! you will put it right?”

Her voice rose into a shrill, despairing cry; then she dropped down helpless, sobbing and moaning, but still holding by Catherine’s hand and her dress, whatever she could grasp at, in a passion of incredulity and despair.

Then Catherine, who had been so stately, sank back into her chair.

“I can’t bear any more,” she said, “I can’t bear any more. For the love of God take her away!”

===Chinese===

“他原也当得起这个念头。”埃伦推开他抚慰的手臂说。“他们原先个个都这么想——人人；如今他们全翻脸骂我，说我挥霍，说我毁了他。哦！我毁了他——我还当自己在把他造就成个人物！凯瑟琳姑姑！你肯让我们人人全当牺牲，只为保爱德华不受伤？”

凯瑟琳·弗农已跌坐回椅中；她脸上却又浮出几分旧日那副观喜剧的神情。暮色初降，他们没有看见那张脸上近乎死灰的颜色——它顶替了人人曾经称道的那副惊人的气色。

“叫她坐下，阿尔杰农，别叫她再撒泼。”她说。“出了什么事？我一无所知。你们对弗农银行若有债权，会同大家的一并偿付——银行站得住，付到最后一便士；倒了，付到能付的极限。再多我说不出。”

两人双双坐下，一脸惊愕地瞪着她；连埃伦的泪也像被法术收干了。她一住口，两人还呆呆地瞪着，像被震懵了。随后埃伦起身，一声狂乱的绝望喊叫，扑倒在凯瑟琳脚前。

“凯瑟琳姑姑！你不会是说，你帮不了我们、救不了我们？哦，凯瑟琳姑姑！别恼我。我没想惹你恼。我一向傻，你知道的。你会帮我们的，你会救阿尔吉，你会把钱付了，对不对？”她挨到凯瑟琳跟前，抓过她的手亲吻，可怜巴巴地仰着脸，泪顺着往下淌。“你会为我做的，凯瑟琳姑姑？哦，我虽傻，我疼我丈夫。他多好；从没说过是我的错。我也一向知道，你会把一切摆平。凯瑟琳姑姑！你会摆平的，对不对？”

她的声音拔成一声尖利的、绝望的喊；随后整个人瘫软下去，抽噎着、呻吟着，手里还死死攒着凯瑟琳的手、凯瑟琳的裙——抓得着什么是什么——在一阵不敢信与绝望的激狂里。

于是一向那样端庄的凯瑟琳，也跌回了椅子里。

“我受不住了。”她说，“我受不住了。看在上帝份上，把她带走！”

===Original===

But it was only the sudden appearance of Harry which put an end to this painful scene. He gathered his sister up in his arms, while her husband was ineffectually intreating and reasoning with her, and carried her out of the room, with a severity and sternness which silenced the young pair.

“Look here,” he said, taking them into the deserted library which had been Edward’s room, “we are all in the same box. He has ruined her and us all. You, out of your own confounded folly, the rest of us﻿—I can’t tell you how. He has ruined *her*. God﻿—forgive him!” cried Harry, with a long pause, bringing out the last words with a violent effort. “But, look here! The only hope we have of pulling through is in her. They can’t let Catherine Vernon be ruined in Redborough. I don’t think it’s in the heart of man to do it; but if we drive her into her grave, as you’ve been trying to do﻿—”

“Oh, Harry, how dare you say so! I only went to her﻿—where should I go?﻿—and I thought it would be all right. I thought it was dreadful, but I never believed it, for I know Aunt Catherine﻿—”

“Ellen, hold your tongue, for God’s sake! If we kill her, it’s all up with us. Hasn’t she got enough to bear? I brought a cab when I knew you were here. Take her home, Algy, and keep her quiet, and let’s meet and talk over it like men,” Harry said, severely.

He had never so asserted himself in all his life before. They hurried her out between them to the cab, much against Ellen’s will, who wanted explanations, and to know if it was true that Aunt Catherine couldn’t, couldn’t if she would; and then told them, sobbing, that if it was so, none of them could afford to pay for a cab, and why, why should ruined people spend a shilling when they had not got it? The cabman heard part of these protestations, and Marshall another part. But on the whole both Algernon and Harry were more occupied with her in her transport, more anxious for its consequences, more tender of her, than if she had been the most self-commanded and heroic woman in the world.

When this tempest of interruption swept away, Catherine was still for a few minutes more. Then she called Hester to her in a voice of exhaustion.

===Chinese===

还是哈里的骤然露面，才了结了这场痛楚的戏。妹夫正徒劳地求她、劝她，他一把将妹妹抱起来，抱出了屋子；那股严厉与冷峻，把这对年轻人全镇住了。

“你们听着。”他说，把两人领进那间空落的书房——爱德华从前那间。“我们全在一条船上。他毁了她，也毁了我们要不——你，毁于你自己那该死的糊涂；我们其余人，怎么毁的我说不清。他毁了*她*。上帝——饶恕他！”哈里喊道，顿了半晌，末几个字是狠挣出来的。“可是听着！我们熬得过去的唯一指望，在她。雷德伯勒容不下凯瑟琳·弗农被毁。我不信人心容得下这个；可我们若把她逼进坟墓——像你们方才试的那样——”

“哦，哈里，你怎么敢这么说！我不过是找她去——我不找她找谁？——我还当会没事的。我当事情可怕，可我从没真信，因为我知道凯瑟琳姑姑——”

“埃伦，看上帝份上闭嘴！我们弄死了她，我们全完。她受的难道还不够？我知道你们在这儿，顺路叫了辆马车。送她回家，阿尔吉，叫她静一静；回头我们碰个头，像男人一样把事情议一议。”哈里严厉地说。

他平生从没这样做过主。两人把她架出门、塞进马车——埃伦老大不愿意，还嚷着要个说法，要弄清凯瑟琳姑姑是不是真的不能、真想也不能；随后又哭着说：若真如此，他们谁也出不起马车钱，为什么、为什么破了产的人还要花手里没有的一先令？车夫听去了这抗议的一半，马歇尔听去了另一半。可总的看来，阿尔杰农同哈里两个，对她这场失态，倒更操心、更怕后果、更心疼她——胜过她是天下最有自制、最英勇的女人时的十分。

这场打搅的风暴卷过去后，凯瑟琳又静了几分钟。随后她用力竭的嗓音唤赫斯特过去。

===Original===

“I think,” she said, “it has done me no harm. Anything is better than that which﻿—is always behind. And I must do nothing to hurt myself before tomorrow. Was not Harry there? He may have something to tell me. Let him come and say it to you. You are quick witted, and you will understand; and if it is worth writing, write it down. I will not take any part. I will keep still here. If it rouses me, so much the better. If not, you will listen for me with your young ears, and forget nothing. I must save myself, you see, for tomorrow.”

“I will forget nothing,” Hester said.

Catherine smiled faintly, with her eyes closed.

“I had thought of making you bring me some wine. There is some Tokay in the cellar; but one always pays for a strong stimulant, and this is the better way. You are young, and you are a Vernon too. Bend your mind to it. Think of nothing but the business in hand.”

“I will,” said Hester, with solemnity, as if she were pronouncing the words before a judge.

Catherine took hold of her dress when she was going away.

“One thing,” she said. “I think you and I have hated each other because we were meant to love each other, child.”

“I think I have always done both,” said Hester.

The faint sound that broke through the stillness was not like Catherine’s laugh. She patted the girl’s arm softly with her hand. Their amity was too new to bear caresses.

“Now go and do your work, for your honour and mine,” she said.

It appeared that Harry had much to say. It was strange to have to say it all to the young and eager listener, her eyes glowing with interest and anxiety, who was not content with any one statement, but questioned and investigated till she had brought out every point of meaning, while the real authority sat by silent, her eyes closed, her hands clasped, like an image of repose. Both the young people kept their eyes upon her. There was not a movement which Hester did not watch, while she exerted her faculties to comprehend everything that Harry told her, and put down everything that seemed at all important. The impulse carried her over her own share of the individual misery. Everything else disappeared before the paramount importance of this. When all that Harry had to say was said, there arose a silence between them which had the effect which nothing before had of rousing Catherine. She opened her eyes and looked at them kindly.

===Chinese===

“我看，”她说，“这一场于我没有坏处。什么都强过那个——总跟在身后的那个。明天之前，我不能伤着自己。哈里不是在那儿吗？他也许有话要对我说。叫他对你说。你脑子快，你听得懂；值得记的，就记下来。我一个字不接。我就这样静着。能提我的神，更好；提不了，你就替我用你年轻的耳朵听着，一字别漏。我得省下自己，你明白，留给明天。”

“我什么也不忘。”赫斯特说。

凯瑟琳阁着眼，淡淡一笑。

“我原想叫你去给我取点酒。地窖里有托卡伊；可烈的提神物，过后总要还账；这个法子更好。你年轻，你也是弗农家的人。把心思弯到这上头来。手里的事之外，什么都不想。”

“我一定。”赫斯特郑重地说，像在法官面前宣蕃。

她要走时，凯瑟琳抓住了她的裙角。

“一句话。”她说。“我想，你我相恨，原是为了注定要相爱，孩子。”

“我想我两样一直都在做。”赫斯特说。

静里透出的那一声轻响，不像凯瑟琳的笑。她伸手轻轻拍了拍姑娘的手臂。她们的交好太新，还经不起爱抚。

“去办你的事吧，为你的名誉，也为我的。”她说。

哈里竟有许多话要说。这一切都得说给那个年轻而急切的听者——她眼里烧着关切与焦灼——听者又不满足于任何一句陈述，追问、追查，直到逼出每一点含义；而真正的权威静坐一旁，阁着眼，交叠着手，像一尊安憩的像。两个年轻人时时望着她。赫斯特一边不漏掉她的一个动作，一边把全部心智用来听懂哈里的每一句，把要紧的一一记下。这股冲劲载着她越过了她自己那一份私人的苦。其余一切，都消失在这件压倒一切的大事后面。哈里的话说尽，两人之间升起一片寂静——这片寂静激起了凯瑟琳，先前什么都不曾这样激起过。她睁开眼，慈和地望着他们。

===Original===

“Everything has been done as I wished,” she said. “I have gleaned something, and the rest you will tell me, Hester, tomorrow. It has been a rest to me to hear your voices. You can expect me, Harry, at the same hour.”

“Is it not too much for you, Aunt Catherine? It is everything for us that you should come.”

“I will come,” she said. “It is easier than staying at home. Fatigue is salvation. Now I am going to bed, to sleep. Oh, I mean it. I cannot do my work without it. You will come too in the morning, Hester, when I send for you? Then, good night.”

They watched her go away with her step still stately. Her faithful maid, whom Mrs. John had found so kind, but who had not always been kind, was waiting for her. The two young people stood and looked after her with eyes of tender respect and awe.

“I thought once,” said Hester, in a hush of subdued feeling, “that she might have died sitting in her chair.”

“Ah,” said Harry, who had a little more experience, “it is seldom that people get out of it so easily as that. I want to tell you something more if it will not﻿—upset you more.”

Hester smiled.

“Is there anything that can upset me more?” she said.

He looked at her wistfully. He did not know what her individual part in this trouble had been; whether Edward was more to her than another, or what the position was in which they stood to each other.

“I don’t know how to take it,” he said, “or how to understand it. There are news of﻿—Edward.”

The last gleam of hope shot across Hester’s mind.

“He is coming back?” she said, clasping her hands.

Harry shook his head.

“Will you come with me to the door? It is such a lovely night.”

She had not the courage or the presence of mind to say no. She went downstairs with him, where the lamps were lighted again, and out to the gate﻿—the same hour, the same atmosphere as last night. Was it only last night that all had happened? She could have turned and fled in the tremor, the horror of the recollection. Just there she lay at Catherine’s feet. Just there Catherine had stood and listened.

“您担得起吗，凯瑟琳姑姑？您肯来，于我们就是一切。”

“我来。”她说。“这比待在家容易。疲惫便是救赎。现在我上床睡觉去。哦，我是认真的。不睡，我做不了我的事。明早我打发人叫你，你也来，赫斯特？那么，晚安。”

他们望着她走开，步态依旧端庄。她那忠心的女仆——约翰太太觉得她顶和气、其实并不一向和气的那位——正候着她。两个年轻人立在原地目送，眼里是温柔的敬与畏。

“方才有一阵我想，”赫斯特压着心绪低声说，“她也许会就死在那把椅子里。”

赫斯特笑了。

“还有什么事能更叫我受不住？”她说。

他怅然望着她。他不知道她在这场祸事里的私份；不知道爱德华于她是否异于旁人，也不知道两人彼此站在什么地界上。

最后一线希望掠过赫斯特心头。

“他要回来了？”她说，双手合在了一起。

哈里摇了摇头。

“陪我到门口走走好吗？夜色真好。”

她没有勇气、也没有镇定说个不字。她随他下了楼——灯又点亮了——走到大门口：同一个时辰，同一片气息，同昨夜一样。这一切都只是昨夜发生的么？在追忆的战栗与恐怖里，她几乎转身逃走。就在那儿，她曾伏在凯瑟琳脚前。就在那儿，凯瑟琳曾立着偷听。

===Original===

Hester stood her ground like a martyr. She knew she must learn to do so, and that it would not be possible to avoid the place made so bitter by recollection. Harry did not know how to speak. He shifted uneasily from one foot to another. “He has been traced to town; he got in at the junction, not here. He reached London this morning, very early﻿—with a lady.”

“With a lady!”

Hester had expected a great shock, but the astonishment of this took its sting away.

“They left this afternoon, it is supposed to go abroad,” Harry said.

“Still with the lady? That is very strange,” said Hester, with a little quiver in her lips.

“There is reason now to suppose that he﻿—married her in the meantime.”

Hester had grasped by accident the post of the gate. She was glad she had done so. It was a support to her, at least. Married her! It gave her no immediate pain in her astonishment, which was unspeakable. In the dusk Harry did not see her face. He had no conception of the real state of the case. The fact that Edward had been discovered with another woman had confused Harry and diverted the natural suspicions which had risen in his mind when he had found Hester so linked with Catherine after the discovery of Edward’s flight. He watched her with a little alarm, wondering and anxious. But the only sign of any emotion was the tightening of her hand upon the iron gate.

“You will know,” he said, “whether it will be best to say anything of this. If it will hurt her more, let it alone till the crisis is past.”

“If it will hurt her﻿—more? I do not think anything﻿—can hurt her more.”

“And you are nearly over-worn,” he said, with a tender and pitying cadence in his voice. “I can’t say spare yourself, Hester. You are the only one she deserves nothing from. She ought to feel that: if he is gone who owes her everything, yet you are standing by her, who never owed her anything.”

赫斯特像殉道者一样站住了。她知道自己必须学着站住；这个被回忆浸得这样苦的地方，躲是躲不开的。哈里不知怎么开口，两只脚不安地倒换。“有人追到了他的踪迹，进了城；他是在枢纽站上车的，不是这一站。今天一早，很早，他到了伦敦——同一位女士。”

“同一位女士！”

赫斯特原等着一场大震；可这一惊的奇，倒把它的毒刺拔了。

“今天下午他们走了，想必是出国。”哈里说。

“还同那位女士一起？这就很怪了。”赫斯特说，嘴唇微微一颤。

“现在有理由认为，他——在此期间娶了她。”

赫斯特恰好一把抓住了门柱。她庆幸抓了。那至少是个撑持。娶了她！这一惊之下，她一时竟不觉得痛——惊愕大得没有言语。暮色里哈里看不见她的脸。他对实情毫无概念。爱德华被查出同另一个女人在一起——这一节搅乱了哈里，也岔开了他心里自然升起的疑心：爱德华出逃的事败露后，他见赫斯特同凯瑟琳那样连在一处，原是起过疑的。他略带惊慌地望着她，又疑又急。可她情绪的唯一迹象，只是那只手在铁门上越攒越紧。

“你自会知道，”他说，“这件事说不说才好。若会更伤她，就先按下，等难关过去。”

“更伤她——？我不认为还有什么——能更伤她。”

“你也快熬到头了。”他说，话音里带着温柔的怜恤。“我不能对你说爱惜自己，赫斯特。你是唯一一个她受之无愧最少的人。她该觉出这一层：欠她一切的那个人走了；从没欠过她什么的你，却站在她身边。”

===Original===

Hester could not bear it any longer. She waved her hand to him and went in﻿—into the house that was not hers, where there was no one who had a thought to bestow upon her. Where was there anyone? Her mother loved her with all her heart, but had nothing to say to her in this rending asunder of her being. She thought she was glad that it was all happening in a house which was not her home, which after, as Harry said, the crisis was past, she might never need to enter again. She went upstairs, to the unfamiliar room in which she had spent the previous night. There she sat down in the dark on the bed, and looked at it all, passing before her eyes, like a panorama. For this was the only description that could be given. The conversation just recorded occurred over again, as if it had been in a book. “With a lady!” “They left this afternoon.” “Reason to suppose that in the meantime﻿—” And then this talk, suspended in the air as it seemed, came to a pause. And Hester, through the interval, saw all her own long stormy wooing, its sudden climax with so much that was taken for granted﻿—“My only love!﻿—and I am your only love.” That was all true. Those agitated scenes, the dances that were nothing but a love duel from beginning to end, the snatches of talk in the midst of the music and tumult, the one strange blessed moment in the verandah at home, the meeting so tragical and terrible of last night. That was a sort of interlude that faded again, giving place to Harry’s steady subdued voice﻿—

“Married her in the meantime! Married her!”

Hester said these words aloud, with a laugh of incredulous dismay and mockery. The sound terrified herself when she heard it. It was Catherine’s laugh made terrible with a sort of tragic wonder. Married her! Had there been no place for Hester at all, nothing but delusion from beginning to end?

赫斯特再也受不住了。她朝他摆了摆手，进屋去了——走进那座不是她的宅子；那里没有一个人，肯为她分出一念。哪里又有呢？母亲全心全意地爱她，可在她这个人被生生撕裂的当口，却对她无一言可施。她想，她倒庆幸这一切都发生在一座不是她家的宅子里——难关过去之后，正如哈里说的，她也许永远不必再跨进这门槛。她上了楼，回到那间陌生的屋子——昨夜过的那一间。她在黑暗里坐到床上，看着这一切从眼前过，像一幅全景画。因为除此再没有别的形容。方才记下的那场对话又演了一遍，仿佛书里的一般。“同一位女士！”“今天下午走了。”“有理由认为在此期间——”随后这场悬在半空的谈话，停住了。在这间歇里，赫斯特看见了她自己那场漫长多风浪的求爱，看见它骤然登顶，带着那么多想当然——“我唯一的爱！——我也是你唯一的爱。”那全是真的。那些激动的场面，那些从头到尾不过是一场爱情决斗的舞，音乐与喧闹中间的片言只语，家中游廊上那个奇异的、蒙福的时刻，还有昨夜那场悲惨可怕的相会。那像一段幕间戏，又淡去了，让位给哈里那平稳压低的声音——

“在此期间娶了她！娶了她！”

赫斯特把这几个字说了出声，带着一阵不敢信的惶乱与讥诮的笑。那声音把她自己都吓着了。那是凯瑟琳的笑，加上一种悲剧的惊奇，变得可怕。娶了她！赫斯特原来连一个位置都没有么？从头到尾，不过一场幻境么？

## XLIV / 四十四
===Original===

The Settlement

The records of the next few days were agitated and full of excitement. Day after day Catherine spent at the bank, immersed in calculations and consultations with everyone who could throw the slightest light upon the matter. Everything oozed out by degrees, and it was said now that Edward was being hunted down by detectives, now that he had escaped altogether, now that his defalcations were so tremendous that nothing but absolute ruin was possible for Vernon’s, now that there was enough left to make a fight upon if only the creditors would be merciful, and give time, and have patience. The usual panic with which such news is received was somehow tempered in this case. It was thought in the district that Catherine Vernon was enormously rich, and independent of the bank, and when it was known that she had not abandoned it, but in her old age had come back, and was in the office every day, struggling to retrieve affairs, there was nobody short of the financial authorities of the place who did not believe that all was safe. Catherine Vernon would not see any harm come to the bank; Catherine Vernon would see everybody paid. This popular faith held up with a certainty of obstinate prepossession which was worth so much solid capital to the tottering house. Catherine herself placed everything she had in the world in the common stock. She it was who took the lead in all the discussions. She rejected the provisions for her own comfort which everybody concerned was anxious to make. The prevailing feeling among all who had any power was at first that the reestablishment of the whole concern was hopeless, but that enough might be saved out of the wreck to enable Catherine to end her days in peace. To this she opposed a determined negative. She would have no arrangement made on her behalf. “Do you think I want,” she cried, “to end my days in peace? I am ready to die fighting, on the contrary, rather than sacrifice the place my father lived and died in and his father before him. Don’t speak of peace to me.” It was when they perceived that she was immovable in this point and was determined to denude herself of everything, that the old contemporaries who had stood by her before in her gallant struggle, and had been her competitors, and had lived to see themselves distanced by Catherine, had felt it impossible to persevere in their refusal to help.

===Chinese===

了局

此后几天的记载满是激荡与兴奋。凯瑟琳日复一日守在银行里，埋在账目同商议中，凡能对这事照进一线光的人，她个个请教。一切都渐渐渗了出来：一时说爱德华正被包打听追缉，一时说他已全身脱逃；一时说他的亏空大得弗农银行除彻底倒闭别无出路，一时又说只要债主们肯发慈悲、肯宽限、肯忍耐，还剩得下足够的一副本钱可以一搏。这类消息照例激起的那场恐慌，这一回不知怎的被冲淡了。地方上都以为凯瑟琳·弗农家财巨万、不靠银行过活；待听说她非但不撒手，反在暮年重返、天天坐镇行里苦撑危局，除了本地金融界的权威们，谁不信一切稳如泰山。凯瑟琳·弗农断不容银行吃亏；凯瑟琳·弗农定叫人人得偿。这份民间的信心，以一股顽强的成见撑持着，于那座摇摇欲坠的老号，抵得上一大笔实打实的资本。凯瑟琳本人把她世上的一切都投进了公账。一切商议都是她领头。人人急着给她安排的那份养尊处优，她一概回绝。起初，凡有权说话的人多半觉得整号重振无望，但残骸里或可捞出一副，够凯瑟琳安然终老。对此她断然说不。凡为她个人打算的安排，她一概不受。“你们以为我想，”她喊道，“安然终老么？我宁可战死，也不肯牺牲我父亲生生死死于斯、他父亲又在他之前生生死死于斯的这个地方。别对我谈什么安然。”及至众人见她在这点上不可动摇、见她决意把自身剥个净尽，那些当年在她那场光荣奋战中同她并肩、做过她对手、又活着眼看自己被凯瑟琳甩在身后的老辈们，便再硬不下心肠拒绝相助了。

She would have no charity, she declared with a flushed cheek. Help for Vernon’s, yes, to set them on their feet again, with a certainty that nobody should lose a penny in the long run﻿—for that she would thank them with a full heart; but help for herself, to keep her in a show of comfort when the reality was gone, no! “not a farthing,” she said. “I am not afraid of the workhouse,” said Catherine, with proud calm, “and I have a right to a Vernon almshouse, the first that is vacant. The old men who had known Catherine Vernon all her life could not withstand this. “We must manage it for her, we must do it somehow,” they said. “Vernon’s is an old name among us. There is no name in all the district that the people have such confidence in. We must try, sir, we must try,” they began to say to each other, “to help her through.” The young men, many of them, were impatient, and would have refused to consider the question at all. What had an old woman to do with business? She ought to be thankful if she was allowed a maintenance, and to terminate her days in comfort. But on this point there was not another word to be said. The Grange and everything in it was to be sold, the White House and the old furniture, part of which Mrs. John still remembered so fondly. There was no question as to that. “We are prepared to sacrifice everything,” Catherine said. “What we desire is not to keep up any false pretence, but to carry on our business and recover ourselves by your help. Dismiss me from your mind. I will take my chance; but think of Vernon’s, which is not hopeless, which has life in it yet.” Old Mr. Rule on his side had pages upon pages of statements to put before the gentlemen. The week was one of terrible suspense and misery, but at the end, though with conditions that were very hard upon the pride of the family, it was decided at last in favour of the bank. Certain great capitalists came forward to prop it up, “new blood” was put into it in the shape of an enterprising manager, who was to guide Harry’s steps. There were bitternesses, as there is in every cup that is administered by strangers. But Catherine had gained her object, and she made no complaint. Vernon’s would continue, and Harry might have it in his power still to retrieve the family fortunes. As for all the rest, what did it matter? She was a woman who was, or thought herself, very independent of material conditions. Whether she lived in the Grange or one of the Vernon almshouses, what did it matter to her? She did not care for fine eating or fine clothing. “Besides, my clothes will last out my time,” she said with a smile. The week’s struggle had been good for her. She had not forgotten the great and enduring grief which lay behind all this. But she had not had time to think of it. She had put it away out of her mind as a strong nature can, till her work was done.

===Chinese===

一辈子认得凯瑟琳·弗农的老人们抗不住这个。“咱们得替她张罗，咱们总得办成。”他们说。“弗农是咱们中间的老名字。全区上下，再没有第二个名字这样得人心。咱们得试试，先生，得试试，”他们彼此说，“扶她过这一关。”年轻人里头不少人不耐烦，本想根本不议这题目。一个老太婆同生意有什么相干？许她一份赡养、容她舒服地了却残年，她该谢天谢地了。可这一点上再没有二话。格兰奇宅连同宅中一切都要卖掉，白宅连同那些旧家具——其中一部分约翰太太至今还满怀眷恋地记得。这没有商量。“我们准备牺牲一切。”凯瑟琳说。“我们要的不是撑什么假场面，而是靠诸位相助，把生意做下去、把元气恢复过来。把我从你们心里划掉。我碰我的运气；你们想弗农银行——它没有绝望，它里头还有活气。”老鲁尔先生那一头，也备下了一页又一页的陈情，摆到诸位先生面前。那个礼拜是在可怕的悬念同悲惨里熬过的；可到末了，尽管条件于这家门的骄傲极其苛刻，事情终于裁断在银行一边。几位大资本家出面扶住它，又注入“新血”——一位有闯劲的经理，来引哈里的路。苦味自然有，凡陌生人递来的杯子里都有。可凯瑟琳达到了她的目的，她毫无怨言。弗农银行存续下去；哈里兴许还有力量挽回家门的财运。至于其余一切，算得了什么？她是个自认——也自以为——丝毫不倚赖物质条件的人。她住格兰奇宅还是住弗农济贫院的一间，于她有什么分别？她不爱美食，不爱华服。“再说我这些衣裳，够我穿到头了。”她含笑说。这一礼拜的苦战于她反倒有益。横在这一切后面的那场巨大而长存的哀痛，她没有忘；可她没有工夫去想。她把它从心里挪开——坚强的天性做得到——直到活儿干完。

It was waiting for her to overwhelm her: but in the meantime she was strong.

Roland Ashton hurried down as soon as the terrible news reached him. He was eager to tell her his own connection with it, to prove to her that it was not he who had led Edward into speculation, that he had done his utmost to restrain him, and had even in his anxiety been willing to embark in what he felt to be a hazardous course in order to save Edward from the rashness he feared. He came down with all his details ready and a burning anxiety to set himself right. But when he reached the scene of all their troubles, Roland never said a word to Catherine on the subject. Such details were beyond the case. She had never willingly spoken of Edward; when it was possible she ignored him altogether; the investigations which had been set on foot, and which had revealed the greater part of his secrets, she had been compelled to know of, but had spoken to no one about them. Since the first day his name had scarcely passed her lips. Harry only had been allowed to tell her that he had baffled all the attempts made to find him, and had escaped. The search after him had been indeed made rather to satisfy anxiety than with any design of punishment, for the other partners in the bank were responsible for everything, and it was on their shoulders that the burden had to fall. He disappeared as if he had fallen into the sea or been lost in a railway accident. The most wonderful complication of all, the companionship in which he had left England, was not told to her then. It threw to all the others a horrible mockery upon the whole story. There was a bitter sort of smile upon Roland’s face when he sat with the old people, and told them all the investigations he had made, the incredulous indignation with which he had received the first idea that Emma’s disappearance could be connected with that of Edward, the growing certainty that it was so, and finally the receipt of her letter which he brought them to read. The old people were very sad for their beloved Catherine and little inclined to laugh, but the old captain indulged in a tremulous roar which was half a groan, and the old lady, who allowed that her sense of humour was small, gave a grieved smile when it was read to her. This is what Emma said:﻿—

它等着她，等她一交差就压上来；可眼下她是强的。

罗兰·阿什顿一得到那个可怕的消息，便急急赶了回来。他急于向她剖白自己同这事的关系，向她证明：不是他把爱德华引上投机的路，他竭力拦过他，甚至出于焦虑，为救爱德华出他不惧的那份莽撞，甘愿自己上一条他明知凶险的船。他带着备好的一应细节、带着一股洗清自己的灼灼急切下了乡。可他一到这片是非场，对凯瑟琳竟一个字没提。这样的细节，于本案已不相干。她从不肯主动提爱德华；能不提，她就当他不存在；那些查出来、揭出他大半秘密的调查，她是被迫知情的，可对谁也没谈论过。自第一天起，他的名字几乎没出过她的口。只允许哈里告诉她一句：追捕他的种种尝试全被他躲过了，人已脱逃。那场追寻，其实为安人心多、为惩办少：银行其余的合伙人对一切负全责，担子要落到他们肩上。他消失了，仿佛掉进了海里，或失事在火车里。最离奇的一层——他离开英国时携的伴侣——那时还没有告诉她。这一层给全案投上一层可怕的嘲弄。罗兰坐在两位老人跟前时，脸上带着一丝苦笑，把他的种种查访讲给他们听：起初听到埃玛的失踪可能同爱德华的有牵连，他怎样不信、怎样愤慨；疑心怎样渐渐坐实；末了收到她的信，随身带来念给他们听。老两口为他们心爱的凯瑟琳难过，笑不出；可老上校放出一阵发颤的大笑、半是呻吟；老太太自认幽默感薄弱，听人念完，哀哀地笑了一笑。埃玛信上是这么说的：

“Dear Roland﻿—I think it my duty to let you know, as it was, so to speak, in your house I was living at the time, how it is that I had to make up my mind at a very short notice, and couldn’t even go through the form of referring Edward to you. I met him in the train, as you will probably have heard. I was rather sorry about leaving Redborough, and so was he too till he saw me beside him. And then it turned out that he had been very much struck with me at Ellen Merridew’s parties, and would have spoken then but for some entanglements that were of old standing, and that he could not shake off. I need not mention any names, but if I say it was someone that was quite out of the question, someone that was detested at the Grange, you will know. He told me he was leaving England forever, and would I come with him? You know I have always thought it my first duty to get settled, being the youngest and without any fixed home. So after thinking it over for an hour or two, and him being so anxious to come to the point, which is generally just where gentlemen are so slow, I thought it best to consent. We were married before a registrar, but he says that is just as legal as in church. It was at the registrar’s in Holywood Street, Trentham Square. We are going to travel, and may be moving about for a good while; but when we settle I shall let you know. I am glad to tell you that we shall be quite well off, and have everything very handsome; and Edward never grudges me anything I fancy. Give my love to them all, and let them know I am as happy as possible, and that I am Mrs. Edward Vernon now, which is one of the prettiest names I know.

Your affectionate sister,

“**Emma**.”
